Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 1: Cohesity 7.4.1
Cohesity is at the forefront of AI-powered data security and management, revolutionizing how organizations protect, manage, and derive value from their data across the data center, edge, and cloud. With a robust ecosystem of partners, Cohesity offers comprehensive solutions that defend against cybersecurity threats through immutable backups, AI-based threat detection, and rapid recovery at scale. Cohesity's innovative approach ensures data security and efficient management, whether delivered as a service, self-managed, or through a Cohesity-powered partner. Dive into our documentation to explore the full breadth of our transformative solutions.
Note: Features and functionalities herein may become subject to a separate license requirement/fee (even if free during an initial period).
Getting Started
If you are ready to: l Set up the Cohesity cluster for the first time, see Hardware Universe l Create users, see Users and Groups l Protect objects, see Protection Overview l View new features, see What's New? l The list of "Fixed Issues" for all the releases are available exclusively in the Fixed Issues Online Help topic under the Release Notes. This information is not included in the offline downloadable PDF version of the Help.
Explore Our Videos
You can learn about Cohesity products and solutions by watching videos on the Cohesity How-to Videos page.

Supported Platforms for Heterogeneous Cohesity cluster
Cohesity supports heterogeneous Cohesity cluster that spans nodes of different Cohesity hardware platforms and Cohesity-qualified partner hardware platforms. Within a heterogeneous Cohesity cluster, you can have a combination of:
l Multiple Cohesity hardware platforms. l Cohesity hardware platforms and hardware platforms from any one partner. l Hardware platforms from a partner. You can create a new Cohesity cluster with heterogeneous nodes or add heterogeneous nodes to an existing Cohesity cluster and combine all the nodes' storage capacities and performance in a Cohesity cluster.
Hardware Compatibility Within a Cohesity cluster
Important: Cohesity recommends using the Sizer tool for guidance on mixing nodes within a cluster.
The heterogeneous Cohesity cluster support has evolved since Cohesity version 6.1. From 6.1 release, more platforms can be combined to form a heterogeneous Cohesity cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 2: Supportability

Supported Platforms for Heterogeneous Cohesity cluster

Note: l Creating a new heterogeneous cluster, or expanding an existing cluster to make it Heterogeneous must only be done after consulting your Cohesity accounts team.
l Creating incorrect combinations of heterogeneous clusters without prior consultation with your Cohesity accounts team risks undesirable consequences. Reverting this can be complicated and time-consuming.
l Use the Cohesity Sizer tool for checking the heterogenous cluster options for both Cohesity C-Series and OEM Hardware platforms.
Before you create a heterogeneous Cohesity cluster, review and follow the guidelines below:
l Cohesity does not recommend mixing All-Flash (nodes with SSDs) and hybrid nodes (nodes with HDDs) in the same Cluster.
l Hardware platforms from only one partner can be combined with Cohesity hardware platforms to form a heterogeneous Cohesity cluster. For example, you cannot form a heterogeneous Cohesity cluster with Cohesity hardware, Cisco, and HPE hardware platforms.
l Performance sizing should be done at 104% of the performance-gated nodes suggested by the sizer, using the highest-performance node.
l Mixing Hybrid Platforms l Equivalent Node Type - Two hybrid node types are considered equivalent if: l Their CPU/SSD ratio is within 10% of each other. l They have the same number of hard disks (HDDs). l The total HDD capacity of the nodes should be within 25% of each other. l Mixing Equivalent Nodes - In a heterogeneous cluster, if two platforms are equivalent, the combined number of total nodes in the cluster should be greater than or equal to the recommended number of nodes per the EC configuration. l Mixing Non-Equivalent Nodes - In a heterogeneous cluster, if two platforms are non-equivalent, then the minimum number of nodes for each equivalence-node type must be as per the EC configuration recommendation. For more details on the recommended number of nodes, see the Disk and Node Resiliency in Cohesity Fault Tolerance--Data Integrity for Modern Web-scale Environments.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 2: Supportability

Agent Compatibility Within a Cohesity cluster
This page details the Linux and Windows agent compatibility within a Cohesity cluster. You must install the Cohesity Agent on Physical servers, SQL servers, Exchange servers, and other Hypervisor environments you want to protect. The Cohesity versions and Cohesity Agent versions specified in the following matrix include their respective minor release versions. For example, Cohesity 6.8.1 version support is also applicable for 6.8.1_u1, 6.8.1_u2, and 6.8.1_ux versions, where x denotes the minor/update release version number. Similarly, Cohesity Agent 6.8.1 version support is also applicable for 6.8.1_u1, 6.8.1_u2, and 6.8.1_ux versions.

Replication Compatibility

Note: l The table above reflects replication compatibility only. It does not indicate restore compatibility between versions.
l If the source cluster adds support for a new workload or a new category within an existing workload and attempts replication, the target cluster must also support that workload or category. If the target cluster is running an older version that does not recognize this capability, replication of such backups fails.
Restore Limitations in Cross-Version Replication Scenarios
Replication between Cohesity clusters running different software versions is supported, as shown in the compatibility matrix. However, restore operations can fail when a restore is initiated on a cluster running an older software version using backups replicated from a newer-version cluster. Restore failures occur because newer Cohesity releases can capture additional metadata for protected sources. Although this metadata replicates successfully to older clusters, the older software may not be able to interpret it during restore operations. This behavior varies by workload type, adapter, and Cohesity release. Once the target cluster is upgraded to the same or a newer software version than the cluster that created the backup, the replicated backups become fully usable for restore operations. To ensure reliable recovery, Cohesity recommends performing restore operations on a cluster running the same or a newer software version than the version that created the backup. If restore operations must be performed while the cluster is running an older software version, Cohesity Support must review the scenario on a case-by-case basis. For guidance specific to your environment, contact Cohesity Support.
Replication 1.0 and 2.0
Replication 1.0 and 2.0 are replication algorithms used by Cohesity to compare and transmit data between the source cluster and the target cluster.
l Replication 1.0 computes the changed files and directories by scanning the entire volume and then transmits the changed metadata to the target cluster.
l Replication 2.0 leverages SnapTree to efficiently determine the changed entries and transmits the changes to the target cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 2: Supportability

Supportability for Qualifications

Note: l Replication 2.0 was introduced in Cohesity version 6.3 and has been the
default replication protocol since then. It is also used for S3 view replication, a capability added in versions 6.5.x and 6.6 for object-store views. l By default, when you upgrade a cluster from a version earlier than 6.3 to version 6.3 or later, a Protection Group begins using Replication 2.0 only after two replication runs complete on the upgraded version. If you want to start using Replication 2.0 immediately after upgrading from a pre-6.3 version, cancel any pending or in-progress replication jobs for backups taken before the upgrade. This ensures that Replication 2.0 is applied immediately, without waiting for two post-upgrade cycles.

Cohesity Cluster Architecture
This section describes the components that make up a Cohesity cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Cluster Architecture

Nodes
A Cohesity node contains CPU with spinning disk or flash storage that is preinstalled with the Cohesity software. A Cohesity cluster can be hosted on:
l Datacenters: Running on x86-based server consisting of three or more physical nodes.
l Edge: A single node ROBO running on x86-based physical servers or a Virtual Edition cluster running on hypervisor with a single node or multiple nodes, depending on the hypervisor.
l Public Cloud: Cohesity Cloud Edition Cohesity cluster deployed on public clouds like Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud Platform.
A node can be in one of the following states:
l Available on the Network but not assigned to the cluster l Assigned to the cluster
Storage Domains
A Storage Domain, formerly known as a View Box, is a named storage location on a cluster. At the storage domain level, settings like fault tolerance, encryption, and storage efficiencies are applied. A Storage Domain contains Views. When you configure a Protection

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Cluster Architecture

Group, you specify a Storage Domain and during a Protection Group Run, the Cohesity cluster stores the Snapshots in that Storage Domain. If Deduplication is on, the Cohesity cluster eliminates duplicate blocks of repeating data stored on the Cohesity cluster, thus reducing the amount of storage space needed to store data. You may want to disable deduplication and here are some possible reasons:
l The speed of backing up on the Storage Domain is more important than conserving the disk space used to store the Snapshots or files. For example the Storage Domain contains a View and you want fast writes to that View (Datastore).
l You are storing backups on the Cohesity cluster that were created by another backup product that already deduplicates the data.
If Inline Deduplication is on, deduplication occurs when the Cohesity cluster writes the data to the Cohesity View. If Inline Deduplication is off, deduplication occurs after the Cohesity cluster writes the data to the Cohesity View.
Views
A Cohesity view provides a storage location with one or more of these protocols namely NFS, SMB, S3 and SWIFT in a storage domain on the Cohesity cluster. The NFS mount path can be mounted onto systems using the NFS protocol. The SMB mount path can be mounted onto systems as an SMB share. You can use the view to store data such as files, backup snapshots, and cloned VMs. Views can only be mounted on any machines specified in the allowlist subnets. A view also acts as a datastore during the VM cloning process and during VM recovery. You can select the SWIFT protocol and a create SWIFT-only view for OpenStack environments. You can create a view for the following three categories:
l File Shares l Backup Target l Object Services
You can select the Read/Write protocol and, optionally, select the Read-only protocol. You can create a Cohesity view only by using a template. The template can be a predefined template or a custom template. For more information, see:
l Create Views Using a Predefined Template l Create Views Using a Custom Template
Note: If you are using Kerberos (AD or MIT), you must create a view using the same storage domain that is mapped to AD/MIT-Kerberos + LDAP.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Cluster Architecture

For more information, see Create Views Using a Predefined Template and Add Subnets to Allowlists.
Views can be used to store data such as files and directories. For example, other backup products can store data on a view that is hosted on the Cohesity cluster. To access a view from your system, you must mount the view.
The table below summarizes the features at the storage domain and view levels, and how they are inherited.

Features Fault tolerance Storage efficiency
Encryption Cloud Tier QoS Policy

Storage Domain

View

Erasure Coding (EC) Replication Factor (RF)

Inherits storage domain fault tolerance settings and cannot be changed for the View.

Deduplication (inline, post-process, or disabled)

OR
Can be overwritten at the View level to be post-process if at the storage domain level is inline, but cannot be disabled.

Enabled or disabled

Inherits storage domain's settings and cannot be changed for the View.

Inherits cluster settings, unless overwritten at the storage domain level.

Inherits storage domain's settings and cannot be changed for the View.

N/A

Set for each View.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Protection Overview

Protection Overview
Cohesity consolidates data protection, management and web-scale storage onto a unified platform. Easy integration with the VMware ecosystem provides a plug-and-play experience for virtualization admins and significantly reduces the complexity of protecting data. With physical workload support as well, Cohesity is an end-to-end data protection solution that enables businesses to instantly see a full index of their environment and choose the objects they want to protect. These objects can then be protected with easy-to-use protection policies that can be customized based on retention period or application group.
Protection is the process of safeguarding your organization's data. Cohesity uses the following terminology for protection components.
l Source: An object in your organization that you want to protect, such as a VM, physical server, Pure Storage volume, MS SQL Server and NAS.
l Agent: The Cohesity software that you install on physical servers and certain VM hypervisors to enable Cohesity to protect them.
l Registration: The process of registering the source with the Cohesity cluster. l Policy: A collection of reusable settings that define how and when sources are
protected, replicated and archived. You select a policy when configuring a Protection Group. l Protection Group: A backup job that runs repeatedly, based on an associated policy, to back up data from a source and store it on the cluster. l Remote Adapter Protection Group: A backup job that runs scripts or executables on a remote Linux machine, typically for sources that are not supported by Cohesity. l External Target: A software environment outside the cluster, such as a cloud or tape management system, which can be used for archiving inactive data for long-term retention on less expensive storage.
For various workloads (sources), Cohesity's incremental-forever strategy relies on change block technology that is either developed by Cohesity or by the vendor Cohesity is integrating with. There are battled-tested technologies and it is highly unlikely that you will ever face data corruption. However, in the case of a mission-critical workload, Cohesity already enables you to mitigate against this in multiple ways with the following existing functionality:
l By performing a backup validation. For example, using Database consistency checker.
l As a part of your regular database restore runs
l As a part of your regular VM or database clones
l You may take a periodic full backup

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Protection Overview

Cohesity recommends a first full and incremental forever approach to backup all workloads (sources) with the exception for Oracle(SBT based backup) and SQL (VDI-based) where Cohesity recommends periodic full backups.
The common high-level steps to protect sources are:
1. Download and install the agent software on the source. This is required only for physical servers and some hypervisors.
2. Register the source with the cluster. 3. Choose a policy provided by Cohesity or create your own. 4. Create a Protection Group to back up the source.
The Backup Manager Service is responsible for handling all the requests from the Cohesity Data Cloud (Self-Managed) and APIs. A multi-node cluster environment with a large amount of data increases the load on the primary instance of the Backup Manager Service which increases the response time of Cohesity Data Cloud (Self-Managed and API calls. For enabling a read-only replica of the Backup Manager Service, see Backup Manager Service Replica.
About Recovering VMs
Cohesity provides the ability to recover Protected Objects (such as VMs) from a Snapshot created earlier by a Protection Group. You can recover VMs from a Cohesity cluster or a currently registered archive. You can recover VMs to their original location or a new location. Follow these procedures to recover VMs from a Cohesity cluster: Recover VMs to the Original LocationRecover VMs to a New LocationYou can also watch the VMware VM Recovery video to learn how to recover a VMware VM to an original or new location..
The Recover task extracts the VM files (such as the VMDK files) stored in Snapshots and creates new instances of the VMs in their original locations or in a new location depending on the options you choose during recovery:
l Recover to the Original Location--Recover the VM files (such as the VMDK files) to their original datastores and create new instances of the VMs in the original Resource Pool available in the original Source.
l Recover to a New Location--Recover the VM files (such as the VMDK files) to an alternate datastore and create new instances of the VMs in an alternate Resource Pool of a registered Source.
l Recover from a Cloud Archive--Recover the VM files from a registered archive (External Target) and place them in a View on the Cohesity cluster.
During recovering VMs, one of the following methods is used to identify the ESXi hosts that have access to the required Datastore:

l If all the hosts have access to the required Datastore then VMware is responsible to select the ESXi hosts based on load balancing.
l If only some of the hosts have access to the required Datastore, a random host from the available list of hosts that have access to the required Datastore is selected.

Recover to the Original Location
While recovering VMs, you can choose to recover the VM files (such as the VMDK files) to their original datastores and create new instances of the VMs in the original Resource Pool of the original Source as described in the figure and procedure below.

numbered time squares: .
The VM Recover task consists of the following actions:
T1) The Cohesity cluster extracts the VM files (such as the VMDK files) stored in Snapshots and places the new VM files in a temporary View. In this example, a new VMDK2 is created from the Snapshot of VM2 made on 03/21/2025 at 02:00 AM.
T2) New instances of the VMs are created in the original Resource Pool by using the new VMDKs from the temporary View. In this example, the new VM2, using VMDK2, is created in the Resource Pool. The View temporarily becomes the datastore for the VMs as represented by the black line between the Resource Pool and View (datastore). The VMs can be used immediately and you do not have to wait until the VMDK files are completely recovered to the original datastore.
T3) The Cohesity cluster migrates the VM files (such as the VMDKs) using Storage vMotion to the original datastore and any changes made to the data on the VM during the recovery process are preserved. The temporary View is deleted when Storage vMotion is completed.
T4) After the VM files are recovered, the VMs use the VM files in the original datastore. In this example, after VMDK2 is fully recovered, VM2 uses VMDK2 located in the original datastore.

About Scale Out

The Cohesity cluster scales out horizontally. To increase the storage capacity and improve performance, you can add additional Nodes to the Cluster as represented by the procedure and figure below. The steps in the following procedure are represented in the figures with
black numbered time squares: .
T1) In this example, all the Nodes in Chassis#1 are assigned to the Cohesity cluster.
T2) Using the Cohesity Dashboard, two Nodes from Chassis#2 are selected to be added to the Cluster.
T3) The Cohesity cluster adds the selected Nodes from Chassis#2 to the Cluster. After new Nodes are added, the disk capacity of the Cluster is immediately increased and available for use by Protection Groups, Clone tasks and Recovery tasks. This addition of more Nodes improves performance because additional CPUs, memory, and disk bandwidth are available to the Cluster. Also, the Cluster distributes the blocks from existing Nodes to the new Nodes. In addition, the Cluster replicates the metadata about the block distribution onto these new Nodes.
The remaining Nodes in Chassis#2 are unassigned. These unassigned Nodes can be added to this Cluster at a later date or used to create another Cluster with the addition of another Node from another Chassis. (A Cluster requires at least three Nodes.)

About Cloud Archival
The Cohesity cloud archive feature enables you to simplify off-site data management by integrating your archive solution with the Cohesity cluster. Archive's benefits include longterm data retention on low-cost storage to meet compliance and retention requirements. Optional incremental archival and source-side deduplication result in lower cloud capacity consumption, faster archive times and lower network bandwidth consumption during archival and retrieval.
Cohesity archive automatically copies an existing Snapshot created by Protection Groups located in a Cohesity cluster and stores it on a registered External Target.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

About Cloud Archival

You specify a protection schedule in a Policy and that protection schedule defines how often a Protection Group using that Policy runs. In the example above, the "Critical_VMs" Protection Group, using a policy with a daily protection schedule, is capturing Snapshots of VM1 and VM2 and storing those Snapshots in the "Dev" Storage Domain. The "Important_ VMs" Protection Group, using a different policy with a monthly protection schedule, is capturing Snapshots of VM3 and storing those Snapshots in the "QA" Storage Domain.
You can optionally specify an archive schedule in a Policy. The archive schedule defines how often Snapshots are copied from a Storage Domain in the Cohesity cluster and saved in an External Target by a Protection Group using that Policy. In the example above, the "Critical_ VMs" Protection Group is making monthly copies of the Snapshots in the "Dev" Storage Domain and storing those Snapshots in the External Target named "EngArchive". The "Important_VMs" Protection Group is making yearly copies of the Snapshots in the "QA" Storage Domain and also storing those Snapshots in the External Target named "EngArchive".
The archive schedule for copying snapshots cannot be more often than the protection schedule for capturing snapshots. For example if snapshots are captured daily, the Cohesity cluster cannot archive them hourly but it can archive them daily or any value less often than daily.
Register an External Target
To specify an archive schedule for a Policy, you must register an External Target in the Cohesity cluster. Registering an External Target makes it eligible to be used by the Cohesity cluster. Data on an External Target resides outside of the Cohesity environment and is separate from the data stored on the local and remote Cohesity clusters. External Targets

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

About Cloud Archival

can be cloud or tape and can be used for archiving or as a Cloud Tier. The Cohesity cluster requires the External Target's login credentials so a handshake can occur. For detailed instructions, see Register an External Target.
External Target Encryption
When registering an External Target so it can receive archive data from your Cohesity cluster, you can choose to turn on encryption. When you turn on encryption, the data is encrypted before it is transferred to the registered Target. Using its own internal key management system, the Cohesity cluster generates a key. This key and data are encrypted and sent to the External Target over a secure channel (SSL).

With this configuration, to accomplish decryption, you do not need to upload keys, nor does the Cohesity cluster integrate with KMS or a similar key management system. When retrieving data from an encrypted External Target, the Cohesity cluster generates a key dynamically (which exists in memory only) that the Cohesity cluster uses to decrypt the key that is stored on the External Target. Only Cohesity knows how to decrypt the data because the key is based on markers within the stored data. Now the Cohesity cluster, and only a Cohesity cluster, can read data from the External Target. Even if an outside entity has access to the External Target, they cannot read the data because they cannot generate a key to decrypt the key stored on the External Target.

You can also restore a Cohesity cluster's archived data from the External Target if you lose access to the Cohesity cluster or data that is on the Cluster. To do this, you must have the lost Cluster's ID and your External Target credentials.
Cohesity recommends you store the cluster ID by registering the cluster at Cohesity Support Portal. Note that performing "clean data" on a Cohesity cluster and then reinstalling changes the Cluster ID. Remember to store this new Cluster ID.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

About Cloud Tier

Additional Security
If you have selected Internal KMS or KMIP Compliant as the Key Management Service (KMS) Type for encryption, then you can enable additional security for the external target. By enabling additional security, you can manage the key manually instead of Cohesity managing the encryption key for data that is transferred out. If you choose to manage the key manually, then after registering the external target with the Cohesity cluster, you must download the key from the external target's details page and store it in a secure location outside of the Cohesity cluster. With additional security, only the Cohesity clusters where you have explicitly provided the encryption key can download data from that external target. However, the source Cohesity cluster (the cluster that archived the data) does not require the encryption key of the external target.
About Cloud Tier
Cohesity Cloud Tier enables an additional storage tier where cold data can be stored. After you register supported existing cloud storage as a Cloud Tier target with the Cohesity cluster, you can enable Cloud Tier to move rarely used and inactive data to the cloud when HDD used capacity exceeds a set threshold (typically 80%). To reduce the storage cost and network utilization, down-tiered data is always compressed in addition to being encrypted regardless of the cluster and Storage Domain settings. For deduplication, however, the down-tiered data in the External Target reflects the same deduplication settings as in the Storage Domain on the cluster. Cloud Tier benefits include utilizing low-cost cloud storage for rarely used and inactive data, allowing you to reclaim Cohesity cluster capacity for often used data. The actual amount of data that can be tiered to Cloud Tier depends on the deduplication ratio of your data. If the deduplication ratio is high, less data can be tiered to the cloud. As a general guideline, however, Cloud Tier roughly doubles your capacity.
The action steps in the following procedure are represented in the figure below with blue
numbered time squares: . The procedure assumes cloud storage is already registered as Cloud Tier and the HDD used capacity is beyond the threshold.
The Cloud Tier process consists of the following actions:
T1) A Cohesity cluster's Storage Domain contains two files, FileA and FileB. Both files contain data blocks that the Cohesity cluster recognizes as cold so it moves the data blocks to the Cloud Tier. Note that files may share data blocks, as indicated by Block#4 in the diagram.
T2) A system accesses FileB data Block#4 and Block#6. The Cohesity cluster recognizes that Block #6 is located on the Cluster and Block#4 is located on the Cloud Tier. The difference in block location is transparent to both the Storage Domain and the system accessing the file. This enables seamless access and simplifies data retrieval.
T3) If, based on additional file access, the Cohesity cluster determines that Block#4 is no longer cold, that data block is moved from the Cloud Tier to the Cohesity cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

About Tape Archival

In the above diagram, white blocks represent data blocks stored on the local Cohesity cluster, and yellow blocks represent data blocks that have been moved to the Cloud Tier external target.

You can also view an overview of Cloud Tier usage in the Storage section of the cluster dashboard once Cloud Tier is enabled.

About Fault Tolerance
Cohesity's highly resilient and fault-tolerant platform ensures organizations can continue conducting business during the following events:
l Hardware or software failure l Maintenance and upgrades with non-disruptive rolling software upgrades
This topic describes how the Cohesity cluster is highly resilient and fault tolerant. Cohesity provides fault tolerance at the following levels:
l Cluster: The failure domain settings at the cluster level protect the cluster against node, chassis or rack failures. You can specify how many node, chassis, or rack failures the cluster can tolerate while continuing to run and maintain strict consistency. For example, a cluster can survive during a catastrophic hardware (motherboard) failure on a node, a chassis backplane failure, or a power outage on a rack.
l Storage Domain: You can configure fault tolerance to survive disk, node, chassis or rack failures at a storage domain level (granular) than at the cluster level (global). A storage domain configured to survive three-disk failures will not lose data even if there are simultaneous three disk failures. In addition, erasure coding (EC) and redundancy factor (RF) levels allow for a further file data resiliency at the stripe level.
l Metadata: The Distributed Metadata Store is a fast key-value store containing all the metadata in the Cohesity cluster. It is a fault-tolerant store that Cohesity uses for keeping track of all the data and other stats in the system. Metadata is stored on SSD for performance reasons. How metadata is replicated depends on the configured resiliency:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

About Fault Tolerance

l 1 Failure: Tolerates either a single node or a single SSD failure. l 2 Failures: Tolerates either two nodes or two SSD failures. For more details on Fault Tolerance and Best Practices, see Cohesity Fault Tolerance-- Data Integrity for Modern Web-scale Environments.
Plan and configure fault tolerance based on your requirements. Use the alerts and advanced diagnostics features to monitor and protect your cluster against failures.

Data Redundancy
The Cohesity cluster provides data redundancy to protect against disk, node, chassis, or rack failures. When files are stored on the Cluster, the Cluster breaks up the data into blocks that are distributed across the Cluster with a replication factor of two. This means that the Cluster stores two copies of each block on different disks and different Nodes. In the example below, one copy of Block#1 is stored on Disk#1 of Node#1 and the second copy is stored on Disk#7 of Node#3.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

About Fault Tolerance

If a block is unavailable because a disk or a Node is unavailable and enough disk space exists on the remaining Nodes, the Cluster creates a new block on a different Node and a different disk from the existing copy of the block --always maintaining the replication factor of two. The Cluster makes itself fault tolerant again and no data is lost during this block restoration process.
Note: The Cohesity rebalancing algorithm always creates a new copy of a block on a different disk and a different Node. Therefore, if a disk or Node becomes unavailable, another copy of the block exists on a different disk and Node or disk.
Disk Resilience
If a disk becomes unavailable, the blocks in that disk are unavailable to the Cluster. The Cluster detects that these blocks are under-replicated and replicates them from existing copies of the blocks in the Cluster as shown in the figures and procedure below. The steps in the following procedure are represented in the figures with orange numbered time squares:
. The data restoration process is described in the following example steps:
T1) When the Cohesity cluster determines that Disk#10 has errors, the Cohesity cluster generates a DiskNotHealthy Alert informing the Administrator of the problem. The

administrator triggers the disk replacement process by marking the disk offline and removing the disk.
T2) The Cohesity cluster periodically scans the blocks and determines that some blocks are under-replicated and replicates them. In this example, the Cohesity cluster determines that there is a single instance of Blocks#5 and Block#6 (because Disk#10 is unavailable) and so it finds the copies of these blocks and replicates them on other Nodes.
T3) An administrator replaces Disk#10 with a new Drive.
T4) The Cohesity cluster assimilates the new disk into the Cluster to restore the disk space capacity. The Cluster also distributes blocks to the new disk to improve performance.
No data is lost during this data restoration process.

Node Resilience

Node Failure or Node Down on a Three-Node Cohesity cluster A three-node Cohesity cluster can sustain a node failure or node down and continues to satisfy the I/O read and write requests. The Cohesity cluster has the ability to automatically switch to an appropriate redundancy during a node failure or node down, and switch back when the cluster is restored back to the original state. For example, if EC2:1 is configured with a fault tolerance setting of 1D:1N, the cluster switches to RF2 to maintain similar levels of data redundancy. Once the node is replaced, the cluster switches back to EC2:1. A node failure or node down on a three-node Cohesity cluster will cause I/Os to fail under the following scenarios:
l The cluster is in the process of healing from a previous disk/node failure If the data is not fully healed, turning off another node will result in data unavailability.
l A node on the cluster is reaching its full capacity - Turning off the node will result in the cluster triggering the healing and filling up space on the other two nodes.
Note: During the above scenarios, the Cohesity cluster can tolerate a quick reboot.
For more details about node resiliency settings, see Disk and Node Resilience Settings.
Chassis Resilience
A chassis is a collection of one or more Cohesity nodes in a single form-factor. A chassis can contain up to four nodes. Cohesity provides protection levels for chassis resiliency that can be set separately for each storage domain. The allowed values depend on the fault tolerance settings. You can select the minimum failures to tolerate and the system adjusts the available options for RF and EC accordingly. For more details about chassis resiliency settings, see Chassis Resilience Settings.
Rack Resilience
A rack is typically a single tower of Cohesity-qualified appliances connected to a top-level switch. A single rack can include one or more chassis. It can also contain client or server machines from other vendors. Cohesity provides protection levels for rack resiliency that can be set separately for each storage domain. The allowed values depend on the fault tolerance settings. You can select the minimum failures to tolerate and the system adjusts the available options for RF and EC accordingly. For more details about rack resiliency settings, see Rack Resilience Settings.

About Fault Tolerance

Usable Storage
The following figure shows the formatted usable capacity based on various EC and RF settings. For example, an EC X:2 scheme provides a lower usable capacity than an EC X:1 scheme but a higher resilience by allowing for two stripe unit failures.

Node VIP Fail-over
The Cohesity cluster maintains a pool of Virtual IP addresses that it assigns to the Nodes as needed. If a Node goes down, the Cluster fails over the VIP to a different Node. Network traffic continues to be routed to the same VIP address but processing occurs on the new Node now associated with the VIP. Therefore, any Protection Groups or Recovery tasks running on the original Node continue to run on the new Node without interruption.
Network Redundancy
Each Node in a Cohesity cluster contains two 10 Gigabit Network Interface Controller (NIC) Cards with either SFP+ or RJ45 ports. If both NIC Cards are cabled into switches and one of the NIC Cards fails, the Node can continue to send and receive network requests using the other NIC card because the two NIC Cards are network bonded. Cohesity recommends cabling the two ports of a Node to different switches, so that if one switch goes down, the network traffic can reach the Node on the other switch.
Memory Redundancy
A dual in-line memory module (DIMM) failure either partial or full is considered a hardware component failure. In such cases, the node cannot function and therefore the failed DIMM must be replaced with a new DIMM for the node to resume memory operations.
CPU Redundancy
Each Node in a Cohesity cluster contains two CPU units housed in two CPU sockets. If one CPU unit fails, the Node can continue to process using the second CPU unit. The CPU units can be easily replaced because they are housed in CPU sockets.
Software and Hardware Failures on Cohesity cluster
The following table describes common software or hardware component failures and their Cohesity remedies. During any of these failures, all operations of the cluster, such as backups and recovery, file IO, replication, and archival are unaffected. For most, the self-

healer automatically heals the failure and brings the Cohesity cluster back to a normal state. The scenarios are listed in the increasing order of ease of resolution.

Failure Rack Failure
Chassis Failure
Node Failure
HDD Failure
SSD Failure

Remedy
Cohesity can sustain up to two simultaneous rack failures. A minimum of three racks in your cluster is required to tolerate one rack failure. File data is reconstructed from the surviving rack that have units from the same stripes as the failed rack. This reconstructed data is placed in racks that have available (spare) capacity.
Cohesity can sustain up to two simultaneous chassis failures. A minimum of three chassis in your cluster is required to tolerate one chassis failure. File data is reconstructed from the surviving chassis that have units from the same stripes as the failed chassis. This reconstructed data is placed in chassis that have available (spare) capacity.
Cohesity cluster can sustain up to two simultaneous node failures. A minimum of three nodes in your cluster is required to tolerate one node failure. Some aspects for a node or a disk failure are:
l Node failure results in both file data and metadata failures. l File data is recovered from the erasure coding or replication scheme. Metadata is recovered from
one of the replicas.
Cohesity cluster can sustain up to three simultaneous HDD failures at any point in time. HDDs are used to store the Distributed File Data. The number of HDD failures that can be tolerated depends on the RF or EC settings. Chunk files are units of replication. Cohesity cluster ensures that there is always a chunk file replica on other nodes, and internal chunk files representing the same user object (or user file) are spread across multiple disks.
Cohesity cluster can sustain up to two simultaneous SSD failures. SSDs are used to store the Distributed Metadata and the Distributed Journal, and are replicated on either 2 or 3 nodes. Parts of the Distributed Metadata and Journal are stored on every node of the Cohesity cluster. An SSD failure can be considered the same as a node failure.

About Fault Tolerance

Failure Network Failure
Boot Device Failure Power Supply Fans

Remedy
Each node gets its own Node IP address, a VIP address, and a hardware management IPMI address. The DNS is set up to do round-robin, which gives each VIP a turn to satisfy client read or write requests and equally distributes them across all the nodes. VIP Failover: Cohesity cluster has a heartbeat mechanism that detects a node failure. If the directly connected network link goes down, the VIP of the failed node gets reassigned to another node, and node re-balancing similar to a node failure is initiated. Cohesity cluster nodes are typically configured with 2x10GbE connected to two separate switches. This allows for failure of a single switch or a single network port, while still allowing continuous operation. For more details, see Optimal Network Designs with Cohesity.
Cohesity cluster boot device is isolated to a separate partition on flash. Since the Cohesity File System is already saved within persistent hard drives, there is no impact on a boot device crash. There is no inconsistency or file system repair required.
Cohesity cluster supports having a redundant power supply per chassis so that if one goes down, the other can still power the nodes.
Cohesity support a fan redundancy of N+1 (there is one extra fan per chassis). Hence, they will support one per node and an extra one to cover for failures.

Other Scenarios
The following table covers several other likely scenarios and how Cohesity cluster responds to each of the scenarios.

Event

Response

Node Addition

Cohesity cluster re-balancing is initiated by the self-healer. Every time a new node is added, part of the existing file data and metadata from the remaining nodes is rebalanced to the new node. This is done at a chunk-file level. The larger the cluster size, the faster the re-balancing.
Common scenarios for node addition:
l Cohesity cluster expansion, for example from 4 to 5 nodes. l Failed node replacement, when the Cohesity cluster size remains the same. For example, one
node in a 4-node cluster fails and is replaced.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Secure Software Development Practices

Event

Response

Node Removal

Node removal involves the removal of a node from the Cohesity cluster. When this happens, the Cohesity cluster re-balancing is initiated.
Similar to a node addition, after a node failure or a node removal, the Cohesity cluster is restored. The file data and metadata are rebalanced on the surviving nodes. If the number of nodes falls to 2, there is an alert and the write policy changes from an EC-to an RF-based one, and writes continue. If a replacement node is added, the file data and metadata are re-balanced back to the replacement node.
If a node goes down, other replicas ensure that newer disks are selected to store the data chunks that were lost from that node.
Common scenarios for node removal from a Cohesity cluster are:
l Node removal (graceful) during a hardware refresh. l Node failure. For example, one node in a 4-node cluster fails and needs to be replaced.

Node is Temporarily Down

This occurs when the node is assumed to be non-responsive after a timeout and re-balance has already kicked-in. The self-healer will stop healing (redistributing) when the node comes back. If the healing process is interrupted, some chunks will be over-replicated compared to others, but those chunks will be cleaned up later by the garbage-collection process

Attached Network is Temporarily Down

The node that is not reachable will be considered to be down. The self-healing process kicks in and rebalances the active nodes. When the network to the node is restored, the extra data and metadata replicas are cleaned up by the garbage collector.

Node Failure and Insufficient Space

If there is a node failure and the remaining nodes do not have sufficient available space to support the file data and metadata from the failed node, the self-healer will not perform re-balancing. In such cases, an alert is raised until a new node is added.

Non-Disruptive and Rolling Upgrades

Cohesity cluster architecture allows for a sequential node-by-node upgrade. Nodes can be upgraded to the latest versions without any interruption to client IOs. Any active IO access through the VIP (Virtual IP address) is transferred as the VIP is seamlessly transferred to another node.

Fault Tolerance with Cohesity for the Edge

Cohesity for the Edge is the virtual platform running as a VM on either VMware vSphere or Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisors using commodity hardware. An environment such as ESX or VMware vSAN with shared infrastructure can provide VM/storage migration capabilities on the underlying host failures.

Cohesity reviews security at each phase of the software development life cycle. Vulnerability scanners are run to assess the state of the operating system, networking layer and services running on the Cohesity cluster. The scan results give the current open ports

Secure Product Development Lifecycle
Cohesity follows a Secure Product Development Lifecycle to deliver secure products with the security vulnerabilities contained throughout the product's lifecycle. Cohesity follows the following six practices for the Secure Product Development Lifecycle (SPDL).

Security Training
Cohesity mandates secure coding training for all the developers to follow security best practices in product development. Teams in Cohesity such as developers, product managers, development managers, release management, and QA are provided with adequate training, awareness, and resources to influence product security during the product development lifecycle successfully.
Security in Design
In the design phase of product development, security is fundamental to develop highly secure systems and applications. To ensure the products' security posture and compliance or certification requirements are maintained with new features, design documents and design reviews are used to align the product design with the current security best practices. Cohesity follows security principles such as secure by default, fail securely, secure crypto algorithms, and so on.
Threat Model
The threat model is an engineering technique used to identify threats, attacks, vulnerabilities, and countermeasures that could affect an application or system. The threat model assists in design practice to meet security objectives in design and reduce risk. The threat model also helps in effective vulnerability management. Cohesity regularly updates the published product threat model based on new features and changes in threats.

Secure Software Development Practices

Vulnerability Management
Cohesity adapts some of the best vulnerability management guidances from ISO 27001:2013 Control A.12.6.1 and NIST Cybersecurity framework Version 1.1 (Controls RA1, RA-5, IP-12, CM-8, MI-3). For vulnerability management, Cohesity follows the following six practices.
Vulnerability Management Policy
Vulnerability management policy defines the severity classification of vulnerabilities based on the CVSS score and SLA for each severity class. It also defines the metrics for the backporting of security defects.
Penetration Testing
Penetration testing of products is conducted using third-party engagement and internal continuous mode using various automated techniques integrated into the release cycle. The potential vulnerabilities found in penetration testing are addressed as per the vulnerability management policy.
Static Code and Binary Analysis
Static analysis security testing (SAST) is an automated testing technique used to analyze source code to identify security flaws. Cohesity conducts static code and binary analysis using well known commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) tools.
Dynamic Scanning
COTS DAST scanners are integrated into the development pipeline to scan all significant development branches. Any vulnerabilities found are addressed meeting the SLA defined in the vulnerability management policy. Automated regression tests of previous vulnerabilities are run to avoid any security regression issues in future releases.
Third-Party Component Security
All imports of third-party components are tested for security risks. The third-party software inventory is maintained to assist in security risk mitigation and third-party component vulnerability patching. Third-party vulnerability patching follows a vulnerability management policy. Third-party component security also covers OEM firmware like BIOS and BMC software.
Product Infra and Tools Support
Engineering infrastructure tools are always maintained up to date, and security protections are configured. Security checks or options for compiler and linker are always enforced.
Secure Software Release
Cohesity follows a secure software release practice that brings predictability to the security posture of software releases. An acceptable level of security quality metrics is defined, and Cohesity ensures that each release meets the minimum goal.

JIRA workflows are defined to track the complete vulnerability life cycle using JIRA labels and fields and hence provide visibility of the release's security posture at any given time.
Product Incident Response

Secure Acceptance Procedure
Cohesity uses the following procedures to ensure the integrity of its hardware and software products.
Hardware
Cohesity products are built by contract manufacturers (CM). CMs ensure the integrity of the products by:
1. Building to controlled specifications documented in Cohesity's Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) system and their shop floor control systems.
2. Performing tests jointly developed by the CM and Cohesity.
Software
The software image provided to customers is protected by using the SHA256 and MD5 hashing technique.
1. The customer logs on to the Cohesity Support Portal. In the downloads section, a link to a software package is provided, along with the corresponding MD5 checksum and SHA256 for the software package.
2. The customer downloads the software package and compares its checksum with the checksum provided on the Cohesity Support Portal. They might use commands such as:
md5sum <software-package>.tar.gz sha265sum <software-package>.tar.gz
3. If the MD5 checksum or SHA256 values do not match, the integrity of the software package may have been compromised. The customer can try downloading the software package again to resolve the issue. If necessary, they can contact Cohesity Support for further assistance.
Cohesity Security Features
This topic explains how Cohesity builds security into the Cohesity cluster and is intended for:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Security Features

l Administrators responsible for the configuration, maintenance and operation of the Cohesity cluster.
l Security engineers reviewing Cohesity for compliance with their company's security policies.
The Cohesity cluster provides the following security features.
Data Segmentation
The Cohesity cluster architecture provides virtual data isolation through Storage Domains. Each Storage Domain encrypts the data stored in it using its own independent keys. During initial cluster setup, encryption can be enabled for the entire cluster so that the data in all Storage Domains will be encrypted. If encryption is not enabled during cluster creation, it can be enabled at the Storage Domain level. Note that once encryption is set during cluster or Storage Domain creation, it can not be disabled later. Each Cohesity View is assigned a Quality of Service (QoS) Policy. A QoS Policy determines the priority of I/O (when contention occurs).
Data at Rest Security
The Cohesity file system provides full at-rest encryption based on the strong AES-256-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) standard. Only 256-bit keys are used for encryption. The encryption architecture provides high security while maintaining the flexibility to optimally leverage the available hardware and software resources. The built-in software-based encryption is hardware-accelerated through the latest Intel processors that support the AES-NI instruction set. Due to hardware acceleration, the software-based encryption route has minimal impact on performance. Keys can be obtained in three ways:
l Internal Key Manager l External Key Manager l Cloud-based Key Manager
Keys can be rotated periodically. The default rotation is set to 90 days. User data is encrypted before it is stored on any storage media used. The data is decrypted after it is read from the storage media in memory. The storage media can be SSD, HDD, tape, and cloud storage. This includes credentials for data sources protected by Cohesity. Physical agents are designed to respond solely to cluster-issued commands. Thus, they do not have the ability to extract data, such as credentials or other sensitive information, from the cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Security Features

Data in Transit Security
The data being transmitted to a Cohesity cluster or being transmitted from a Cohesity cluster to External Targets is encrypted for security. Examples of data movement are ingesting data from a primary site, replicating between remote offices or transmitting data to public cloud. The agent encryption cipher in use can be viewed in the Pulse logs or the agent report per the UI changes.
Primary Site to a Cohesity cluster
When the Cohesity backup software ingests data from the primary storage, it first establishes a secure connection with the primary storage over HTTPS. Cohesity backup software determines which data blocks have changed from the previous backup run by communicating with the primary storage over the secure connection, and then transfers all the changed blocks over the HTTPS connection. Communication between the Cohesity cluster and Cohesity backup service (agent) is secured using SSL/TLS integrated transport. They perform mutual authentication and all data exchanged is encrypted. The encryption is done using the Advanced Encryption Standard-256 protocol. The cipher suites used for backups through agents are:
1. TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 2. TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA38 3. TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384.
Replication from One Cohesity cluster to Another
A source Cluster starts a replication session by initiating a handshake with the target cluster over an HTTPS connection. Upon receiving the handshake request, the target Cluster obtains a session key from its local Key Management Server and sends it to the source cluster over the HTTPS connection. The source Cluster stores the received session key in its local Key Management Server and completes the handshake. At this point, both the source and the target Clusters have the session key. The source Cluster uses the session key to encrypt the data and transfer it securely for that replication session. The encryption uses Advanced Encryption Standard-256 protocol in Galois/Counter Mode ( AES-256-GCM).
Data in Cloud Security
The cloud can be used:
l As another tier of storage (Cloud Tier) l To store long-term retention copies (CloudArchive)

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Security Features

l Archive data directly to an external target without retaining a copy of the data on the cluster (CloudArchive Direct).
Cohesity supports all the major cloud vendors, including Amazon, Microsoft Azure, Google and Oracle, and any S3-compatible storage.
l You register the cloud storage as an External Target on the cluster and provide the cloud storage access keys. The access keys are encrypted and stored on the Cohesity cluster using AES-256 encryption in Galois/Counter Mode (AES-256-GCM). You can update the access keys from the Cohesity Dashboard or by using the Cohesity REST API. (Cohesity does not rotate the access keys.)
l Though the access keys are specific to the cloud storage provider, the Cohesity's key storage security is the same regardless of the cloud provider. Cohesity is FIPS certified and has an internal software-based key management system (KMS) that stores the key encryption key (KEK).
l Cohesity establishes a connection to the External Target only when making REST API calls to perform an archive or recovery operation.
l Cohesity does not include the External Target access keys in the API request. The request is signed using the External Target's access key and the signature is sent using the Authorization request header.
l Cohesity uses TLS 1.2 to encrypt in-transit data. Currently, Cohesity does not use mTLS (2-way SSL) in communication with External Targets.
CloudArchive and CloudArchive Direct use their own encryption, independent of data-atrest encryption. The cipher suite used for encryption is AES-256-GCM.
l Cloud Archive encryption is on by default but can be turned off. Cohesity recommends keeping it on.
l Both the data encryption key (DEK) and KEK are encrypted, distributed for resiliency across the cluster and stored in SSD.
l The cluster creates a new DEK for each External Target. Cohesity provides two options. You can: l Store the data, metadata and encryption keys (DEK/KEK) in the External Target.
l Store the data, metadata, and DEK only in the External Target. This requires the KEK to be downloaded and stored outside of the cluster. Without the downloaded keys, future CloudRetrieve operations will not be possible.
For Cloud Tier, encryption is always on and cannot be turned off.

Cluster Management Methods
The Cohesity cluster can be managed using the following methods:
l The Cohesity Dashboard web browser interface. l The command line interface (CLI) available for Linux, Windows and iOS systems. l The REST API endpoints on any platform using a REST client.
All access methods listed above require an SSL connection, and the Cohesity cluster prioritizes TLS 1.3. For backward compatibility, TLS 1.2 ciphers are also supported, but administrators can disable TLS 1.2 for enhanced security. The connection uses strong ciphers for the established session. To update the cipher list, see iris_cli cipher update. When the Cohesity cluster is created, a self-signed X.509 certificate (PEM format only) is generated for this purpose. The certificate must have the "Common Name" field set to the server's hostname (for example, a VIP's DNS name). Certificates are stored in the boot disk. They are replicated to other Nodes as part of Cluster formation using RPC calls. When the key expires, the web browser marks the session as invalid. Users can import new certificates to re-establish the session. Users can overwrite this X.509 certificate according to their company policy.
Authentication
Authentication is required for all management methods (the Cohesity Dashboard, CLI and API). Only a user with an account on the Cluster can authenticate to the Cluster. Cohesity supports three types of accounts.
l Local User Account--A user account is created locally on the Cluster. This user can access only this Cluster. When the account is created, a password is assigned to the user and required to authenticate to the Cluster. This password is stored on the Cluster.
l Active Directory--A user account that exists on an Active Directory server. This user can access all the Clusters that have joined the Active Directory. The user uses the Active Directory password to authenticate to the Cluster. The Cluster authenticates the user with Active Directory. The password is not stored on the Cluster.
l Single Sign-On - A Single Sign-on (SSO) user account that uses the supported

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Security Features

Identity Provider (IdP) to authenticate to the Cohesity cluster. Cohesity supports major IdP vendors such as Okta, Duo, Ping, and Azure AD.

Protocols and Authentication
The Cohesity cluster can authenticate users defined locally in the Cluster and users defined in Active Directory. NFS uses allowlist-based access control. SMB uses Active Directory for authentication and authorization. Anonymous access, which doesn't require authentication, is not allowed for SMB.
Kerberos Authentication Protocol
Kerberos can be enabled for stronger authentication for SMB by joining the Cohesity cluster to Active Directory. Cohesity supports only Active Directory-based Kerberos authentication.
Client Side Protocols
Cohesity supports the SMB, NFS and S3 protocols.
SMB Protocol Security
Cohesity supports two types of authorization data on a file: Windows-style access control lists (ACLs) and POSIX mode bits (UNIX permissions). ACLs are used when a file is accessed from SMB. POSIX mode bits are used when a file is accessed via NFS.

Mixed SMB and NFS Environments
Beginning with version 6.0, support for mixed-permission environments is available. The supported scenarios are:
l A UNIX client can store and access a file over NFS. l A Windows client can store and access a file over SMB. l A UNIX client can connect by NFS to a file that was stored on the Cluster by a Windows
client over SMB and access it based on the permissions. l A Windows client can connect by SMB to a file that was stored on the Cluster by a
UNIX client over NFS and access it based on the permissions. l Data can be written at the same time to a file via NFS or SMB.
AWS S3
Cohesity supports: l S3 server over HTTPs. l Authentication with AWS Signature Version 2 and Version 4. l AWS ACLs. l Access controlled via allowed subnets.
Authorization
Authorization is implemented at two levels. l The operation level, where operations are restricted to authorized users only. l The object level, where objects are restricted to authorized users only.
The Cohesity cluster can also be added as an Active Directory domain. Role Based Access Control (RBAC) A role is a collection of operations, such as creating a View or deleting a Protection Group. A role grants authorization to perform one or more operations. Cohesity provides default roles such as Admin, Operator, Viewer, and Data Security. Customers can create custom roles. A user can have multiple roles but must have at least one role to log in to the Cluster. A user can be assigned a set of objects on the Cluster. The user is authorized to access only those objects and perform operations on them allowed by the role assigned.
Accounting
Accounting is implemented at two levels. l The operation level, where each operation is tracked. l The file level, where each file access is tracked.

Audit Trail
Every user operation that changes the Cluster is audited and the audit log is saved. The log contains the original value and the value after the operation. For a list of logged operations, see Audit Logs. Cohesity stores audit logs on the Cohesity cluster. Users can read them using the standard NFS, SMB and S3 protocols and can export the logs to a syslog server.
Compliance
The following sections explain how Cohesity addresses various guidelines and specifications.
Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) Compliance
The Cohesity cluster is FIPS 140-2 certified. The encryption module has been validated on the Cohesity cluster with NIST for FIPS certification. The encryption module always operates in FIPS mode. You can find detailed information in the Cohesity FIPS 140-2 Non-proprietary Security Policy on the NIST website.
Common Criteria (EAL2+ Certification)
Common Criteria is an internationally recognized set of guidelines for evaluating IT security products. Common Criteria:
l is a catalog of criteria, and a framework for organizing a subset of the criteria, into security specifications
l is a methodology for evaluating security features l can be applied to hardware, software, firmware or a combination thereof l allows vendors to describe a product's security functionality with proof to support
their claims
Cohesity realizes the value of being a Common Criteria participant. To view the CC certificate, see MyCC.
DoDIN APL Certification
Cohesity is DoDIN APL certified. The Department of Defense Information Network (DoDIN) Approved Products List (APL) is the single consolidated list of products that have completed Cybersecurity (CS) and Interoperability (IO) certification. DoD customers are allowed to select products for purchase from this list. The DoDIN APL process is a rigorous security testing, validation, and certification process. This certification's security functional requirements come from a best practices guide called Security Technical Implementation Guides (STIG). It includes application security, OS hardening, web server security, and networking security as well. Cohesity adheres to these highest security standards. As part of the DoDIN APL requirements, Cohesity provides the following security features:

WORM (Write Once Read Many SEC 17a-4(f) Certification)
Long-term records retention is mandated by regulations and compliance rules, for example:
l In the financial services industry, SEC Rule 17a-4(f) specifies that "electronic records must be preserved exclusively in a non-rewriteable and non-erasable format."
l Other industries must meet similar requirements when they store mission-critical information.
WORM technology addresses these requirements by providing immutable locking and secure data retention capabilities.
Cohesity implements WORM as DataLock Views. DataLock Views are locked (read only) for a user-specified time period. Any user who has access to the View can clone a copy of the View as a DataLock View and set the lock retention time. During that time period, only users with Cohesity Data Security privileges can delete the cloned View, extend the lock period (it cannot be reduced) , add allowlisted IPs, change the QoS and change the description of the View. After the lock period expires, the View can be deleted by any user who has permission to delete it.
A replicated or archived DataLock View retains its DataLock properties. A DataLock View can be cloned to a regular or DataLock View.
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
GDPR is an EU regulation designed to strengthen data protection for residents of the EU. It became effective on May 25th, 2018, and applies to any company controlling or processing Personally Identifiable Information (PII) of EU residents, regardless of the location of the company.
GDPR imposes a broad set of legal, governance and technical requirements on companies processing personal data. A subset of these requirements--those related to data protection and data management--are particularly relevant for storage platforms used to store personal data.
Cohesity has a strong vision to enable our customers to be at the top of their GDPR compliance. The tools and product functionality that Cohesity provides as part of its vision fall into the following categories:

Secure Data from Ransomware Attacks
Threat Defense Architecture Cohesity's Threat Defense architecture is designed to help you combat threats against your data in the cluster by enabling you to achieve outcomes related to data protection, compliance, operational resiliency, and defense against sophisticated attacks. For instance, these outcomes include:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Security Features

l An ability to rapidly recover from a ransomware attack. l Resilience of the data against aggressive attacks that actively target the data
protection platform. l An ability to recover from both operational and data center failures. l Compliance through immutable and tamper-resistant data archives.

Cohesity Data Cloud At its core, Threat Defense architecture is about providing a highly resilient platform that ensures confidentiality, availability, and integrity of the data with encryption, fault tolerance, and immutability built into the Cohesity Data Cloud. The Cohesity Data Cloud is built around a hardened, self-contained Linux-based operating system (CohesitySpanOS) specifically designed to serve as a data management platform.
Note: Cohesity's data protection application does not run on general-purpose operating systems such as Windows.
The SpanOS kernel operates with SELinux extensions enabled in enforcing mode by default. This helps restrict privilege escalation and file modification, and confine access to services to ensure zero-trust security. Cohesity SpanOS is not accessible to users.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Security Features

Services
Services and subsystems on the Cohesity Data Cloud remain isolated with established APIs and other secure communication mechanisms used for service-to-service communications. Services that are essential to the operation of the cluster are installed and enabled, and other services included in general-purpose Linux distributions are not included on the Cohesity Data Cloud. This helps minimize the attack surface area of the Cohesity Data Cloud. Cohesity Data Cloud includes an in-built firewall that minimizes the network surface area of the cluster, therefore, only exposing ports and services necessary for cluster operation based on the configured operation.
Cohesity SpanFS
Cohesity SpanFS is an immutable file system. It ensures strict consistency of data across nodes within a cluster to provide data resiliency. Immutability ensures that WORMprotected data cannot be deleted or modified by any process or user including cluster administrators. Only the backup service running on the Cohesity cluster can write to the file system through trusted APIs.
DataLock
DataLock enables your storage to be WORM-compliant (Write-once-read-many) and restricts any modification of backup snapshots. You can refer to Create or Edit a Standard Policy to learn more about creating or editing policy that includes DataLock.
Data Operations
In a Cohesity cluster, data integrity is maintained through multiple integrity checks whenever data is read or written. Data is securely written to the Cohesity Data Cloud. This means data is always written in empty space and never overwritten.
Note: Every read or write operation to internal views is sandboxed.
Encryption
Data at rest and data in-flight encryption using FIPS-validated cryptography are employed with support for external key management.
Air Gap Protection
Cohesity Data Cloud can be configured to achieve air-gap protection that allows you to maintain a physically isolated network. Refer to Cohesity's Solutions for Air Data Protection to learn more about air-gap protection.
Zero Trust Access Control
Data resiliency is further augmented with comprehensive access control capabilities that ensure that entities accessing the data management platform conform to Zero Trust

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 3: Data Protection Key Concepts

Cohesity Security Features

principles.
Authentication
Cohesity supports a wide range of user authentication options, including a local user store (with in-built support for multi-factor authentication), integration with external identity providers, and certificate-based authentication (including support for smart cards). Besides native, in-built support for multi-factor authentication, Cohesity can also integrate with SAML-based authentication providers.
Access Control
Administration relies on role, object, and tenant-level access controls to ensure that Cohesity users are provided with the least privilege on the system. Access to the shell via SSH is disabled by default and can be controlled with organizational security policies. By default, you have read-only permission. Multi-man approval protocols are required for sensitive operations such as escalating privileges. Cohesity Support cannot access a cluster for troubleshooting unless explicitly granted limited-time permission by a cluster administrator. By default, read-only permission is granted.
Credentials Management
Each locally managed credential on the Cohesity Data Cloud is securely stored as a cryptographic representation of the credential and not in plaintext format. Therefore, you can reset it from factory defaults. In addition, security policy, which is enabled by default, can enforce password length and complexity rules and force password changes regularly to minimize the risk of brute force attacks.
Access to API
User and API access to the Cohesity Data Cloud are strictly controlled. Cohesity conforms with Zero Trust principles. This means that a user can access the Cohesity cluster only if they have the required permissions on the objects and files, and have been authenticated through any authentication protocol in the cluster. You can additionally control access to Cohesity APIs with rotatable API access tokens and user credentials.
Auditing
User activity is recorded in an audit trail that can be automatically shipped to an external log repository.
Analytics and Detection
The Threat Defense architecture incorporates additional layers of protection, including AIdriven detection and analytics. It combines a set of advanced capabilities ranging from threat detection to data anomaly detection.
Threat Detection
The Cohesity Data Cloud detects threats and vulnerabilities in several ways.
