Networking Workflows

Configure a Non-routable Primary Network for Cluster Creation and Expansion
A few customer environments have a dedicated storage network where the traffic is not routed outside of that network. In such a scenario, you can use the instructions in this topic to deploy Cohesity cluster data traffic on an isolated (non-routable) primary network and use the secondary interface for replication traffic.

Important: In cases where data traffic is isolated on a primary interface, the gateway is configured on the secondary interface. Ensure that NTP and other ports are reachable via the secondary interface.
Creating a Cohesity cluster 1. Install 6.6 on Cohesity cluster nodes. 2. Launch all cluster nodes' IPMI remote console. (ssh to nodes is not possible.) 3. To create a cluster, you can use one of the following steps on each node: a. Use the following command to configure the IP on a routable secondary interface. iris_cli ip config interface-name=<primary_interface_name> ifaceips=xx subnet-gateway=yy subnet-mask-bits=zz mtu=qq(optional)
Example: Iris_cli ip config interface-name=bond1 interface-ips=10.1.1.19 subnet-gateway=10.1.0.1 subnet-mask-bits=20

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

b. Use the following command to set the secondary interface used as the default route: Iris_cli route add dest-network=0.0.0.0/0 interface-name=xx nexthop=yy
Example Iris_cli route add dest-network=0.0.0.0/0 interface-name=bond1 next-hop=10.1.0.1
4. Use secondary interface IP or the Cohesity Dashboard and start cluster setup.

5. Assign node IP after the node selection (non-routable primary interface IP).

6. Continue with cluster setup and leave the Cluster Subnet Gateway field blank as the gateway is not available on the primary node IP network.

Set MTU
A maximum transmission unit, also called MTU, defines the largest size of the packet that can be transmitted as a single entity in a network connection. The size of the MTU determines the amount of data that can be transmitted in bytes over a network.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

Note: Ensure that the MTU is set with the same value end to end and there is no mismatch.
To enable jumbo frames, ensure the following: l Switch ports have the MTU set to 9000 l Every network hop between client hosts, such as any cluster nodes, hypervisor hosts, Windows or Linux hosts, and the Cohesity cluster have the MTU set to 9000
After setting the MTU on the path between all hosts and the Cohesity cluster, follow these steps to manually set the MTU size to 9000 on each node of every required network interface:
1. Log in to the iris_cli as an Admin user. 2. Stop the cluster services by running the following command:
admin> cluster stop 3. Check the cluster status by running the following command:
admin> cluster status
Note: Before proceeding, ensure the cluster status is as follows:
l SERVICE STATE SYNC: DONE l CLUSTER HEAL STATUS: NORMAL
4. Update the MTU for a node in the Cohesity cluster, using the interface-name parameter in the CLI interface update command, where the interface-name is the name of the interface group: iris_cli -username=<username> interface update interface-name=<name of the interface-group> mtu=<new value of mtu> Example: iris_cli -username=admin interface update interface-name=intf_group1 mtu=9000
5. Enter the password. 6. Start the cluster services by running the following command:
iris_cli -username=<user> cluster start 7. Enter the password.

Dual-Stack Network Configuration
Dual-stack network configuration enables Cohesity clusters to support both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses on the same network interfaces. This setup allows for a smooth transition between IP protocols and ensures compatibility with different network environments. Process Overview A quick overview of the process is as follows:
l Dual stack configuration for New clusters l Configure IPv6 and IPv4 on Free Nodes l Create Cluster
l Dual stack configuration for Existing clusters l Configure dual-stack networking with changing IP family preference l Configure dual-stack networking without changing IP family preference
l Create IPv6 and IPv4 subnet for Marketplace Apps l Enable Apps Management on the Cohesity Cluster l Install NoSQL and Hadoop Service Dual stack configuration for New clusters This topic provides detailed instructions for configuring dual-stack networking on new Cohesity clusters. It includes guidance on setting up IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and managing network settings. Configure IPv6 and IPv4 on Free Nodes You need to configure the IPv6 and IPv4 command on the primary interface of the free nodes using iris_cli command.
Note: You must configure IPv6 address first and then followed by IPv4.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

Run the following command to configure IPv6: iris_cli ip config interface-name=<primary_interface_name> family=2 interface-ips=<IPv6_address> subnet-mask-bits=<subnet_mask> subnet-gateway=<gateway> Example admin@127.0.0.1> ip config interface-name=bond0 family=2 interfaceips=fc00:10:95:160::18 subnet-mask-bits=64 subnet-gateway=fc00:10:95:160::1 Success: Ip configured successfully Run the following command to configure IPv4:
Note: You must configure a private IPv4 address for internal communication within Cohesity cluster nodes.
iris_cli ip config interface-name=<primary_interface_name> family=1 interface-ips=<IPv4_address> subnet-mask-bits=<subnet_mask> Example admin@127.0.0.1> ip config interface-name=bond0 family=1 interface-ipss=10.95.160.18 subnet-mask-bits=20 Success: Ip configured successfully. Description

Cluster Name

Specify a unique name for the Cohesity cluster. Only alphanumeric characters and hyphens are allowed. A hyphen cannot be the first or last character. Length cannot exceed 32 characters. No other characters are allowed.

Cluster Domain Name

The fully qualified domain name for the Cohesity cluster.

Cluster Subnet Gateway

Specify the IPv6 address of the Subnet Gateway for the Cohesity cluster.

Cluster Subnet Mask

Specify the Subnet Mask for the Subnet that the Cohesity cluster is a part of.

IPMI Subnet Gateway (optional)

Specify the IPv4 address of the subnet Gateway for the IPMI or iRMC network interfaces
Note: You can either specify the IPMI configuration while creating the Cohesity cluster or after creating the cluster.

IPMI Subnet Mask (optional)

Specify the IPv4 Subnet Mask for the IPMI or iRMC Subnet.

IPMI Username (optional)

Specify the IPMI username to connect to the IPMI interface for each of the nodes in the Cohesity cluster. The cluster uses the IPMI username to get system health information about the nodes in the cluster.
All nodes in the cluster must use the same IPMI username and IPMI password.
Only alphanumeric characters and hyphens are allowed, but a hyphen cannot be the first character. The length cannot exceed 32 characters.
The default IPMI username is admin.
The Cohesity cluster does not depend on the IPMI configuration to get system health information about the nodes. For ease of managing the nodes remotely, you can configure IPMI.

IPMI Password (optional)

Specify the IPMI password to connect to the IPMI interface for each node in the Cohesity cluster. All nodes in the cluster must use the same IPMI username and IPMI password. The password can be 8 to 16 characters. It cannot include the following characters: dollar sign ($), asterisk (*), quote ("), single quote (`) or backslash (\). The default IPMI password is admin. The Cohesity cluster supports AES256 software encryption. The Cohesity cluster provides a built-in Key Management Service (KMS) that automatically generates keys. After Encryption is turned on, the following option is available:
l The Rotation Period is how often the Cohesity cluster's encryption key is rotated. After the time period is reached, the old encryption key is replaced by a new key and the data on the Cohesity cluster remains as it was originally encrypted. The Rotation Period default value is 30 days. You can change this to the desired value.

Enable Apps Management on the Cohesity Cluster

Before you can install and run apps, the cluster must be enabled to support app management.
Perform the following steps to enable app management:

1. Log in to the Cohesity cluster with valid credentials. 2. Navigate to Marketplace > My Apps. 3. Click the My Apps tab and then click App Settings located at the top right of the
page. 4. Turn on the Enable Apps Management toggle.

You can also Enable Apps Management using the iris_cli command. Run the following command:

iris_cli apps update-apps-settings marketplace-apps-mode=kBareMetal

Example

admin@127.0.0.1> apps update-apps-settings marketplace-apps-mode=kBareMetal

APPS MODE

: BareMetal

MARKETPLACE APPS MODE

: BareMetal

Install NoSQL and Hadoop Service

You need to download the NoSQL and Hadoop Service and install it on the cluster. Perform the following steps:

1. Obtain the NoSQL and Hadoop Service package from your Cohesity Accounts contact. The app package format is app1011-700xxxx.pkg where 700xxxx is the version number.
2. Download the package to a location from where you are planning to connect to the Cohesity Platform.
3. Log in to the Cohesity Platform with valid credentials.
4. Navigate to Marketplace > Apps.
5. Under the My Apps folder, click Upload App and navigate to the location where you have downloaded the app package, and select the app package.
6. Click Upload and Install.
7. Once the upload is complete, click Run App to launch the app.

Use a Proxy Server
The Cohesity cluster supports routing network traffic to a proxy server for:
l getting upgrade packages from Cohesity l sending proactive monitoring (Helios) diagnostics from the Cluster to Cohesity l connecting to the Cluster via the Cohesity Support Channel (if a proxy server is
configured for the Cluster as described below, the Support Channel will use the proxy server)
This functionality has been qualified with the Squid3 proxy server. Configure this functionality using the following CLI commands: cluster update-proxyserver, cluster rm-proxy, cluster ls-proxies and cluster edit-proxies. To learn more, log in to the Cohesity CLI and enter the name of the command followed by help such as: cluster update-proxy-server help. To configure a proxy for outbound Web traffic using Squid, see the How to configure a proxy for outbound web traffic using Squid KB article.

Verify NTP Setup and Detect Issues
Starting with Cohesity cluster version 7.2.2, Cohesity will transition from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7.9 OS to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9.2 as the Host Operating System. Chronyd is now the default time daemon, replacing ntpd. When a Cohesity cluster is first created, it must have connectivity to an NTP server. Common public NTP servers that can be used:
l time.nist.gov l time.google.com
Verify the Cluster Can Query the NTP Server
Perform the following from the Cohesity node that is used to create the Cohesity cluster. ssh to a Cohesity Node with the support user and run the chronyd -Q command:
#chronyd -Q `server <hostname_of_ntp_server> iburst'
For example:
#chronyd -Q `server time.nist.gov iburst'
If the NTP server is reachable, expect the following output:
[root@f7e746e6 ~]# chronyd -Q `server time.nist.gov iburst' 2025-08-21T03:26:23Z chronyd version 4.5 starting (+CMDMON +NTP +REFCLOCK +RTC +PRIVDROP +SCFILTER +SIGND +ASYNCDNS +NTS +SECHASH +IPV6 +DEBUG) 2025-08-21T03:26:23Z Disabled control of system clock 2025-08-21T03:26:27Z System clock wrong by 0.000159 seconds (ignored) 2025-08-21T03:26:27Z chronyd exiting [root@f7e746e6 ~]#

Detect and Resolve NTP Synchronization Issues

NTP time synchronization is critical to Cohesity clusters. A cluster's opclock, which is a vector clock, relies on strict NTP synchronization. If time services become out of sync, they can shut down all I/O operations if a metadata opclock out-of-order condition occurs.
NTP out of sync condition symptoms include:

l Cluster creation does not complete. An error of "kClusterBringup" may be reported. l After entering Node and IPMI IP addresses in the initial setup wizard, the screen
begins to flicker and ultimately returns to the login prompt. l Cluster creation fails with "WARNING | CE00411001 - FrequentProcessRestarts |
Process bridge_exec is restarting frequently". l "An internal component may be down" message is reported.
l The Cohesity Bridge service experiences FATAL errors with the following message:

F1013 01:21:08.107616 120432 client_base_op.cc:247] Server asked the client to crash. Timestamp in the request is 10001 msecs in the future. Please check the time difference between nodes. logs/bridge_exec.FATAL (END)

Change operations may not be allowed within the Cohesity cluster. For example, the time cannot be set earlier because of the opclock dependency.
There are multiple ways to check the NTP server configuration and current state. This following information describes how to check an chronyd configuration and status.

l Verify the time difference on multiple Nodes:

[cohesity@9166193e ~]$ allssh.sh "date"

=========== 10.10.10.10 ===========

Mon Oct 12 16:27:48 PDT 2015

|-- NTP master is faster than other

nodes

=========== 10.10.10.11 ===========

Mon Oct 12 16:25:51 PDT 2015

=========== 10.10.10.12 ===========

Mon Oct 12 16:25:50 PDT 2015

=========== 10.10.10.13 ===========

Mon Oct 12 16:25:50 PDT 2015

l Verify the chrony.conf on all Nodes:

[cohesity@9166193e ~]$ allssh.sh "less /etc/chrony.conf" =========== 10.10.10.10 =========== # /etc/chrony.conf, configuration for chronyd

#------------------------------------------------# DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE - it is machine generated # Don't change config without validation for security holes

Manage VLANs
After the initial setup of a Cohesity cluster, you can extend your existing on-premise VLANs into the Cohesity cluster to logically separate traffic and improve performance. After you add a VLAN to the Cohesity cluster, users can select the VLAN when recovering VMs, files, folders, Pure Storage volumes, NAS volumes, or when cloning a vCenter Source. Some recovery and clone tasks can auto-select the appropriate VLAN for the task, but users can override the selection. The Cohesity cluster supports a maximum of 4094 VLAN IDs irrespective of the cluster size. The following diagram shows an example Cohesity environment using VLANs.

Add a VLAN Perform the steps in this section to add a VLAN.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

Note: Cohesity recommends the following:
l Do not configure a VLAN gateway if you want to use global static route for outgoing traffic from the Cohesity cluster.
l Enable a separate VLAN gateway (different from the default VLAN gateway) to route incoming traffic to the Cohesity cluster via a VLAN IP address such as NFS or UI. Static routes are required only for outgoing traffic, and the Default Gateway setting of the VLAN is only for incoming traffic regardless of Static Routing.
1. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Networking and then select the VLANs tab.
2. Click Add VLAN. 3. Provide the following information:
l Interface Group: Select the interface group to use for the VLAN. l VLAN ID: Specify the ID of the VLAN you want to add. l Subnet: Specify the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the subnet mask bits for the VLAN. l Gateway: Optional. Specify the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the subnet gateway for
the VLAN. l Enable For All Organizations:Optional. Toggle this setting on if you want to
enable VLAN for all organizations. For more information, see Enabling VLANs for all Organizations. 4. Click Save.
The VLAN is added to the Cohesity cluster and available for the supported recovery and clone tasks. To add optional virtual IP addresses (VIPs) to the VLAN, select Settings > Networking and then select the VIPs tab. From the Interface Group drop-down, select intf_group1.

icon ( ). 3. Change the settings as needed. Note the following:

Manage VIPs
When a cluster is created, every node in the cluster is assigned a Node IP (or static IP) address. However, if the cluster goes offline, the Node IP addresses become inaccessible and go down as well. Virtual IP (VIP) is assigned to the cluster nodes after the cluster is created. Even if the cluster goes down, the assigned virtual IP remains available.
Add a VIP
You can add IPv4 or IPv6 virtual IP addresses (VIPs) to an interface group. To add a VIP:
1. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Networking and then select the VIPs tab.
2. Select the VIP type you want to add, IPv4 or IPv6. 3. Interface Group: Select an interface group from the drop-down. 4. Provide the following information:
l Subnet: Specify the IP address of the subnet mask bits for the interface group. l FQDN: Specify the fully qualified domain name associated with the interface
group. l Gateway: Optional. Specify the IP address of the subnet gateway for the
interface group.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

l VIP Address or Range: Optional. Specify a single virtual IP (VIP) address or a range of addresses assigned to the interface group and then click Add VIP or Range. If providing a range, enter a complete address in the first field and just the upper limit of the range (such as 5) in the second field. For the non-primary interface group, the number of VIPs must be equal to or greater than the number of Nodes in the Cluster. If you provide a number of VIPs equal to or greater than the number of Nodes, the VLAN is automatically added to the Cluster. For the primary interface group, the number of VIPs can be lesser than the number of Nodes in the Cluster.
Note: VIPs cannot be assigned to two interfaces within the same subnet.
5. Inbound DNS (Optional)Type Zone name and Zone Server VIPs. Click the (+) icon to add multiple zones.
Note: Use this option to use the Cohesity cluster as an internal DNS server. For more information, see Internal DNS for Load Balancing.
Configuring it helps in load balancing by selecting available VIPs for balancing network traffic. A Zone name consists of an internal DNS name and a client-side DNS name. For example, Testintdns.storage.eng. In the example, storage.eng is the DNS zone in the client environment and Testintdns is the child zone hosted on Cohesity cluster.
Note: You should know your DNS server name to add the zone name and can use one of the VIPs as Zone Server VIP. You cannot delete a VIP that is used as a Zone Server VIP.
6. Click Update.
Note: If you have updated any of the above mentioned fields, you must click Update before proceeding.
Delete a VIP You can delete IPv4 or IPv6 virtual IP addresses (VIPs) from an interface group.

To delete a VIP: 1. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Networking and select the VIPs tab.
2. In the list of VIPs, click the delete icon ( ) to delete the VIP.
Internal DNS for Load Balancing
The Domain Name System (DNS) in the Cohesity cluster helps in load balancing by selecting available VIPs for balancing network traffic on VLANs. From release 6.6 onwards, your Cohesity cluster can act as a DNS server. You can configure your cluster as a DNS server by configuring In Bound DNS option and creating DNS load balancing zones in the Cohesity Cluster. The configured DNS load balancing zones are valid with a VLAN. You can configure the In Bound DNS when creating a VIP. Cohesity uses the round-robin technique for managing the client's requests. You should register one cluster serving VIP on a DNS server (client-side DNS) in your environment. The Cohesity cluster acts as a subdomain for your DNS server. The configured DNS server inside the cluster addresses the issue of updating the client-side DNS when you add or remove a node in the Cohesity cluster or add a new VIP. Advantages of DNS Load Balancing The advantages of DNS load balancing are:
l You do not need to add all VIPs on the client-side DNS server for mapping. l Map a single VIP with the client-side DNS. Prerequisites l Access to external DNS server Considerations l You can't delete a VIP configured with an external DNS server. l A single FQDN can resolve only with one zone.
l The View mount paths for SMB, NFS, and S3 do not show paths for other DNS zones when you have a single FQDN and. the cluster is not registered with AD.
l In a multitenancy environment, DNS load balancing is supported only for VLAN-based organizations (tenants).

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

Create DNS Load Balancing Zone
DNS load balancing zone assigns available VIPs to clients using the round-robin method and manages network traffic. When you configure the DNS load balancing zone on your Cohesity cluster, available VIPs are linked to a load balancing zone in a VLAN. You need to configure the client-side DNS server to delegate all DNS requests to the DNS load balancing zone on the Cohesity cluster. You can create a DNS load balancing zone when creating a VIP. For more information, see Manage VIPs.
Configuration on Client-Side DNS Server
Create a new delegation zone in the DNS Server for the child domain that you have created on the Cohesity cluster. When you create a delegation, any request to your DNS server is forwarded to the DNS load balancing zone created on your Cohesity cluster.
Add A-record and Delegation Zone on Client-Side Windows DNS Server
You need to add an address mapping record ('A' Record for IPv4) or `AAAA' (for IPv6) record in the client-side DNS server and add a delegation. For example, we have this client-side DNS server zone.com and you added an internal DNS zone on your Cohesity cluster: cohesityV4dns.zone.com with VIP 10.1.1.1. Now you need to make an 'A' record in the zone.com DNS for the VIP 10.1.1.1 and add a delegation using the 'A' record and the internal DNS zone name: cohesityV4dns.zone.com. Prerequisites
l Cohesity DNS zone name. l VIP address used for creating the DNS zone on the cluster.
To add a delegation zone on the client-side Windows DNS Server:
1. Log in to your Windows Server. 2. Navigate to Windows Administrator Tools > DNS Manager > Forward Lookup
Zones. 3. Select the required domain and add an A or AAAA entry for one of the VIPs from your
Cohesity cluster. 4. Enter a name for the Cohesity internal DNS server. 5. After adding the A or AAAA record entry, add a DNS delegation. 6. Right-click the domain and select New Delegation. 7. In the New Delegation wizard, enter the DNS zone name that you added in the
cluster. Enter the A or AAAA record name that you added to the DNS server. 8. Complete the instructions in the wizard to add the delegation.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

Once the A or AAAA record is added and delegation is created, any requests to the clientside DNS Server are forwarded to the DNS zone created on the Cohesity internal DNS server. Add or Remove Inbound DNS Zone You can add or remove a load balancing zone. To add or remove DNS zone:
1. In the Cohesity cluster Dashboard, navigate to Settings > Networking and then click the VIPs tab.
2. In the Inbound DNS (Optional) section of the page, click the (+) icon to add multiple zones or click (-) to delete a zone.
3. Click Update.
Manage Host Mappings
Use the Cohesity cluster to provide Cluster-wide /etc/hosts entries that map IP addresses to domain names. Using the dashboard ensures that the entries are centrally stored in the Cluster and propagated to all existing Nodes and to any new Nodes added to the Cohesity cluster. The entries are also preserved during Cohesity cluster upgrades. On a new or newly upgraded Cohesity cluster running release 6.5.1 or later, the Clusterwide file is initialized automatically. The Cluster then monitors the Nodes at regular intervals for changes to /etc/hosts and propagates the changes to the other Nodes within a few seconds. For an upgraded Cohesity cluster, any existing /etc/hosts entries are retained and uploaded to the Cluster-wide file.
Note: Do not directly edit the /etc/hosts files on the Nodes in the Cohesity cluster.
Manage /etc/hosts Entries You can manually enter the host names and IP addresses or upload a host file with the mappings between them. To manually enter the host names:
1. Select Settings > Networking and then select the Host Mapping tab.
2. Click the Edit icon ( ) next to Host Mapping. 3. Enter the IP addresses and host names. 4. Click Save. To upload entries from a host file (in *.txt format):

1. Select Settings > Networking and then select the Host Mapping tab. 2. Click Upload hosts file. 3. Browse to open your text file that has the IP address vs. host name mapping. The IP
address and hostnames must be separated by a space or tab, as shown below. Comma-separated values are not supported.

Configure a Non-native VLAN for Cohesity cluster Creation and Expansion
Create a Cohesity cluster 1. Install 7.4.1 on Cohesity cluster nodes. 2. Launch all Cohesity cluster nodes' IPMI remote console. (ssh to nodes is not possible.) 3. To create a Cohesity cluster, you can use one of the following methods: 1. Through iris_cli. Perform these steps on all nodes: a. Use the iris_cli add vlan command to set up the non-native VLAN to be used for the Cohesity cluster create workflow. iris_cli vlan add interface-group=<name of the interface group> id=<VLAN-ID> subnet-mask-bits=<Subnet-Mask-Prefix>
Example: iris_cli vlan add interface-group=intf_group1 id=5 subnetmask-bits=20

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

b. Use the following command to set the non-native VLAN logical bond interface as primary. Replace vlan_id with the ID of the VLAN you added.
iris_cli ip config interface-name=<bond0.vlan_id> interfacerole=primary
Example:
iris_cli ip config interface-name=bond0.5 interfacerole=primary
Alternatively, to configure the IP on each node and access the node using the IP (not required if using Avahi to discover all nodes), use this command:
iris_cli ip config interface-name=<bond0.vlan_id> interfaceips=xx subnet-gateway=yy subnet-mask-bits=zz interfacerole=primary
Example:
iris_cli ip config interface-name=bond0.5 interfaceips=10.5.1.5 subnet-gateway=10.5.0.1 subnet-mask-bits=20 interface-role=primary
2. Through configure_network.sh script: Perform these steps on all nodes. Use configure_network.sh option 10 to add VLAN and follow the prompts to complete VLAN addition on the desired network bond. Location: /home/cohesity/bin/network/configure_network.sh
4. Restart the Cluster Manager Services:
sudo service nexus restart
5. Run ifconfig and ensure Avahi runs on the non-native VLAN bonded interface. Cohesity relies on Avahi for node discovery. Sample output from a node running on the primary non-native VLAN 5
bond0.5:avahi: flags=4163<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,MULTICAST> mtu 1500 inet 169.254.7.187 netmask 255.255.0.0 broadcast 169.254.255.255 ether a4:bf:01:2d:7e:b2 txqueuelen 1000 (Ethernet)
6. Perform these steps on any one node: If an IP was assigned on the VLAN interface, access the UI using the assigned IP on the VLAN interface. Otherwise, complete these steps: a. Connect the Mac laptop to the node for Avahi discovery for Cohesity cluster create.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Networking Workflows

b. Perform discovery through the browser, using this URL format: https://chassis-<chassis_serial_number>-<node_number>.local
7. On any node, start the Cohesity cluster create workflow and provide Cohesity cluster IPs from the configured non-native VLAN.
Note: If necessary, the user can configure Cohesity cluster IPs and VIPs from the non-native VLAN and retain the IPMI in the native VLAN or some other subnet.

Using the Cohesity Dashboard or CLI, you can configure application-based firewall rules and manage incoming traffic on a Cohesity cluster. Manage Application-Based Firewall Rules
Firewall restricts network access and manages inbound traffic on Cohesity cluster. It allows you to secure your cluster from unauthorized access and malicious traffic. Cohesity lets you configure application-based firewall rules using firewall profiles. Firewall profiles are rules that define whether data from specific applications, ports, protocols, and ipsets (source IP address sets) are allowed or denied through one or more interface groups. You can

Configure Firewall Rules
Using the Cohesity Dashboard or CLI, you can configure firewall rules and apply them to one or more interface groups on a cluster.
Note: If you configure multiple bond interfaces on a cluster for various traffic types, ensure that you configure the same bond interfaces on the free nodes before adding them to the cluster.
To configure firewall rules using the supported profiles:
1. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Networking and then click the Firewall tab. The Rules page appears and displays all the supported firewall profiles. By default, all the incoming application traffic listed in the firewall profiles are allowed on all the available interface groups.
2. Click the edit icon ( ). 3. Provide the details in the applicable fields for the application traffic you plan to
manage: l Application: Predefined name of the firewall profile. Specifies an external service or a source of the incoming traffic. l Interface Group: Select one or more interface groups from the drop-down menu. By default, all the interface groups are selected.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Manage Firewall Rules and Ports

l Client's IPSet: Select Custom IP/Subnet from the drop-down menu and specify the IP address and subnet mask bits of the source network. You can enter multiple IP addresses and subnet mask sets. For example, 10.1.1.2/24 and 10.2.3.2/16. By default, the All IP Addresses option is selected.
l Action: Select Allow or Deny from the drop-down menu to allow or restrict the traffic. By default, the Allow option is selected.
4. Optional. Repeat Step 3 to customize the firewall profiles and manage other network traffic types based on your requirements.
5. Click Apply to save the configuration and apply the firewall rules. Restore Firewall Rules to the Default Settings If you misconfigured firewall rules or if you want to reset all your firewall settings, you can restore the configured firewall rules to their default settings.
Important: If you restore firewall rules to default, all the configured firewall rules will be lost.
To restore firewall rules to the default settings: 1. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Networking and then click the Firewall tab. The Rules page appears and displays all the supported firewall profiles.
2. Click the reset icon ( ). 3. Click Restore to confirm the reset operation. You can also use the Cohesity CLI to configure the firewall rules or restore the rules to their default settings. For more details, see Cohesity CLI Commands Used to Manage Firewall Ports.
Manage Firewall Ports
You must open certain ports in the firewall to allow the Cohesity cluster to transmit and receive data. The cluster sends the following types of traffic over the network. You can isolate traffic on physical or logical networks to improve performance and security.
l IPMI traffic for admins to access nodes, typically for pre-boot BIOS access and postboot console access.
l Management traffic: l from Nodes to external services such as Active Directory, DNS, NTP, and SNMP l for admins to access the Cohesity cluster
l Backup and restore traffic for moving data between protected sources and the cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Manage Firewall Rules and Ports

l Replication traffic for replicating data from one cluster to another cluster. l Data access (NAS) traffic for accessing data on the cluster by using protocols such as
NFS, SMB, or S3. l Archive and tiering traffic for moving data to external targets such as a cloud or tape
system. l Support Channel traffic between nodes and the Cohesity Support servers. l Internal traffic between nodes on a cluster.
Note: Note the following when applying firewall rules on a Cohesity cluster:
l Cohesity uses Virtual IPs (VIPs) to manage incoming traffic to the cluster. l Cohesity uses Host IPs (node IP addresses) for outgoing traffic and node-to-
node communication within the cluster. l When setting up replication on a Cohesity cluster, you can specify either the
VIPs or node IP addresses of the remote cluster. Cohesity recommends specifying VIPs, as they can failover to other nodes if a node becomes unreachable or goes down. l Do not enable Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) for replication workflows and Teleport support traffic, as it can degrade replication performance and impact Teleport functionality. l Ensure to have network connectivity between the source and the cluster.

Identify Source IP of Outgoing Traffic
The source IP of outgoing traffic depends on the matching static route's outgoing interface. If there is no static route, the source IP depends on the default route's outgoing interface. Use the route list command to view the list of routes configured on an interface in a Cohesity cluster and the IP address of the destination network.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Manage Firewall Rules and Ports

Source
Cohesity cluster

Destination

Destination Port

Cohesity Agent 50051*

Protocol TCP

Usage Notes

Type of Traffic

Used for Cohesity Agent and agentless data transfer to the cluster. Needs to be open on all nodes on the cluster and any backup target using the Cohesity Agent, such as SQL servers, physical servers, and VMs running the Cohesityinstalled Agent.
Cohesity clusters pick any available ephemeral port to initiate communication with the agent service via port 50051. The firewall needs to allow the connection request from the Cohesity nodes if the destination port is 50051.
*By default, Cohesity uses port 50051. This port isn't reserved exclusively for Cohesity, so if another application on your network already uses it, you can use port 21213 instead. IANA reserves port 21213 for Cohesity in its service registry. You can select the port during installation, and only one port is active at a time. Open only the port that your deployment uses. You don't need to open both.
Port 21213 is an early access feature. To enable it, contact your Cohesity account team. Add port 21213/TCP to your firewall only after you enable this feature, to avoid requesting unnecessary firewall rules from your network, firewall, or security teams.

Backup and Recovery

No specific ports need to be opened to protect Microsoft Exchange Servers, provided the following requirements have been met as part of your cluster configuration:

*By default, Cohesity uses port 50051. This port isn't reserved exclusively for Cohesity, so if another application on your network already uses it, you can use port 21213 instead. IANA reserves port 21213 for Cohesity in its service registry. You can select the port during installation, and only one port is active at a time. Open only the port that your deployment uses. You don't need to open both.
Port 21213 is an early access feature. To enable it, contact your Cohesity account team. Add port 21213/TCP to your firewall only after you enable this feature, to avoid requesting unnecessary firewall rules from your network, firewall, or security teams.
Cohesity CLI Commands Used to Manage Firewall Ports
For on-premises clusters, you can use the following Cohesity CLI commands to manage the cluster firewall configuration. For more information, see Using the Cohesity CLI and List of Cohesity CLI Commands.
The firewall commands use the following terminology: Active Cohesity rules are called attachments. An attachment includes a profile and multiple ipsets. A profile is a group of TCP or UDP ports. An ipset is a subnet with the format of <IP/prefix>. An attachment can be on one or more specific network interfaces, or it can apply to all interfaces when no interface is specified.

CLI Command firewall-profile activate firewall-profile add firewall-profile deactivate firewall-profile delete

Description Activates a profile on a list of interfaces with a list of ipsets. Adds a collection of service ports with the protocol of each port for the firewall. Deactivates a list of active firewall profiles. Removes a list of firewall profiles.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

CLI Command

Description

firewall-profile list

Lists the groups of firewall profiles.

firewall-profile list-active

Lists all the active firewall profiles. Each attachment activates a profile on specific network interfaces and ipsets.

firewall-ipset list

Lists the IP sets for a firewall.

firewall-profile activate revertto-default

Reverts all the firewall rules to the default settings.

To list the parameters for each command, type help after the firewall-profile <option> or firewall-ipset <option>. For example:
admin@node-1> firewall-profile activate help

Access Management
Cohesity Access Management ensures secure and efficient access control by allowing only authorized users to interact with specific resources. It is designed to enforce User Authentication, Authorization, Access Control, and Security Settings, ensuring users have the necessary permissions to perform their roles.
The Users & Groups tab in the Access Management page lists all local users, Active Directory users, and SSO users and groups that can access the Cohesity cluster. Administrators can assign roles to users and groups to grant specific privilege levels. For detailed instructions, see Users and Groups. You can also edit or delete existing users.

Key Components of Access Management
User Authentication and Authorization
User and Group Management: Administrators can create and manage user accounts and groups, specifying roles and permissions that determine access levels to various Cohesity resources.
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Organization admins can add and manage users through role-based access controls (RBAC). Applying principles of least privilege and separation of duties is simple with fine-grained control over standard and custom defined roles.
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Multi-factor Authentication (MFA) is an additional layer of security used to verify the identity of a user. Cohesity strongly recommends enabling Multi-factor Authentication for Local and Active Directory Users for all users and groups for enhanced security. After the administrator enables MFA, users are prompted for

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

an additional authentication factor along with the Cohesity cluster user credentials during the sign-in process. Single Sign-On (SSO): Streamlines the login process by allowing access to all the Cohesity resources with a single set of credentials, reducing the risk of password fatigue and enhancing user convenience. For more information, see Single Sign-On (SSO).
Users and Groups
Cohesity allows adding users with different privileges by assigning them various roles within the cluster. These users and groups can manage data and view statistics based on their assigned roles. Cohesity supports the following types of users and groups. Except for the support user, all user types can log in to the Cohesity Dashboard to manage data on the Cohesity cluster and view statistics, depending on their role.
l Local users: Local users exist on the Cohesity cluster only. l Local groups: You can define groups by adding local users and Active Directory
principals. l SSO users: If the Cohesity cluster is configured to use an identity provider for single
sign-on access, you can add SSO users and assign them roles. For more information, see SSO Users. l Active Directory principals: If the Cohesity cluster is joined to an AD domain, you can assign roles to principals in the AD or the AD's trusted domains, which determine the Cohesity cluster access. For more information, see Active Directory (AD). l Support user: Used to access the bash shell of the Cohesity cluster using SSH. The support user account is disabled by default. For more information, see Manage Support User.
Types of Users and Groups
Local Users
Local users are exclusive to the Cohesity cluster. They can be created and managed directly within the system.

Add a Local Administrator Group Using the CLI
You can use local administrator groups to grant SMB access to views and/or administrative access to the Cohesity cluster.
The Cohesity cluster has a built-in local administrators group called Administrators. By default, the group has only SMB Security privileges and the standard Windows administrator Security ID (SID) S-1-5-32-544. You can use and modify the Administrators group, or create your own local administrator groups and assign roles and SIDs by using the Cohesity CLI.

Enable User Account Lockout
The admin user can enable account lockout on the user account. User accounts can get locked after a threshold number of failed login attempts. The user cannot log in to the Cohesity Dashboard after three consecutive invalid login attempts for 15 minutes.

Note: You can enable account lockout only for non-admin local users.

Perform the following steps to enable user account lockout: 1. Navigate to Settings > Access Management. 2. Select the Users & Groups tab.

Change Local User Password

Using the Cohesity Dashboard, you can change your local user password. By default, the new password must replace at least eight characters with the current password.
Using the following Cohesity CLI command, you can define the number of characters you have to replace in your existing local user password:

iris_cli security-config update num-diff-chars=<number_of_characters>

For example:
If you want to restrict those six characters in your existing local user password must be replaced while changing the password, then use the following command:

iris_cli security-config update num-diff-chars=6

Note: The restriction is not applicable if the admin user wants to change the password of other local users in the Cohesity cluster.
To change the local user password: 1. Navigate to Settings > Access Management.
2. Click the actions menu ( ) next to the user and click Edit. 3. In the Edit Local User: <user> page:
1. Enable Change Password. 2. Enter the Current Password and then enter and confirm the new Password. 3. Click Save Changes. Optionally restrict access to specific Objects and Views only by toggling this option on. By default, the allowed actions apply to all Source Objects registered with the Cohesity cluster and all Views. After restricting access, you must specifically add Objects and Views through Add Registered Object(s) and Add Cohesity View(s). The user or group does not have access to any Objects or Views until you add them. When a user has access to an Object, that user also has access to all previous Snapshots of that Object and any Objects added to the selected Source folder in the future. For example, if a user has access to an ESX host, they will also have access to VMs added to the host later. Users that have access restricted to specific Objects cannot modify users or Sources even if their role grants them these privileges. Object permissions are replicated for Virtual Machine Objects but not currently for physical Server and View Objects. When Snapshots are replicated from a local to a remote Cohesity cluster, the Object permissions for AD users or groups are also replicated. However, the privileges for an AD user or group are not replicated. For example, if an AD user called Fred has permission to access the Virtual Machines called VM1, VM2 and VM3 on the local Cohesity cluster, when Snapshots of those Virtual Machines are replicated to a remote Cohesity cluster, those Object permissions are also replicated. However, an administrator on the remote Cohesity cluster must add the AD User called Fred or an AD group that includes Fred and grant him privileges so Fred can access and recover from Snapshots of these VMs on the remote Cohesity cluster. AD users inherit the permissions of the Restricted Objects provided to the Restricted AD Groups to which the users belong.
Optionally add a description.

Support User
The support user account is designed for accessing the bash shell of the Cohesity cluster through SSH for troubleshooting and support purposes. This account is disabled by default for security reasons.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

Manage Support User
Cohesity provides a support user account for improved security and you need to use the support user account to log in to the Cohesity cluster bash shell using SSH. By default, the support user account is disabled on the Cohesity node that is part of a Cohesity cluster. You need to enable the support user account by setting a password for the user account in the Cohesity Dashboard. Also, you can Enable Linux Sudo Access for the support user account.
Set the Support User Password for the First Time
Using the Cohesity Dashboard or Cohesity CLI, you can set the password for the support user. You cannot retrieve the password once it is set. Therefore, ensure that you set a strong password that is longer and easy to remember. In case, if you want to reset the support user password and have forgotten the existing password then contact Cohesity Support. Perform the following steps to set the support user password:
1. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Access Management and click the Support tab.
2. Under Linux Shell Password, click Set Password and perform the following steps: a. In the New Password field, enter the new password. The password requirements are: l Must be at least 15 characters long. l Must contain at least one digit, one special character, one uppercase & one lowercase character.
Note: Do not use !, `," and \.
l Do not use more than two of the same characters in a row. For example, 123aa is allowed. 123aaa is not allowed.
l Do not use more than four identical consecutive character types (digit, special character, uppercase and lowercase character). For example, 123aa is allowed. 12345aa is not allowed.
b. In the Confirm Password field, enter the new password. c. Click Set.
Note: By default, the support user logs in to the secure shell and access to the host shell is restricted through SSH. For more information on how to enable host shell access using the support user account, see Enable Host Shell Access.

Manage Roles
The Manage Roles page lists all defined roles that you can assign to users and groups. From the Manage Roles page you can add and edit custom roles. For detailed instructions, see Create or Edit a Role. You can also delete existing custom roles. For users with restricted access, their allowed actions can be performed on the explicitly selected object set only; they do not have access to other objects. This restricted access protects your data from any ransomware attack because the data is managed only by the users who have the necessary privileges on your cluster.
Note: Admins can create and modify custom roles. Pre-defined system roles cannot be modified.
Pre-defined System Roles
Admin
Users with the Admin role have full access to all actions and workflow within the Cohesity UI and Cohesity CLI except for changing DataLock Views and setting their expiration dates. For example, a user assigned the Admin role can create backups, recover Snapshots and files from backups, add sources, delete sources, set up and manage the Cohesity cluster, manage Nodes, manage Views, resolve Alerts, etc. A user with the Admin role can also add and delete users. By default, the Cohesity cluster is preconfigured with a default System Admin user called admin that has the same privileges as a user with the Admin role. This default System Admin account (admin) cannot be deleted.
Viewer
Users with the Viewer role have read-only access for all workflows within the Cohesity Dashboard.
Operator
Users with the Operator role have Viewer role privileges and the following additional privileges:
l Run existing Protection Groups. l Create and Manage Clone tasks. l Create and Manage Recover tasks.
A user with this privilege cannot download files from a snapshot and cannot recover from External targets.
SMB Security
Users with the SMB Security role have all SMB privileges when accessing data over SMB.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

SMB Backup Operator
Users with SMB Backup Operator role have the privilege to perform SMB backup and SMB restore.
Self Service Data Protection
Users with the Self Service Data Protection role have Viewer role privileges and the following additional privileges:
l Create and Manage Protection Policies. l Create and Manage Protection Groups. l Create and Manage Clone tasks. l Create and Manage Recover tasks l Create and Manage Cohesity Views.
Data Security
Users with the Data Security role have all privileges granted by the Self Service Data Protection and Viewer roles and the following additional privileges:
l Create DataLock Views and set DataLock expiration dates. l Create a Protection Group. l Start an on-demand protection run and edit a protection run. l Delete protection runs and snapshots. l Add and remove Legal Hold to existing snapshots.
Replication
Users with the Replication role have basic privileges for replication. This role allows the user to perform replication of data to other clusters. A user with this privilege cannot log in to the Cohesity Dashboard.
FortKnox Self Managed Vault Admin
FortKnox Self-Managed vault admin users have full access to create, update, and delete FortKnox Self-Managed cluster pairing. Create or Edit a Role Use this page to create or edit a custom role. For example, you can create a user with the Operator role and certain admin privileges such as Upgrade Cluster and Manage Cluster. All custom roles have Viewer role privileges.
Note: Admins can create and modify custom roles. Pre-defined system roles cannot be modified.

privileges, see Privileges.
Tip: In the Cohesity Dashboard, hover your mouse over the privilege name to display its description in a pop-up tooltip.
4. Click Create Role or Save Changes. Role and privilege updates for currently logged-in users take effect after logging out and logging in again. Updates for users that are not currently logged in take effect when they log in.

Single Sign-On (SSO)
You can configure the Cohesity cluster to use an Identity Provider (IdP) for single sign-on (SSO) access to the cluster. For a multitenancy-enabled cluster, you can configure SSO for an organization defined in the cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

Important: If you are using SSO for authentication, Cohesity recommends that you enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) for your SSO system.
First, add the cluster as an application to your IdP and get an SSO URL and certificate file. Then configure the SSO in the cluster and provide the SSO URL and certificate file. After the integration is configured, users can sign in to the cluster using the following methods:
l Use the IdP sign-in page. l Use the Cohesity cluster sign-in page. Click the Sign in with SSO link at the bottom
of the cluster sign-in page.
Note: Cohesity supports any Identity Provider (Idp) as long as it uses SAML 2.0 based SSO. The Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) url and Entity ID for any IdP is https://cluster_fqdn/idps/authenticate.
Integrate an Identity Provider You have to integrate an identity provider to configure SSO. The following identity providers are supported and you can follow the documentation link to learn more about how to integrate it with the Cohesity.
Note: You can configure multiple Identity Providers (IDPs) when using Organizations. Each organization can have one IDP configured at the cluster level.

Identity Provider

Documentation Link

Active Directory Federation Services (ADFS) Integration with Active Directory Federation Services for SSO

Azure Active Directory

Integration with Azure Active Directory for SSO

Duo Single Sign-on

Integration with Duo for SSO

Ping Identity

Integration with Ping Identity for SSO

Okta Single Sign-on

Integration with Okta for SSO

Add an SSO Provider to the Cohesity cluster
1. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Access Management and select the SSO tab.
2. Click Add SSO.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

3. Select one of the following options:
l SAML: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an XML-based protocol used for SSO login.
l OpenID Connect: OpenID Connect is an open authentication protocol that uses OAuth2.0 framework.
4. If you select SAML, then refer to the following table:

Name

Description

SSO Domain

Your choice of domain name, such as abc.com. This name must be unique within the cluster.

SSO Provider

Your choice of provider name, such as Okta.

Assign to Organization

Optional. In a multitenant-enabled cluster, you can configure SSO for an organization that has been added to the Cohesity cluster. Select an organization from the drop-down.

Single Sign-on URL

Paste the URL that you copied from your IdP. For example: https://mycompany.okta.com/app/cohesitymycompany_clusterapp/******/sso/sam

Provider Issuer ID

Paste the issuer ID that you copied from your IdP. For example: http://okta.com/*****

X.509 Certificate

Click Select File and browse to the location to select the file you downloaded and renamed previously. For example, okta.pem. Select Edit to edit the certificate.

5. Click Add. If you select OpenID Connect (OIDC), perform the following steps and then refer to the table: Prerequisites: 1. Create the OIDC app within your Identity Provider (IdP). For more information, see Create OIDC app integrations.
Note: OIDC is an open standard and Single-Sign-On with Cohesity Platform is intended to work with any OpenID Connect supported Identity Provider. For setup details, refer to your Identity Provider's documentation.
2. Map the OIDC configuration details from Okta IDP to Cohesity Platform side configurations:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

1. To get the Issuer ID: 1. Navigate to Security > API. 2. On the API page, click Authorization Servers. You can find the issuer ID in the Issuer URI section.

2. To get the Client ID: 1. Navigate to Applications. 2. On the Helios Test OIDC App page, click General.
3. To generate the JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) URL: 1. Construct the URL as follows: Format: <issuer ID>/.well-known/openid-configuration For example: https://***00000000.okta.com/oauth2/default/.well-known/openidconfiguration. 2. Enter the constructed URL in the address bar of the browser and JSON output will be displayed.

Name

Description

OpenID Server Domain Enter a unique domain name.

OpenID Server URL for the public (JWKS)

Enter the JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) URL. You can get this URL from your identity provider.

Polling Interval (Hours) Specifies the caching duration for responses from the JWKS endpoint.

Audience IDs

Enter the IDs verified against the 'aud' field in the JWT. The 'aud' in the JWT must align with one of the strings listed in the Audience IDs field.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

Important: When enabling signed requests in Okta (or any SAML identity provider), you must explicitly set the following values:
l Signature Algorithm: RSA-SHA256 l Digest Algorithm: SHA256
6. Click Add.
Important: Make sure to add an SSO user before you add the SSO provider. For more information, see Add SSO Users.
The cluster validates the connection to the IdP. If the connection succeeds, the SSO provider is added to the provider list and you can edit, delete or deactivate it as described in the following sections. Active Directory (AD)
Active Directory (AD) in Cohesity Access Management is a directory service implemented by Microsoft that provides several services such as LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), Kerberos, and DNS. It is used for user and group identity management and authentication within a Cohesity cluster. You can join the Cohesity cluster to one or more Active Directory (AD) domains. Joining to AD allows the following:
l Existing AD users and groups can be assigned Cohesity roles l SMB shares created by the Cohesity cluster can be authenticated based on AD
credentials
Cohesity Roles
Once the Cohesity cluster is joined to an AD domain, existing AD principals can be added assigned different roles so they can access the Cohesity Dashboard. For example, you can assign the View role to the AD group "ITGroup." This gives all group members read-only access to the Cohesity Dashboard. You can also assign the Admin role to the AD user "ITManager."

numbered time squares: . The procedure assumes the Cohesity cluster is already joined to an Active Directory domain. Client access to an Active Directory-joined Cohesity cluster SMB share consists of the following actions:
T1) A client requests access to a Cohesity cluster SMB share. T2) The client attempts to perform an operation on the Cohesity cluster SMB share. T3) Active Directory authenticates the client's membership within a group that can
perform the requested operations on the Cohesity cluster SMB share.

Join Active Directory
This topic explains how to configure a Cohesity cluster to use Active Directory (AD) credentials for SMB access to views and to access the Cohesity Dashboard. (For information about protecting Active Directory domain controllers, see About Active Directory Data Protection.)
Joining the Cohesity cluster to an AD domain is optional. You can join the Cohesity cluster to one or more AD domains to enable:
l existing AD users can access Cohesity cluster SMB shares based on their AD credentials
l existing AD users and groups can be assigned Cohesity roles and access the Cohesity Dashboard
On Cohesity clusters that are not joined to AD, all views are accessible as SMB shares and there is no authentication. If the AD administrator blocks NTLM, the shares on the Cohesity cluster are not accessible.
All accounts and Cohesity cluster SMB share privileges for users in AD are managed through Active Directory or where the SMB shares are mounted. Non-admin AD users must be granted backup and restore privileges on Windows clients explicitly. This is in addition to backup and restore privileges for the Cohesity cluster.

Trusted Domains
After the Cohesity cluster joins the Active Directory domain, you can add trusted domains to the allowlist or denylist. By default, all trusted domains are used for authentication unless added to the denylist. You can add trusted domains to the allowlist so that only trusted domains added to the allowlist are used for authentication.
Note: If the domain controller is not functioning correctly, the discovery of trusted domains may take a relatively long period of time or may provide inconsistent results. Therefore, a trusted domain might not be discovered at all. You must manually enter such domains in the allowlist or denylist.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

A trusted domain forest can have multiple trusted domains. To provide optimized access, you can use a subset of trusted domains so that the Cohesity cluster does not send group membership queries to all trusted domains. You can choose a subset of trusted domains by using one of the following modes:
l Denylist--Ignores specified trusted domains. For example, if there are three trusted domains T1, T2, and T3 and if T2 is added to the denylist, T1 and T3 are the trusted domains used for authentication.
l Allowlist--Allows only specified trusted domains. For example, if there are three trusted domains T1, T2, and T3 and if T1 and T2 are added to the allowlist, T1 and T2 are the trusted domains used for authentication.

Click + to add another domain. Cohesity recommends adding at least one domain or switching to a denylist. 5. Click Save. The trusted domain is added to the allowlist.

One-Way Trust
A one-way trust is a unidirectional authentication path created between two AD domains. In a one-way trust, the trust relationship is only one way. The following is an illustration of one-way trust and the direction of access:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

As shown in the above figure:
l domain2.ad.local has a one-way trust with domain1.ad.local. domain1.ad.local does not have a trust relationship with domain2.ad.local. Users in domain2.ad.local can access resources in domain1.ad.local. However, users in domain1.ad.local cannot access resources in domain2.ad.local.
l domain3.ad.local has a one-way trust with domain2.ad.local. domain2.ad.local does not have a trust relationship with domain3.ad.local. Users in domain3.ad.local can access resources in domain2.ad.local. However, users in domain2.ad.local cannot access resources in domain3.ad.local.
In a one-way trust, the direction of trust is the opposite of the direction of access. An outgoing trust allows incoming access and an incoming trust allows outgoing access.
If one-way trust is enabled on the AD domain, trusted domains are listed in the following way in the Cohesity cluster:
l If the Cohesity cluster joins domain2.ad.local and if trusted domains are enabled:
l domain1.ad.local is displayed as a trusted domain because domain1.ad.local trusts domain2.ad.local

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

l domain3.ad.local is not displayed as a trusted domain because domain3.ad.local does not trust domain2.ad.local
l If the Cohesity cluster joins domain3.ad.local, both domain2.ad.local and domain1.ad.local are displayed as trusted domains because domain2.ad.local trusts domain3.ad.local and domain1.ad.local trusts domain2.ad.local.
l If the Cohesity cluster joins domain1.ad.local, no domain is displayed as a trusted domain because domain1.ad.local does not have a trust relationship with domain2.ad.local or domain3.ad.local.
Two-Way Trust
Two-way trust refers to the trust relationship between two domains where each domain trusts the other. Users and resources in both domains can access resources in the other domain. In a two-way trust relationship, authentication requests can flow in both directions, allowing users from one domain to access resources in another and vice versa without encountering authentication issues. For example, if domain A establishes a two-way trust with domain B, it implies that domain B reciprocally trusts domain A. As a result, both domains can seamlessly share resources.
Cohesity supports the following types of two-way trust:
l Parent-Child Trust
l Tree-Root Trust
Parent-Child Trust
A parent-child trust is a two-way, transitive trust relationship between a parent domain and its child domain within the same forest. The parent domain sits atop the forest and governs its child domains. A child domain is a subdomain established beneath its parent, inheriting policies and settings while also capable of possessing its distinct policies and objects.
This trust relationship facilitates seamless access for users, groups, and computers within the child domain to resources located in the parent domain, and vice versa. Tree-root trust is bi-directional as it allows authentication and authorization traffic to flow in both directions between the parent and child domains.
Tree-Root Trust
A tree-root trust is a two-way, transitive trust relationship automatically established between a new domain tree and the forest root domain when the tree is added to a forest. Users from any domain in the tree can access resources in the forest root domain and vice versa, without needing additional trust relationships. Tree-root trust is bi-directional as it allows authentication and authorization traffic to flow in both directions between the two forests.

Certificate-Based Authentication
If the Cohesity cluster is joined to an Active Directory domain, certificate-based authentication can be enabled for the Cluster, requiring users to sign in using a digital certificate instead of a user name and password. For added security, if you want to determine if the incoming certificate is from a trusted source, you must set up a trust store in the Cohesity cluster and add trusted root certificates to the trust store. For more information, see Trust Store in Cohesity Cluster. Prerequisites and Considerations
l The Cohesity cluster must be joined to an Active Directory domain. For more information, see Join Active Directory.
l Active Directory should have Certificate Services installed if you plan to use selfsigned certificates. For more information, see Install the Certification Authority.
l Each user must have a valid self-signed certificate or Authority-issued certificate in .pem format. The key resides on the user's computer.
l An AD user or group must be mapped to one or more Cohesity roles. For example, you might map the Administrators group to the Cohesity Admin role to grant users in the group Admin privileges in the Cohesity cluster. See the following procedure for details.
l If an AD user is defined in different AD groups and those groups are mapped to different Cohesity roles, the user will have the privileges for the combined roles on the Cluster.
To enable certificate-based authentication:
Note: Enabling or disabling certificate-based authentication automatically restarts the Cluster and signs out all users. The Cluster restart can take a several minutes to complete.
1. In Active Directory Certificate Services, map the certificates to users. 2. Make sure Cohesity users have access to their certificates so they can install them
when prompted to do so.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

3. Map each AD user or group to one or more Cohesity cluster roles: a. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Access Management. b. Click Add AD Users & Groups. c. Select Active Directory Users & Groups. d. Select a domain from the Active Directory Domain dropdown. e. Select a user or group from the User(s) or Group(s) dropdown. f. Select one or more roles for the group or user in the Roles dropdown. g. Click Add.
4. Enable certificate-based authentication for the Cohesity cluster: a. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Summary and click Configure. b. Toggle on Enable Certificate-based Authentication. c. Respond to the confirmation prompt.
You and other users will be automatically signed out of the Cluster when it restarts. After the Cluster restarts:
l Users defined in AD are prompted to install the certificate the first time they access the Cohesity Dashboard. Once the certificate is installed and the user is authenticated against AD, the Cohesity Dashboard is displayed (the user bypasses the sign-in prompt).
l Users who attempt to sign in with an invalid certificate will see a 403 forbidden error and message indicating that certificate authentication is enabled.
l Users who attempt to sign in with no certificate are presented with the sign-in prompt, but no AD domains are shown in the prompt.
l Local users (defined locally in the Cluster) can continue to sign in as usual with their user name and password.
To authenticate using the Cohesity CLI: If certificate-based authentication is enabled on the Cohesity cluster, users who want to use the Cohesity CLI must first authenticate to the Cluster by using the following command:
iris_cli --server=<ip address> -cert <absolute path to public key file> -key <absolute path to private key>
A sample command is shown below:
./iris_cli --server=192.0.2.3 -cert /a/b/c -key /a/b/c
The command options are:
l -server The IP address or hostname of the Cohesity cluster. l -cert The absolute file path for the public key file (.pem). l -key The absolute file path to the private key file (.key) that corresponds to the
certificate file.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

To change the authentication type via the Cohesity CLI: In addition to enabling and disabling certificate-based authentication in the Cohesity Dashboard, you can use the following Cohesity CLI command. Note that the Cluster must be restarted after changing authentication with the CLI command.
iris_cli cluster update authentication-type=<string>
Specify one of the following options for <string>:
l password-only Disables certificate-based authentication. All users must provide passwords to sign in.
l certificate-only Enables certificate-based authentication. Users defined in the joined AD domain must have certificates to sign in to the Cluster. Local users must provide passwords.
Certificate Mapping-Based Authentication
If the Cohesity cluster is joined to an Active Directory (AD) domain, Active Directory (AD) users can authenticate to the Cohesity cluster using certificate mapping-based authentication. In certificate mapping-based authentication, the AD user is authenticated based on the attribute mappings you have configured for the certificate and AD. In the Cohesity cluster, you can define the following attributes of the certificate and AD that must map for the user authentication:
l Certificate Attributes: l CommonName l EmailAddress l UserPrincipalName
l Active Directory Attributes: l SamAccountName l UserPrincipalName
Configure the Authentication Attributes
In the Cohesity cluster, you can define the certificate and AD attributes that must map for user authentication. To configure the authentication attributes:
1. Start the Cohesity CLI remotely or locally as described in the Cohesity CLI Reference Guide. Specify the static IPv4 or IPv6 address of one of the Cohesity nodes. For example, if the CLI was downloaded to a Linux system, you might use the following command. Provide a Cohesity cluster username and password.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

./iris_cli -server 172.16.3.101 -username=admin
2. To define the certificate and AD attributes that must map for user authentication, run the following command:
iris_cli security-config update ad-mapping=<AD_attributes> certificatemapping=<cert_attributes>
Where: l <AD_attributes> - Any one of the following AD attributes: l SamAccountName l UserPrincipalName l <cert_attributes> - Any one of the following certificate attributes: l CommonName l EmailAddress l UserPrincipalName
Sample:
iris_cli security-config update ad-mapping=UserPrincipalName certificate-mapping=EmailAddress
Enable Certificate Mapping-Based Authentication
In the Cohesity cluster, you can enable certificate mapping-based authentication using the Cohesity CLI. To enable certificate mapping-based authentication:
1. Start the Cohesity CLI remotely or locally as described in the Cohesity CLI Reference Guide. Specify the static IPv4 or IPv6 address of one of the Cohesity nodes. For example, if the CLI was downloaded to a Linux system, you might use the following command. Provide a Cohesity cluster username and password.
./iris_cli -server 172.16.3.101 -username=admin
2. To enable certificate mapping-based authentication, run the following command:
iris_cli security-config update enable-mapping-based-auth=true
The AD users are now authenticated to the Cohesity cluster using certificate mapping-based authentication. For added security, if you want to determine if the incoming certificate is from a trusted source, you must set up a trust store in the Cohesity cluster and add trusted root certificates to the trust store. For more information, see Trust Store in Cohesity Cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

Trust Store in Cohesity Cluster
Note: This is an Early Access feature. Contact your Cohesity account team to enable the feature.
For security purposes, you can set up a trust store in the Cohesity cluster and add trusted root certificates or certificate authority (CA) to the trust store. If the incoming certificate forms a valid certificate chain with at least one of the trust store certificates, then the incoming certificate is determined to be from a trusted source. Once the AD users are authenticated using certificate mapping-based authentication and the digital certificate is determined to be from a trusted source, the AD user can log into the Cohesity cluster.
Set Up Trust Store
You can set up a trust store in the Cohesity cluster using the Cohesity CLI.
Prerequisites
Ensure that: l The certificate is in PEM format. l You copy the certificate to the Cohesity cluster.
To set up a trust store: 1. Start the Cohesity CLI remotely or locally as described in the Cohesity CLI Reference Guide. Specify the static IPv4 or IPv6 address of one of the Cohesity nodes. For example, if the CLI was downloaded to a Linux system, you might use the following command. Provide a Cohesity cluster username and password. ./iris_cli -server 172.16.3.101 -username=admin
2. Validate the certificate. Run the following command: iris_cli trusted-cas register name=rootCert desc=testing filepath=rootCert.pem only-validate=true
3. If the certificate is valid, add the certificate to the trust store. Run the following command: iris_cli trusted-cas register name=rootCert desc=testing filepath=rootCert.pem
4. You can view the added certificates to the trust store using the following command: iris_cli trusted-cas ls

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

5. Enable the feature that validates if the incoming certificate forms a valid certificate chain. Cohesity Support to enable the feature.
6. If you have not enabled certificate-based authentication or certificate mapping-based authentication on the Cohesity cluster, enable it. For more information, see Certificate-Based Authentication or Certificate Mapping-Based Authentication.
The AD users are now authenticated to the Cohesity cluster based on the type of authentication you have configured, such as certificate-based authentication or certificate mapping-based authentication. And, the user can log in to the Cohesity cluster using only the trusted certificates. Kerberos Cohesity supports Kerberos authentication using both NFSv3.0 and NFSv4.1. Kerberos prevents unauthorized users from accessing Cohesity NFS exports. Kerberos is a network authentication protocol that allows users to securely access services over a physically insecure network. Kerberos has three parts:
l Client l Server l Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) - KDC mediates between client and server. Clients obtain tickets from the Kerberos Key Distribution Center(KDC), and they present these tickets to servers when connections are established. For more information, see Kerberos.
Supported Kerberos Flavors
Cohesity supports the following two flavors of Kerberos: l Microsoft AD Kerberos l MIT Kerberos
Kerberos Terminology
Realm A network that uses Kerberos, composed of one or more servers called KDCs and a potentially large number of clients. Key Distribution Center (KDC) A service that issues Kerberos tickets, usually run on the same host as the Ticket Granting Server.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 4: Cluster Administration

Access Management

Ticket Granting Service (TGS) A server that issues tickets for the desired service which are in turn given to users for access to the service. The TGS usually runs on the same host as the KDC. Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) A special ticket that allows the client to obtain additional tickets without applying for them from the KDC. Principal A user or service that can authenticate using Kerberos. A principal's name is in the form root [/instance]@REALM. For a typical user, the root is the same as their login ID. The instance is optional. If the principal has an instance, it is separated from the root with a forward slash ("/"). An empty string ("") is considered a valid instance (which differs from the default NULL instance), but using it can be confusing. All principals in a realm have their own key, which is derived from their password or randomly set for services. For more information on Service Principal Name and Host Principal Name, see Service Principal Names. Client An entity on the network (a user, a host, or an application) that can get a ticket from Kerberos.
Microsoft AD Kerberos
Kerberos is the authentication service in Microsoft Active Directory.
