Customize Indexing

By default, the root directory (/) is included and entire file system is indexed. When a directory is indexed, its sub-directories are also indexed. You can limit indexing to a specific set of files and directories to minimize the disk space used by the index. For example, you could add two additional rules to the first default rule:
l include / l exclude /var l include /var/log
In this example, all files in the / root directory are indexed except the files found in the /var directory. However, the files in the /var/log are indexed because there is an explicit include rule. Include and Exclude Rules:
l Use forward slashes (/) for both Windows and Unix as the separator character. l Do not specify the drive letter and colon in front of the directory path for Windows. l Drive letters are allowed for Windows systems to limit the drives searched for a
specified path. l If no drive is specified then all drives for which the path is found are indexed.

Examples /C/Users /Users /var/log

Description
On Windows, include or exclude Users directory in C:\Users
On Windows, include or exclude Users directories in all drives, i.e. C:\Users, D:\Users.
On Linux or Unix, include or exclude /var/log directory.

The default directory inclusion/exclusion list are as follows: l include / l exclude /$Recycle.Bin l exclude /Windows l exclude /Program Files l exclude /Program Files (x86) l exclude /ProgramData l exclude /System Volume Information

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 8: Manage Protection Policy

Configure Pre & Post Scripts

l exclude /Users/*/AppData l exclude /Recovery l exclude /var l exclude /usr l exclude /sys l exclude /proc l exclude /lib l exclude /grub l exclude /grub2 l exclude /opt/splunk l exclude /splunk
Excluding Pseudo Filesystems from Indexing
In a Linux operating system, specific filesystems, such as /sys, /proc, /dev, /run, /tmp, /dev/pts, and /dev/shm, are dynamically generated by the kernel during system boot. These filesystems are commonly referred to as 'pseudo filesystems' or 'virtual filesystems.' Their contents are unique to the system and temporary, meaning they do not persist beyond system reboots. Due to their transient nature, Cohesity does not recommend indexing these pseudo filesystems. Attempting to index them not only lacks practical utility but may also result in inaccurate or inconsistent indexing outcomes.

Configure Scripts for Sources with Agent Installed
Out of the supported sources for pre and post-scripts, physical servers and databases require Cohesity Agent to be installed on the source. Following are the settings required for configuring the pre and post scripts for sources with Agent installed:
Pre-Script
l Script Path: Depending on the agents, specify the full path or name of the script as mentioned in the Note section below. A script matching the specified name must be available in the user_scripts directory found in the agent installation directory on the protected server. (See the table below for details about the directory path.) The script can be in any format, for example: shell script, batch file, executable (.exe), etc. The script must be configured with the permissions to allow execution (+x).
Note: l For Physical servers, MS SQL server and Oracle, only the script name is required (provided the script is available in the user_ scripts directory found in the agent installation directory).
l For NAS and SAN sources, the absolute/full path to the script is required.
l On Windows platforms, PowerShell, Python, or Perl scripts (any script that is not a .exe file) must be embedded within a .bat script before they are called.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 8: Manage Protection Policy

Configure Pre & Post Scripts

Important: Cohesity does not validate the content of the script and is not responsible for the content of the script or any actions done by the script. You must verify the script actions before a script or executable is run.
l Script Params: Optional field for passing one or more parameters to the script. All specified parameter values are passed as a single string to the script.
l Timeout: Optional field for specifying how long a script is allowed to execute before the Cohesity cluster stops the execution of the script. By default, the timeout is 15 minutes. If no value is specified, there is no timeout and the script is not stopped. This can cause a protection run to hang if the script never completes. The timeout is applied from the moment the script starts. For example, if the timeout is set to 15 minutes but the script takes 20 minutes to complete, it will be stopped after 15 minutes. Therefore, users should set the timeout based on the expected runtime of the script to avoid premature termination.
l Continue Backup if script fails: This toggle applies only to Pre-Scripts and is enabled by default. When this toggle is enabled, the Protection Group backs up the objects even if the Pre-Script fails. If this toggle is disabled and the Pre-Script fails, the backup is canceled but the Post-Script still runs.

l Script Path: Depending on the agents, specify the full path or name of the script as mentioned in the Note section below. DataLock
DataLock is the Cohesity WORM (write once read many) feature that locks and retains files for compliance and regulatory purposes and to protect the files from accidental deletion.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 8: Manage Protection Policy

DataLock

DataLock enables your storage to be WORM-compliant to ensure the snapshot is not aged prematurely. When it is enabled, your data such as backups and archives cannot be deleted by anyone, including administrators, until the DataLock expires. This retention lock helps to prevent ransomware attacks on your clusters.
Note: The contents of backups cannot be modified because of Cohesity SpanFS's immutable file system design.

The Cohesity Dashboard displays a lock ( snapshots.

) icon to indicate DataLocked policies and

Features of DataLock
l You can apply DataLock for each schedule (such as backup, extended retention, archive, and replication) defined in the Protection Policy.
l You can specify DataLock duration in days, weeks, months, or years for each schedule defined in the Protection Policy.

Considerations
l The DataLock expiry date is set at the time of snapshot creation and does not change afterward.
l Extending snapshot retention--whether for runs created before or after the change--does not extend the DataLock expiry.
l Modifying snapshot retention after creation does not alter the originally configured DataLock expiration.
l Using DataLock with longer snapshot retention periods and for auto-protected sources can result in the cluster running out of space.
l DataLock retention must be less than or equal to backup retention.

Snapshots selected for extended retention are retained for a longer time than defined in the protection schedule. You can retain the first snapshot of the backup run taken on the specified hours, every run, days, weeks, months, or years for a longer period of time.

7:00PM (Day 3) - The snapshot captured is retained for an extended period of 28 days.
7.00PM (Day 4) - The snapshot captured is retained for 14 days.

The first snapshot captured during the specified week is retained for the number of days as mentioned in the extended retention policy. Every subsequent snapshot captured is retained for the number of days specified in the backup policy.

Define a backup policy that captures every day and retains it for 14 days. Specify an extended retention policy to capture the first snapshot taken every week and retain the snapshot for 28 days.
Assuming the week starts on Sunday:
Week 1, Sunday 6:30PM - The snapshot captured is retained for 28 days.
Week 2, Sunday 6:30PM - The snapshot captured is retained for 28 days.

You can create one or more extended schedules. For example, you could define a protection schedule that captures snapshots every hour and retains them on the Cohesity cluster for 1 day. This protection schedule retains 24 sets of snapshots on a rotating basis, each hour a new set of snapshots are retained and the oldest set of snapshots is deleted. If you want to retain a subset of these snapshots for a longer period of time, you could define an additional extended retention schedule to retain a single subset of snapshots daily for 90 days. This extended retention schedule retains 90 sets of snapshots on a rotating basis, each day a new set of snapshots are retained and the oldest set of snapshots is deleted.
Note: If you specify multiple extended retention rules for the same set of snapshots with different retention periods, the snapshots are retained for the longest specified time period. For example if you define two extended retention rules that retain the same set of snapshots but one rule specifies a retention period of 90 days and another specifies a retention period of 180 days, the set of snapshots are retained for 180 days.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 8: Manage Protection Policy

Extended Retention

The extended retention schedule for backups is based on calendar-based scheduling for weekly, monthly, and yearly. For archive, replication, and CloudSpin; the extended retention schedule is as follows:
l Weekly: The first successful run that started on a Sunday or later. l Monthly: The first successful run that started on the first day of the month or later. l Yearly: The first successful run that started on the first day of the year or later.
For backup schedule, Cohesity allows you to set the day for weekly backup and any day of the week for monthly backup.
Note: If a backup fails, the extended retention is applied to the next scheduled snapshot taken by the Cohesity cluster. However, if a manual backup was run in place of the failed backup after selecting "all objects" when selecting the VMs, extended retention is applied to the manual snapshot. For example, you've set the extended retention to be applied on the first snapshot on the first of every month. The scheduled backup on Feb 1st fails. After selecting all the objects (VMs), you run a manual backup successfully. The extended retention is applied to the snapshot of the manual backup.

SmartFiles (File and Object Services) Overview

SmartFiles (File and Object Services) Overview
Cohesity SmartFiles is an enterprise-class, software-defined, data-centric, multiprotocol file and object solution for the enterprise that transcends traditional offerings in terms of manageability, scale, security, efficiency and multi-tiered data management. SmartFiles modernizes and simplifies data and application management by providing one platform for multiple workloads. It is a modern converged target for consolidating data silos and securely managing unstructured content and application data, including digital libraries, archives, rich media, video surveillance, big data, and backup data sets.
You can use Cohesity file and object services for the following use cases:
l Backup targets--Store backups from other products, such as Veeam. Reduce storage requirements with automatic deduplication and compression.
l Home directories--Create personal folders for Windows and Linux users. Use ID mapping to ensure consistent access control. Establish view user quotas and block certain file types. Create share aliases to simplify access.
l Corporate file shares-- Store, access and share company files and documents. Lock and retain files for compliance and regulatory purposes.
l Video and image stores--Stream videos and store images of virtually any file size. l Archiving and tiering--Archive infrequently used data to public clouds for long-
term retention. Use cloud tiering for seamless capacity expansion into the cloud. Replicate into the cloud for disaster recovery and test/dev operations. l PACS images--Store digital medical images for compliance and disaster recovery purposes. Use built-in antivirus software to protect against any viruses and ransomware. Lock and retain files for HIPAA compliance. l AWS S3 integration--Use Cohesity cluster instead of S3 buckets.
Key Components
SmartFiles uses the following Cohesity cluster components:
l Storage domains--A named storage location on a cluster. When a cluster is created, it contains a default storage domain. You can create additional storage domains and customize them for the intended use case.
When you create a storage domain, you define its options, including deduplication, compression, encryption, quotas, fault tolerance and erasure coding. Storage domains contain views.
l Views--A named storage location in a storage domain used for storing user data such as files, backup snapshots, objects and cloned VMs.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

SmartFiles (File and Object Services) Overview

When you create a view, it inherits some options, like deduplication and compression, from its storage domain, but you can override them. You also define attributes such as access protocols, a Quality of Service policy, security settings, quotas, WORM (DataLock), file filtering and more. Views are automatically assigned protocol-specific mount paths so they can be used as NFS exports and SMB shares. Before a client system can mount a view, the client system's subnet must be added to the allowlist in the Cohesity cluster. l Allowlists--Lists of subnets. Systems with IP addresses in those subnets can mount and access views. The Cohesity cluster supports global, view-level and share-level allowlists.
Supported Access Protocols
SmartFiles supports the following protocols for accessing views from client systems:
l NFS 3.0 and NFS 4.1--Mount a View Using NFS l SMB 3.0 and SMB 2.x--Mount a View Using SMB l AWS S3--Objects (S3)
Optimize for the Use Case
You can and should configure storage domains and views for the expected use case. For example, the data stored in a view can be written to faster SSD storage or slower, less expensive HDD storage, depending on the use case. The view's Quality of Service (QoS) policy determines the type of storage used and the latency factor in writing data to the view. The following use cases demonstrate why you might choose one QoS over another.
l Videos--Let's say you plan to store surveillance videos from security cameras that are continually streaming videos to a view. This workload entails sequential writes (recording the video) and sequential reads (video playback). Because this workload is not latency-sensitive, the data can be written to slower HDD storage. You can accomplish this by configuring the view with the appropriate QoS policy. In this case, you would use one of the Backup Target QoS policies.
l Home directories--Let's say you plan to set up home directories for university students to store their work in. This workload entails random reads and writes. Because this workload is latency-sensitive (students are actively accessing their work), the data should be written to faster SSD storage. In this case, you would use one of the TestAndDev QoS policies.

Fundamentals of SmartFiles
The following topics introduce you to key file and object services concepts:
About Deduplication
Deduplication eliminates redundant copies of data to reduce storage usage on the Cohesity cluster. Redundant data blocks are replaced with a pointer to the unique data copy, which ensures that only unique instances of data are transferred over the network and retained on storage media. When you create a storage domain, you choose one of the following options:
l Inline deduplication: Data is deduplicated as it is written to the Cohesity cluster. Generally, Cohesity recommends inline deduplication. It is the default when creating a storage domain.
l Post-process deduplication: Data is deduplicated after it is written to the Cohesity cluster, which can improve the speed of I/O operations.
l No deduplication: Data is not deduplicated at all. You may want to disable deduplication if access speed is more important than conserving disk space, or if you are storing data that has already been deduplicated by another product.
Storage domains contain user-created views. The views inherit the deduplication setting from the storage domain. If inline deduplication is enabled for the storage domain, you can override it and always use post-process deduplication for the view.
Tip: If the expected workload for a view is latency sensitive, Cohesity recommends post-process deduplication because it improves the speed of I/O operations to the view.
For more information about deduplication, see the white paper Cohesity Fault Tolerance -- Data Integrity for Modern Web Scale Environments.
QoS Policies for Cohesity Views
You can assign a QoS policy to a view. A Cohesity view provides a storage location with NFS, SMB, and S3 mount paths in a storage domain on the Cohesity cluster. A QoS policy optimizes the view's performance in terms of throughput, IOPS, and latency for different workloads. The policies also let you prioritize I/O operations for certain views above others.

There are two basic QoS policies, Test And Dev and Backup Target, and each has variants by storage media and priority.

QoS Policy
Test And Dev
Backup Target

Optimized for I/O Workload Type

Priority

Mixed I/O workloads such as file shares. Best for writes and sequential single stream reads and writes. Recommended for Cohesity SmartFiles.

High Low

Best for sequential, multi-stream reads and writes. Recommended for Cohesity DataProtect and Cohesity Archive. Recommended for Cohesity SmartFiles when used as a backup target.

SSD High Low

Be sure to select an appropriate QoS policy for the view. By specifying a priority and the type of workload you expect, the Cohesity cluster can optimize how it processes data in regard to latency, throughput, and priority.
The following table lists the QoS policies in the decreasing order of QoS priority.

QoS Policy

Description

Journaled Sequential Dump

Use this policy for workloads that write large amounts of data sequentially to a very small number of files and do not keep many I/Os outstanding. By default data is written to the SSD and has the highest priority and low latency.

TestAndDev High

Use this policy for workloads that require lower I/O latency or do not keep many I/Os outstanding, as the I/Os are given higher priority compared to other QoS policies. Data is written to the SSD.

TestAndDev Low

The same as TestAndDev High, except that the I/Os with this QoS policy are given lower priority compared to I/Os with TestAndDev High when there is contention.

Backup Target CommVault

Use this policy to intelligently detect and exclude application-specific markers to achieve better deduplication when CommVault backup application is writing to a Cohesity View. Data is written to SSD and has the same priority and latency as TestAndDev High.

Backup Target Auto

(Applicable only for Cohesity C6000 series) Use this policy for workloads such as backups, which keep many I/Os outstanding. This policy distributes I/Os across SSDs and HDDs to achieve maximum performance based on the current usage. The priority for processing workload with this policy is lower than Journaled Sequential Dump, TestAndDev High, and Backup Target CommVault.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Fundamentals of SmartFiles

QoS Policy

Description

Backup Target SSD

Use this policy for workloads such as backups, which keep many I/Os outstanding, but in this case, Cohesity sends both sequential and random I/Os to SSD. The latency is lower than other Backup Target policies.The priority for processing workload with this policy is the same as Backup Target Auto.

Backup Target High

Use this policy for non-latency sensitive workloads such as backups, which keep many I/Os outstanding. Data is written to HDD and has higher latency compared to other QoS policies writing to a SSD The priority for processing workload with this policy is the same as Backup Target Auto.

Backup Target Low

The same as Backup Target High, except that the priority for processing workloads with this policy is lower than workloads with Backup Target Auto / High /SSD when there is contention.

Cohesity allows you to pin views to the SSD tier. For more information, see Pin Views to SSD.
In hybrid nodes that have both SSDs and HDDs, QoS policies use the storage media differently to optimize performance and life of the media. Many factors such as I/O block size and I/O pattern are considered. In general, Test And Dev uses SSDs for accelerating overall write performance. Backup Target often reads and writes directly from HDDs. For sequential reads, all QoS policies prefetch data intelligently into RAM and/or SSDs.

ID Mapping for Multi-Protocol Views
ID mapping maps Unix and Windows identifiers to provide consistent access control to files on shared storage, such as Cohesity views. Specifically, the Unix user and group IDs (UIDs/GIDs) are mapped to Windows user and group Security Identifiers (SIDs).
Tip: ID mapping is used only for views that support both the NFS (Unix) and SMB (Windows) protocols and that have the Security Style set to either Unified or NTFS, as described later in this topic. ID mapping is irrelevant to views that support just one protocol.
You can use your organization's existing ID mapping in an external server or configure the Cohesity cluster to maintain internal ID mapping, as described in the following sections.
External Server ID Mapping
If the Cohesity cluster is joined to an Active Directory (AD) domain controller and your organization has existing ID mapping on any of the following servers, you can configure the Cohesity cluster to use that mapping for access to multi-protocol views. The administrator of the external server maintains the ID mapping.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Fundamentals of SmartFiles

l RFC2307 within AD l SFU within AD l Centrify l LDAP
You can also configure fallback mapping in case the external server is not available.
Internal ID Mapping
If the Cohesity cluster is joined to AD but your organization does not have an existing ID map, you can still configure the Cohesity cluster to use one of the following basic mapping types. The ID mapping will be stored internally on the Cohesity cluster.
l Fixed - A user-defined UID and GID are applied to all files created on the view. l RID - The relative ID of the SID is used as the UID or GID.
Required Configuration for ID Mapping
To use ID mapping, do following in the Cohesity Dashboard:
l Configure a mapping type for the AD domain controller(s) on the Active Directory page. For more information, see Join Active Directory.

l Configure the following options for multi-protocol views. For information, see Create Views Using a Predefined Template.
l Read/Write Protocol must be set to the required protocol (NFS, NFS v4.1 or SMB).

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Fundamentals of SmartFiles

Optionally S3 access is selected. It is the default Read-Only Protocol. You can disable the access if you need it. ID mapping is irrelevant if Read/Write Protocol or Read-Only Protocol is set to NFS only, SMB only or S3 only. l Security Style must be set to Unified or NTFS. Unified means that Unix and Windows permissions are kept consistent; when one is changed, the other is automatically changed. NTFS means that access via SMB and NFS is controlled by the Windows ACL on the file/folder. ID mapping is irrelevant if Security Style is set to Native.
User and Directory Quotas for Views
In addition to the storage domain quotas, you can enable user quotas and/or directory quotas at the view level.
User Quotas
User quotas limit how much view capacity a user can use. After a view is created, you can set a default quota for all users and override the default for individual users.
Note: If the view is used through both NFS and SMB, Cohesity strongly recommends using ID mapping to ensure accurate quota accounting. For more information, see ID Mapping for Multi-Protocol Views.
When a user reaches 85% of the quota, an alert (UserExceededQuotaAlertLimit) is triggered in the Cohesity cluster. If email notifications are configured for alerts, emails are also sent. To know more information, you can use the User Quotas. Individual users will also receive an email if the Cohesity cluster joins an Active Directory domain and the user's email address is defined in the AD. NFS users will receive an email if they are mapped to an AD user whose email address is defined in the AD. Alert emails are sent to the addresses specified in the notification rule. AD users who wish to receive these emails must configure their email addresses in the notification rule. For more information about configuring alert notifications, see Configure Alert Notification Settings. When the user reaches 100% of the quota, the (UsersExceededQuota) alert is triggered and the user cannot use additional capacity in the view until they reduce their usage or the quota is increased. To enable user quotas:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Fundamentals of SmartFiles

1. Navigate to SmartFiles > Views. 2. On the Views page, click on a view name to navigate to the corresponding view
details page. 3. Click the Quotas tab.
4. In the User Quotas section, turn on the Enable toggle. The default logical quota for all users and the alert threshold are displayed.
5. To change the default quota for all users, click the edit icon, select different values and click Save.
6. To override the default quota for an individual user:
a. Click Add. b. In the Add User Quota Override dialog, select a local user, AD domain, or
Unix user ID from the Principal drop-down.
If the view's storage domain is mapped to an AD domain, you can select only that AD domain and its trusted domains.
c. Enter an AD user or a Unix ID. d. Select different values for the Quota Override. e. Click Add. f. Repeat these steps to add additional user quota overrides.
You can also use the iris_cli user-quotas commands to manage user quotas. For example, you can change the default 85% alert threshold. For more information, see Using the Cohesity CLI and List of Cohesity CLI Commands.
Directory Quotas
Directory quotas limit the capacity of directories in a view. You can set different quotas for different directories. For example, you can set a quota on the parent directory /home/sales, and set different quotas on the sub-directories /home/sales/kane and /home/sales/reynolds.
If a quota is set on a parent directory, the data usage in any of its nested sub-directories contributes to the quota for the parent. So if the data usage for /kane is 20 GiB and /reynolds is 10 GiB, they contribute 30 GiB to the quota set for /home/sales.
If the view is replicated to another Cohesity cluster, the directory quotas are available on that Cohesity cluster.
When a directory reaches the alert threshold (by default, 90% of its quota), the DirectoriesExceededQuota alert is triggered in the Cohesity cluster but data can still be written to the directory.
When the directory reaches 100% of its quota, the DirectoryExceededQuotaAlertLimit alert is triggered and data cannot be written to the directory until files are deleted or the quota is increased.
If email notifications are configured for alerts, emails are also sent.

l After enabling the quota for a directory experiencing high IOPS, it is important to allow the current storage usage to be calculated before accessing the directory again. This allows the quota settings to be accurately applied and ensures proper management of storage usage within the directory.

File-level DataLock for NFS and SMB Views
DataLock is the Cohesity WORM (write once read many) feature that locks and retains files in a view for compliance and regulatory purposes.
This topic describes the file-level DataLock setting, which differs from the view-level DataLock setting available when cloning a view.
When you create a view, you can enable the File DataLock setting to make the files in the view immutable based on the following settings:
l whether files are automatically locked after a specified period of I/O inactivity, based on the last modified time stamp
l whether files are manually locked when users or applications change the file permissions to read only or change the last accessed time, for example, by using the following Linux and Windows commands.
Using NFS:
chmod -w <filename>

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Fundamentals of SmartFiles

touch -at YYYYMMDDhhmm.ss <filename>
Using SMB, from PowerShell:
# (dir filename).Attributes = "ReadOnly"
# (dir filename).LastAccessTime = "YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss"
In addition to file system locking, the Cohesity REST API can be used to lock files, update time stamps and get file lock status. Contact your Cohesity account team for details on the REST API. You can also set: l a default retention period for locked files l an overriding lock expiration date for files For more information about the File DataLock settings, see File DataLock. If File DataLock is enabled for a view, the files in the view are in one of the following states: unlocked, locked or lock expired. The following table lists the actions permitted for each state.

Permitted Action Unlocked

Change the file

yes

Delete the file

yes

Locked no no

Lock Expired no yes

Note: The File DataLock option is only applicable for NFS and SMB View types.

Snapshot Self-Service
The Snapshots Self Service option enables the users to retrieve files and folders from the backup snapshots without depending on the administrator for retrieval.
You can enable the snapshot self-service for Views supporting SMB/NFS protocols when creating or editing a View. For more information, see Create Views Using a Predefined Template.
When you enable the Self-service option on a View, a hidden snapshot directory is created and the backup snapshots are listed in the hidden directory.
Using the snapshots from the hidden snapshot directory, users can copy/restore the files or folders that may have been deleted accidentally or corrupted.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Fundamentals of SmartFiles

Note: The Self-service option applies to the Views that are protected. You can set the Snapshot Self-service option on Views without protection job enabled. However, the snapshots directory will be empty without the backup snapshots.
For NFS and SMB Views, you need to enable the Enable Snapshot Directory option. When you enable the option with default settings, a .snapshot directory is created for NFS Views, and ~snapshot directory is created for SMB Views. You can customize the Snapshot directory name for NFS and SMB. NFS users/clients can access the .snapshot directory and SMB users/clients can access the ~snapshot directory and copy the required files or folders. For NFS Views, the .snapshot directory may not be visible on the Linux server after being mounted. To navigate to the .snapshot directory, run the cd .snapshot command inside the mount path. The snapshot retention period in the protected views depends on the protection policy.
Note: When you are using a name of your choice for the snapshot directory name, ensure that it is a unique name. If the name of the snapshot directory is the same as one of the folders in your View, you will not be able to see the backup snapshots.
Show Previous Versions The Show Previous Versions option is available for SMB Views. This is another option to restore files and folders.
Note: When you upgrade from any previous versions to Cohesity 6.6 or later, by default, the Show Previous versions option is enabled with access to Everyone.

required files or folders. Restoring Files or Folders from Previous Versions via SMB To restore a file or folder:

Cohesity Views
A Cohesity view provides a storage location with NFS, SMB, and S3 mount paths in a storage domain on the Cohesity cluster. You can use the NFS protocol to mount the NFS mount path onto systems. You can mount the SMB mount path onto systems as an SMB share. You can use the view to store data such as files, backup snapshots, and cloned VMs. Views can only be mounted on any machines specified in the allowlist subnets. A view can also act as a datastore during the VM cloning process and during VM recovery. You can select the SWIFT protocol and a create SWIFT-only view for OpenStack environments. You can create a view for the following three categories:
l File Shares l Backup Target l Object Services You can select the Read/Write protocol and, optionally, select the Read-only protocol. You can create a Cohesity view only by using a template. The template can be a predefined template or a custom template. For more information, see: l Create Views Using a Predefined Template l Create Views Using a Custom Template
Note: If you are using Kerberos (AD or MIT), you must create a view using the same storage domain that is mapped to AD/MIT-Kerberos + LDAP.
Navigate to the SmartFiles > Views page to perform the following actions: l Create views using a predefined template or custom template. l Create custom view templates. l Manage share aliases--View and manage Cohesity-created shares and any usercreated shares on the Shares tab. For more information, see Manage Share Aliases. l Configure global settings--Enable Active Directory authentication for SMB shares.

Glance Bar
The glance bar provides a summary of the views:

The following details are displayed:
l Total--The total number of views.
l Protected
l The number of views taking snapshots.
l The number of views replicating data out of the cluster.
l The number of views replicating data into the cluster.
l Consumption
l Logical--Size of total unique logical data of active file system as residing on Cohesity. This does not count the space consumed by the Data Protection runs (i.e. snapshots) that may be protecting the active file system.
l Data Reduction--The ratio of Data In to Data Written. This ratio reflects the data deduplication and data compression operations, and demonstrates the true power and value of the Cohesity.
l Physical--This number reflects unique data written, before resiliency operations. This is the unique logical data has been reduced by data deduplication and data compression by Cohesity.
l Resiliency Impact--The space required to honor resiliency settings (Erasure Coding / Replication Factor) in addition to the data written. For example, if the Data Written is 100 GB and resiliency setting is RF3, the Resiliency Impact is 200 GB. That is, to honor the resiliency setting, you will need an additional 200 GB on top of the 100 GB for the Data Written.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

l Storage Consumed--The total size of data stored on the Cohesity file system after all operations on the data (data deduplication, data compression, and data resiliency) have been accounted for. This data can be stored either all locally or as a combination of local storage and in the Cloud Tier (if Cloud Tier is enabled). For example, if the Data Written is 100 GB and resiliency is set to RF3, leading to the need for an additional 200 GB of space, the resulting Storage Consumed is 300 GB. If the Data Written is 100 GB and resiliency is set to EC4:2, leading to the need for an additional 50 GB (as for every 4 data fragments, 2 parity fragments are added), the resulting storage consumed is 150 GB.

Storage Lifecycle Management Rules You can reduce storage space utilization by managing the file timestamp attributes. You can define criteria for identifying aging files and specify actions to take upon meeting these conditions. By automating the deletion of aged files, storage lifecycle management ensures optimal performance and resource utilization, enabling you to reclaim valuable storage space.
Important: Cohesity strongly recommends enabling File Services audit logs on Views on which storage lifecycle management is enabled.
Click No Lifecycle rules have been added yet and click Add Rule:

In the Add Storage Lifecycle Management Rule dialog, do the following:
l Name--Enter a name for the rule. l Type--Select one of the following:
l Allow Rule--Files matching this rule are deleted. l Deny Rule--Files matching this rule are excluded from storage lifecycle
management, even if the files match other rules. l Scope--Select one of the following:
l Select the Apply to all files in the View option to apply this storage lifecycle management rule on every file within the View.
l Select the Limit the scope of this rule using filters option to limit the scope by using the following filters: l Filter by File Extension--Enter the file extension. For example, you can enter .pdf to restrict the scope to only PDFs stored in the View. l Filter by Minimum File Size--Specify the minimum file size limit. l Filter by Maximum File Size--Specify the maximum file size limit.
l Aging Policy--Select one of the following: l Number of Days--Specify the number of days. l Date--Select a date. l None--If you have selected the type as Deny Rule, choosing None ensures that the aging policy is not applied to the deny rule.
To calculate aging, you can select Last Modification Time or Creation Time. l Creation Time--Refers to the timestamp when a file is initially created and saved to the storage medium. l Last Modification Time--Refers to the most recent timestamp when a file's data was modified. This timestamp updates whenever you modify the data in the file.
All the rules added are listed in the Storage Lifecycle Management Rules section.

Important Points to Note
l When specifying file extensions, make sure to include the period (.) before the extension. For example, use ".pdf" instead of just "pdf".
l Regardless of the sensitivity of the View, file extensions are treated as caseinsensitive and are handled the same way. For example, if a case-sensitive View contains files named f1.pdf, f2.PDF, and f3.Pdf, and a rule specifies to preserve only ".pDf" files, then all three files (f1.pdf, f2.PDF, and f3.Pdf) will be preserved.
l If a file meets the criteria for deletion based on a storage lifecycle management rule while it is open, the system still proceeds with deleting the file.
l Cohesity strongly recommends backing up Views on which storage lifecycle management is enabled. If any files are unintentionally deleted, you can recover them from the backup.
l The system honors File DataLock settings and storage lifecycle management rules are only applied to files that are not locked.
l If you replicate a View that includes storage lifecycle management rules, the rules are disabled since the View is read-only on the remote cluster. If you intend to use this View by cloning it, note that the storage lifecycle management rules will be present, but you must manually enable them on the View.
Note: If the remote cluster does not support Storage Lifecycle Management, the storage lifecycle management rules are not replicated to the remote cluster.
l When you archive and subsequently restore a View, the storage lifecycle management rules are not restored along with the View.
l When you clone a View, the storage lifecycle management rules associated with that View are also cloned and lifecycle actions are executed on this cloned View according to the rules.
l Users with the privilege to edit a View can add or update Storage Lifecycle Management Rules on that View.
l Storage lifecycle management rules applied to a View are executed on all eligible files within that View, regardless of the individual file's access permission settings.
l If you intend to enable Storage Lifecycle Management Rules on a View designated as a down-tiering target, Cohesity recommends not to enable lifecycle management on this target View if the down-tiering task uses the Tier with symbolic links option. Enabling lifecycle management under such circumstances may result in dangling symlinks on the primary source when files are deleted by lifecycle management on this target View. For more information about Symbolic Links, see Configure a Down-Tiering Task.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

l By default, lifecycle job execution occurs across the cluster every seven days. During this process, the job identifies all Views governed by lifecycle policies and identifies files eligible for deletion according to the policy of each View. If a significant number of files are eligible for deletion, it may take multiple runs of the lifecycle job to remove them all. Cohesity focuses on prioritizing other critical workloads on the server; as a result, the job refrains from being more aggressive in deleting all files in a single run. Therefore, if a lifecycle job does not delete all files in one go, note that the subsequent job runs will eventually complete the task. Although Cohesity can schedule the lifecycle job to run daily, doing so would consume resources needed by active and higher-priority workloads on the Cohesity server. Hence, the default periodicity of once every seven days is maintained.
Lifecycle Management Details in Audit Logs
The Cluster audit logs feature captures all events that occur at the cluster level. To review storage lifecycle management details, you can download the CSV file from the System > Audit Logs > Cluster tab.
The following is an example of an audit log record:
filerLifecycleManagement: rules: - agingPolicy: agingCriteria: LastModificationTime days: 180 fileFilter: fileExtensions: - .docx - .pdf fileSize: maxBytes: 1073741824 minBytes: 1048576 name: rule1 status: Enabled type: Allow
The File Services audit logs feature allows you to capture and monitor events happening on your SMB and NFS Views. These logs document actions such as file deletions, last modification times, creation times, file sizes, and other pertinent details. Timestamps are included in these logs, enabling you to cross-reference with cluster audit logs and determine the most recently active storage lifecycle management rules.
The following is an example of a File Services audit log record:
{"Timestamp" : "2023-12-12T17:35:33.918Z", "RecordID" : "2cda:6b", "Protocol" : "SnapFS", "RequestType" : "Delete ClientIP" : "10.14.52.77", "ViewName" : "test_view2", "Fsid" : 8817 ", "Result" : "Ok", "EntityType" : "File", "EntityPath": "f_100kb_90day.pdf", "EntityInode" : 8035, "EntityModifyTimestamp" : "2023-09-12T01: 30:09.000Z", "InodeSizeBytes" : 102400, "SourceParentEntityInode" : 8815, "LCMRuleName" : "r1", "EntityCreationTimestamp" : "2023-12-12T17:29:51.860Z"}
l EntityPath displays the name of the file that is being deleted.
l LCMRuleName displays the name of the storage lifecycle management rule.

Security
Configure the security settings for the view. You can add and manage Global IP Allowlist, Netgroup Allowlist, and select Security Style for the view.
IP Allowlist
1. Select Override Global IP Allowlist to ignore the global IP allowlist and honor only specific entries provided in the view. Select Extend Global IP Allowlist to honor the global IP allowlist and the specific entries provided in the view.

Security Style
Select the Security Style for the view. This setting is available only if you select both NFS and SMB protocols.
l Native--Windows and Linux permissions are stored separately. l Unified--Windows and Linux permissions are kept consistent such that when one
changes, the other is modified automatically. l NTFS--Access via SMB and NFS is controlled by an SMB ACL present on the file.

Alert Threshold File DataLock Turn on the File DataLock toggle to make the files in this view immutable based on the settings described below. File-level DataLock is typically used for compliance and regulatory purposes.
Important: You can enable File DataLock only while creating the View. You cannot enable File DataLock on an existing View.
Note: The File DataLock option is only applicable for NFS and SMB view types.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

l File DataLock Mode--Select one of the following modes:
l Compliance--Once File DataLock is enabled for the view, it cannot be disabled by anyone. However, a Cohesity user with the Data Security privilege can edit other DataLock settings. A user with the Data Security privilege can extend the override date into the future, but no one can shorten the date. Compliance mode means the view complies with SEC Rule 17a-4.
l Enterprise--A Cohesity user with Admin privileges or Data Security privileges can rename the view, delete the view, extend or shorten the override date, switch to Compliance mode, and edit the File DataLock settings. This mode is useful for giving storage administrators additional control over the view.
Note: o Apart from the local admins, Domain Admins also can delete files in a view with File DataLock enabled and operating in Enterprise Mode.
o Enterprise mode is supported on 6.4.1 and later clusters. If the view is replicated to a pre-6.4.1 cluster, Enterprise mode is automatically changed to Compliance mode. If the view is then replicated back to a 6.4.1 or later cluster, it retains the Compliance mode setting.
l Default Lock Period--Indicates the default time period that locked files remain locked if a user or application does not specify a default retention period. When the time period ends, files can be deleted but not changed. If you set the Default Lock Period to Forever, you cannot override it by enabling the Override (Lock all files until a specific date) option.
l Autolock Files--Indicates whether files are automatically locked after the specified period of I/O inactivity (based on the last modified timestamp). Override is supported only if Autolock Files is enabled. If Autolock Files is disabled, override cannot be used as legal hold.
l Manually Lock Using--By default, manual file locking occurs when a user or application sets the file's read-only attribute. Select one of the following:
l Read-Only--Locks files when the file permission is set to read-only. For example, set the Windows file properties attribute or use the Linux chmod command.
l Future ATime--Lock files when the last access time (atime) is set. For example, use Windows PowerShell commands or the Linux touch command.
Auto lock and manual lock are not mutually exclusive. You can have both the options active at the same time.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

l Minimum Lock Period: Optional. Indicate a minimum time for which the files remain locked if the user or application does not specify a default retention period. If an application or user locks the files for a default period and the application locks the files for a minimum period that is less than the default period, the request is silently rejected and the files remain locked as per the default retention period.
l Maximum Lock Period: Optional. Indicate a maximum time to ensure that a file's last access time cannot be set outside this period. A request to do so results in a permission denied error if the manual locking mode is FutureATime. Otherwise, the request will be silently rejected and the file will be locked for the default retention duration. This is useful for storage administrators to reclaim the storage space by specifying a maximum lock period after which the files can be either deleted or archived.
Note: By default, the Maximum Lock Period is set to None and cannot be edited if the Default Lock Period is Forever.
The Minimum Lock Period and Maximum Lock Period fields are valid for both FutureATime and Read-Only manual lock.
l Override (Lock all files until a specific date)--Indicates whether the lock on files expires on a specific date. This setting is typically used for legal hold purposes. Files in a lock expired state cannot be deleted until this date. If the Default Lock Period is set to Forever, overriding only extends the period for the defined amount of time and does not actually override the files.
File Filtering
Turn on the File Filtering toggle if you want to block or allow files with specified file extensions from being written to this view. Select one of the following options:
l Denied File Types--If you want to specify a list of file extensions for files that are blocked from being written to this view. For example, if you specify a list with the .exe and .dll extensions, files with these extensions cannot be written to this view.
l Allowed File Types--If you want to specify a list of file extensions for files that are allowed to be written to this view. For example, if you specify a list with the .cvs and .txt extensions, only files with these extensions can be written to this view.
Note: Special characters are not permitted in file extension names.
Enter file extensions separated with commas, spaces, tabs, or newlines and click Add.

SMB Options
Click the SMB Options to enable or disable the following SMB options:
l Browsable Shares--Turn on the toggle if you want shares of this view to be discoverable by the Windows net view command.
Windows behavior prevents Cohesity SMB shares from being automatically discoverable. Use the net view command to probe the cluster explicitly using \\<Cluster-machine-account-name> or \\<Cluster-vip-FQDN> or \\<Cluster-VIP>.
l Access Based Enumeration--If this setting is enabled, then when a user browses an SMB share, only the files and folders that a user has privileges to access are displayed.
l SMB Encryption--Turn on the toggle to enable encryption. Turn on the Enforce Encryption toggle to disallow any SMB2 or SMB3 connections that do not have encryption enabled. Turn off the toggle to allow all connections.
l Fast Durable Handles--Turn on this toggle to improve performance, but continuous availability is lost. For more information, see Fast Durable Handles.
l SMB Oplocks--By default, the SMB Oplocks toggle is turned on when you create a view. If SMB Oplocks is enabled:
l Client-side caching of read-ahead, write-behind, and lock information improves SMB share performance.
l File and directory leasing also gets enabled on newer clients such as Windows 2012 or later or Windows Server 2012 R2 or later. SMB leasing enables the client to cache file and directory metadata, which improves the overall file sharing performance.
For more information, see SMB Oplocks.
l Offline File Caching--The SMB offline feature allows the SMB client to use files offline when the SMB clients are disconnected from the network. For more information, see SMB Offline.
l NTFS Root Permissions--For an SMB share, by default, everyone has full control permissions for the view. You can optionally define custom permissions for the view. Search for and select the principal (user or group) that you want to define permissions for. Select Allow or Deny. Then select the permissions and the folder/file level to apply them to. Click Add. Permissions adhere to the prescribed behavior of ACEs in a DACL. For more information, see Manage Access Using NTFS Permissions.

Cohesity Views

Note: While editing a view, changes to the permissions apply only to new files and folders that are created after the change. Changes to permissions are not applied recursively to the view's existing files and folders.
If the view's storage domain is mapped to an AD domain, you can select only that AD domain and its trusted domains.
l Share Level Permissions--For an SMB share, you can optionally define custom permissions for the share. The share-level permissions are stored on the cluster as view metadata and are independent of the NTFS permissions. Search for and select the principal (user or group) that you want to define permissions for. Select Allow or Deny. Click Add. Permissions adhere to the prescribed behavior of ACEs in a DACL.
l Super Users--An SMB Super User is a privilege for AD users and groups, and local SMB users and groups. Select the AD domain and principal (user or group). Click + to add additional super users. A user with this privilege has complete access to view or share content overriding any assigned ACLs. However, the privilege cannot override the global allowlist and filelevel data lock permissions. The privilege is set at the share-level for a view and not as NTFS root permissions. When the Super User privilege is assigned to a user for a specific view or share, the user has complete access to all the contents of the view or share. For more information, see SMB Super User.
Note: The most restrictive permissions are applied. The permissions can be Full Control, Modify, Read Only, or Super User. For example, if NTFS permissions are Read and Write, but the share permission is Read, the Read permission is applied.

NFS Squashing
You can configure NFS root squash or all squash at the subnet, netgroup, or view level. Subnet/netgroup level squashing supersedes view-level squashing. Root Squash By default, root squashing is enabled on a Cohesity view and root user requests are processed as though it is made by the anonymous user (UID=65534). If you disable squashing, the root user on the client gets the same level of access to files as the root user on the Cohesity view. Root squashing allows the root user (UID=0) to be trusted by clients defined in a given allowlist. All Squash All squash maps all users, including root, to a defined UID/GID. The default UID used for squashing is 65534.

Pin Views to SSD
Cohesity allows you to pin views to the SSD tier. This feature enables you to pin views to the SSD tier so that critical data and data that has to be retrieved quickly are not downtiered to HDD or cloud. You can do the following:
l Pin a view to an SSD when you create the view. l Edit an existing view and pin the view. In this case, only the new data written after the
view is pinned is retained on the SSD tier. l Pin a view for an indefinite period of time. Select Forever if you want to set this
option. The data resides on the SSD forever. l Pin a view for a definite period from the time of its last access. You can select Hours,
Days, Months, or Years and specify an appropriate number in the field. The view is pinned for the specified duration from its last access time. After the specified period, the data is automatically downtiered to HDD. l Only the following QoS policies support pinning views:
l Test And Dev High l Backup Target SSD For more information, see QoS Policies for Cohesity Views. l Unpin a view from an SSD.
Note: If the system has used the reserved SSD capacity, view pinning is not honored and the data is downtiered to HDD.
Pin a View to the SSD To pin a view when creating a view, complete the following steps:
1. Navigate to SmartFiles > Views > All Views. 2. Click Create and select View.

l Test And Dev High l Backup Target SSD 6. Enable the Pin View to SSD toggle button. 7. Select one of the following options to set the duration: l Forever--Pins the view forever. The data resides on the SSD forever. l Hours--Enter the number of hours for which the view should be pinned. l Days--Enter the number of days for which the view should be pinned. l Months--Enter the number of months for which the view should be pinned. l Years--Enter the number of years for which the view should be pinned.

Clone a View
You can make a clone of an existing view. After cloning, the two versions of the data are unique. Changes made to the data in the new view are not replicated in the original view and changes made to the original view are not replicated in the new view. Data within a DataLock view is immutable. You can also clone a view from a view Snapshot. For more information, see Clone a View From a Snapshot. To clone a View:

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

1. Navigate to SmartFiles > Views.
2. Hover over the view that you want to clone, click and select Clone.
3. Select the clone's Purpose.
Select Clone as DataLock View if you want to clone a view as write once read many. Data within a DataLock view is immutable, and most view properties cannot be edited. (Note that view-level DataLock is different than file-level DataLock, as described in File-level DataLock for NFS and SMB Views.)
4. In the Task Name field, you can optionally change the default name for the clone task.
1. View Name: If you are creating or cloning a new view, specify a name for the view. Forward slashes (/) are not allowed in the view name.
Important: Renaming a view changes its default share name. Clients won't be able to mount the view unless they use the new share name. Clients using a share alias are not affected by the rename.
For a DataLock view, select a date for lock expiration. During the lock period, data within the view cannot be edited by any user.
During the lock period, users with Data Security privileges can delete the view (unless File DataLock is enabled for the view, in which case the view cannot be deleted), extend the lock period (it cannot be reduced) , add IPs in the allowlist and change the description. After the lock period expires, the view can be deleted by any user that has permission to delete it.
5. The Storage Domain is already selected. The new view is always created in the same storage domain as the original view.

If Inline Deduplication is on, deduplication occurs when the Cohesity cluster writes the data to the Cohesity View. If Inline Deduplication is off, deduplication occurs after the Cohesity cluster writes the data to the Cohesity View.
For more information, see About Deduplication.
1. QoS Policy: A QoS Policy determines to which storage media data is written and the priority of I/O when contention occurs. Select an appropriate QoS policy for the view. throughput, and priority.

Clone a View From a Snapshot
You can clone a view directly from a snapshot of the type view. This clone action creates a new view with a copy of the data captured in the snapshot. After cloning, the two versions of the data are unique. Changes made to the data in the new view are not replicated in the original view and changes made to the original view are not replicated in the new view. Data within a DataLock view is immutable.
You can clone a view from a snapshot created using any of the following actions:
l A snapshot captured directly from a view on the current Cohesity cluster.
l A snapshot located on a remote Cohesity cluster that was replicated (copied) from the Cohesity cluster that captured the snapshot. When the first Snapshot is replicated to the remote Cohesity cluster, a DR view is created on this remote Cohesity cluster. A DR view is a placeholder view that does not store data and cannot be cloned or mounted. You can use this DR view to access the replicated Snapshots using the Cohesity UI on the receiving (remote) Cohesity cluster. You can create a new view on the remote Cohesity cluster by cloning a replicated Snapshot associated with the DR view. In addition, when the first Snapshot is replicated to the remote Cohesity cluster, an Inactive Job is also created on the remote Cohesity cluster. You can use an Inactive Protection Group of type View to access the replicated Snapshots using the Cohesity UI on the remote Cohesity cluster that received the Snapshots. An Inactive Protection Group of type View is a placeholder Job and you cannot failover this type of Inactive Protection Group.
While creating a Protection Group for a view, if you have enabled the option to create a view on the remote Cohesity cluster, then along with the snapshot, a view will be created on the remote Cohesity cluster from the latest snapshot during the first Protection Group run. The same view will be reused and will always point to the latest snapshot after every run
To learn more, see Protect Cohesity Views.

Clone the Contents of a Directory in a View
You can recursively clone (copy) the contents of a directory in a View to a new directory in the same View or a different View using the view clone-directory Cohesity CLI command. Limitation The default value for the maximum number of files in the source hierarchy that can be atomically cloned together is 8192. Contact Cohesity Support to increase the maximum number of files in the source hierarchy that can be atomically cloned together. To copy the contents of a directory in a View:
1. Start the Cohesity CLI remotely or locally as described in the Cohesity CLI Reference Guide. Specify the static IPv4 or IPv6 address of one of the Cohesity nodes. For example, if the CLI was downloaded to a Linux system, you might use the following command. Provide a Cohesity cluster username and password.
./iris_cli -server 172.16.3.101 -username=admin
2. Clone the contents of a directory using the Cohesity CLI view clone-directory command:
admin>view clone-directory destination-directory-name=<DestDirName> destination-directory-path=<DestPath> source-directorypath=<SourcePath>
Tip: You can use the CLI Help feature to view the view clone-directory options by entering the following command: view clone-directory help.

Protect Cohesity Views
You can protect the data in a view by capturing snapshots of the view. A view Protection Group captures snapshots according to the protection schedule defined by the associated protection policy. Snapshots can be used as follows:
l The snapshot can be cloned into a new view that is stored in the same storage domain as the original snapshot. The new view contains the version of the files and directories as they were captured when the original snapshot was created.
l The snapshot can be replicated (copied) to another storage domain on a remote Cohesity cluster. The replication schedule is defined by the protection policy associated with the Protection Group.
Other backup products, such as Veeam, can store data in a view.
The steps below provide a sample scenario of how view snapshots are captured, cloned and replicated:
1. A view Protection Group captures a snapshot of all files and directories stored in a view. In this example, all the files and directories currently stored in the myView view are captured in the 3/21/24 01:00 AM snapshot.

2. If a replication schedule is defined for protection policy associated with Protection Group that created the snapshot, then the following would be created on the remote Cohesity cluster ("EngReserve, below):
l A copy of the snapshot is replicated from the Cohesity cluster capturing the snapshots ("EngMain", below)
l A DR view is created when the first snapshot is replicated to the remote Cohesity cluster. A DR view is a placeholder view that does not store data and cannot be cloned or mounted. You can use this DR view to access the replicated

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

snapshots using the Cohesity UI on the receiving (remote) Cohesity cluster. You can create a new view on the remote Cohesity cluster by cloning a replicated snapshot associated with the DR view. In addition, when the first snapshot is replicated to the remote Cohesity cluster, an Inactive Job is also created on the remote Cohesity cluster.
l A new view with Read-Only permission is created from the latest replicated snapshot (if you have enabled the option to create view on the remote Cohesity cluster). This view can have any user-specified name provided while creating Protection Group for a view and will always point to the latest replicated snapshot. If a disaster strikes, you can clone this view instead of the latest snapshot. However, if you want to restore a data set that is not the latest, then you must clone the view from the respective snapshot.

3. In the original myView view, a new file called Eng_400_backup.vbm is created at 1:30 AM.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

4. At 2:00 AM, a new view snapshot is captured. The 2:00 AM snapshot has captured the new file called Eng_400_backup.vbm but the original 1:00 AM snapshot does not have the file.

5. You clone the 1:00 AM snapshot in the capturing Cohesity cluster. A new view (called myViewClone) is created with the versions of the files and directories as originally captured by the 1:00 AM snapshot. The new view is always created in the same

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

Storage Domain as the original view. The new view (called myViewClone) does not contain the Eng_400_backup.vbm file.

6. As defined by the replication schedule of the Job, along with the latest view a second copy of the snapshot is replicated to a remote Cohesity cluster at 2:15 AM. In this example, every snapshot captured on the Cohesity cluster ("EngMain", below) is replicated to the remote Cohesity cluster ("EngReserve", below).

7. If disaster strikes and the original view is no longer available, you can recover from the disaster by cloning the snapshot stored on the remote Cohesity cluster. When the View Snapshot is cloned, a new View is created that contains the version of the files and directories as they were captured when the Snapshot was created. In this example, since the new view created on the remote Cohesity cluster ("EngReserve",

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

below) was replicated from the second snapshot, the new view (called myBckVM) contains the Eng_400_backup.vbm file.

Add or Edit a Protection Group for a View
The Protection Group captures snapshots of views and snapshots of views are required for the following tasks:
l creating a new view from a view snapshot l replicating snapshots l archiving snapshots
The Cohesity cluster supports backing up the following entities stored in the view:
l ordinary files l directories l symbolic links l hard links
These entities can be captured in a view snapshot and restored to a new view. The backup and recovery of the following special files is supported: pipes, block devices, sockets and character devices. To create a Protection Group for a view:
1. Navigate to Data Protection > Protection and do one of the following: l To create a Protection Group--Click Protect on the top-right of the page and then select the type of Protection Group.
l To edit a Protection Group--Click the action icon ( ) next to the Protection Group and select Edit.
2. If creating a new job, select Protect > Cohesity View.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

3. Views: Select the view that you want to protect and then click Save Selection. The list shows the Storage Domain that contains the view. View Snapshots are always stored in the same Storage Domain as the original view.
4. Name: Enter a name for the Protection Group. The name can contain alphanumeric characters, underscores, dashes, and periods.
5. Policy: Select an existing protection policy or create a new one by selecting New Policy.
6. Remote View: This option is available only if the policy you selected has replication enabled. In the Remote cluster fields, enter a name for each view that will be created on the remote Cohesity cluster corresponding to the views on the primary Cohesity cluster. Ensure that the name provided for the views are unique and are not the same as any other view names on the remote Cohesity cluster. If the name provided is not unique, then on the remote Cohesity cluster, a new view will be create with"-1" appended to the provided name. In the next protection run, the views in the remote Cohesity cluster will be overwritten by the latest replicated snapshot of the view on the primary Cohesity cluster.
1. End Date: Optional. Toggle on and select the date when the Protection Group stops capturing snapshots. A protection run that starts prior to this date runs until completion even if it completes after this date.
7. Start Time: Indicates when the Protection Group should run. The current time is displayed by default but you can change it. Enter the hour and minutes or use the up and down arrows on your keyboard. Verify the AM or PM setting.
The default time zone is the browser's time zone. You can change the time zone by selecting a different time zone.
8. Indexing :Indexing is enabled by default and is required for file recovery. Optionally customize by adding indexing rules. Type index text. Click Add under Include and Exclude fields to add more index terms.
9. Priority: Select a priority for the Protection Group execution. Cohesity supports concurrent backups, but if the number of Protection Groups exceeds the ability to process them, those with High priority are given the highest priority to execute, Medium the second-highest priority, and Low the lowest priority.
10. Cancel Runs at Quiet Time Start: Available only if the selected policy has at least one quiet time period. Toggle it on to specify that all currently executing protection runs should abort if a quiet time period specified for the Protection Group starts. By default this toggle is off, which means after a protection run starts, it continues to execute even when a quiet time period specified for this protection run starts. However, a new protection run will not start during a quiet time period.
11. Alerts: Optional. Select one or more of the following settings if you want Alerts to be created for the following triggers:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

l Success: Create an Informational Alert when a Protection Group completes successfully. Emails are not sent when Informational Alerts are created.
l Failure: Create an Critical Alert if the Protection Group fails to complete. Emails are sent when Critical Alerts are created.
For more information about Alerts, see Alerts. 12. Description: Optional. Click the plus sign and enter a description for the Protection
Group. 13. Click Protect.
The Protection page is displayed and includes the new Protection Group.
Recover Files or Folders
You can now recover the files and folders of a view that has been protected. You can either recover the files and folder of a view to an alternate view or to the same view. This section describes how to perform the recovery of a view.
Considerations
l You can select only those views as targets that have the Case Sensitive File or Folder Names option same as the source view. For example, if the file of a view you selected for recovery has the Case Sensitive File or Folder Names option disabled, then from the Select View drop-down, you can select only those views having the Case Sensitive File or Folder Names option disabled.
l You can recover files or folders from a view having the File DataLock option enabled. However, you cannot recover files or folders to a view having the File DataLock option enabled.
l The target view and the source view must belong to the same storage domain. l You can recover files or folders from an NFS view to an SMB view and vice-versa.
However, symlinks will not be preserved for cross protocol recoveries. l You can recover files or folders from an archive and replicated view. l You cannot recover files or folders to a Read-only view. l You cannot recover files or folders from an S3 view or to an S3 view.
Recover to the Original View
To recover files and folders to the original view:
1. Navigate to Data Protection > Recoveries. 2. Click Recover located at the top right of the page and then select Cohesity View >
Files or Folders. 3. Select any one of the following options to search for the file or folder:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

l Browse: Allows you to search and recover files using the name of the view or Protection Group from any backup available on the Cohesity cluster.

Character replacement explanation for : and \ in file and directory names in zip files
If the original file or directory name contains a `:' , it is replaced with `_COLON_' in the archive. Example:
l The original name is "a:b" then the archived name is "a_COLON_b" l The original name is "a:b:c" then the archived name is "a_COLON_b_
COLON_c"
If the original file or directory name contains a `\', it is replaced with '_BACK_ SLASH_' in the archive. Example:
l The original name is "x\y" then the archived name is "x_BACK_SLASH_y" l The original name is "x\y\z" then the archived name is "x_BACK_SLASH_
y_BACK_SLASH_z"

7. Optional. Edit the default settings of the following Recovery options:
l Overwrite Existing File/Folder: By default, this option is disabled to create the files and folders in the specified location. Any duplicate files are skipped. Enable this option to overwrite the existing files and folders.
Consider this example, you are recovering a file, 1.txt from the source view V1 to the root directory of the target view V2. If a file, 1.txt already exists in the root directory of the target view V2, then the Overwrite behavior is as follows:
l If the Overwrite option is enabled during recovery, the 1.txt in the target view is overwritten with the data in the 1.txt file of the source view V1.
l If the Overwrite option is disabled during recovery, the 1.txt in the target view V2 will not be overwritten with the data in the 1.txt file of the source view V1.
If Overwrite is enabled, recovering a file to the source when the file is in use may cause the open file to be overwritten. Whether overwriting occurs depends on the application using the file.
l Preserve File/Folder Attributes: This option is not applicable for the file or folder recovery of a view.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

l Continue on Error: By default, this option is enabled to continue the recovery even if one of the objects encounters an error. Disable this option to discontinue the recovery task if one of the objects encounters an error.
l Cluster Interface: By default, the Auto Select option is enabled and the recovery task automatically selects the correct VLAN. If you disable this option, then select a configured interface group from the Interface Group drop-down.
l Task Name: Change the default name of the recovery task. l Save Success Files: Enable this option to download the success logs for a
recovery run. 8. Click Recover.
The recovery task is initiated. You can monitor the recovery task from the Recoveries page.

Restore Previous Versions of SMB Files and Folders
You can restore previous versions of files and folders that are in Cohesity-protected SMB Views. This feature enables you to perform the restore from the system where the Views are mounted and provides the same functionality as the Windows "Restore previous versions" function.
The snapshot to be restored is generated only when the backup task is performed on the SMB view.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

Note: l The file or folder you want to restore must have already been backed up by a previous View Snapshot on the Cohesity cluster.
l The versions available for restore are determined by the snapshots stored in the Cohesity cluster. For example, if the retention period specified in the Protection Policy retains snapshots for only two days, then only the versions from the past two days are available for restore.
To restore a previous version: 1. On the system, right-click the file or folder that is under a backed up view and select Restore previous versions. 2. Click the Previous Versions tab. 3. Select the version you want to restore to and click Restore.
Lock or Unlock Cohesity View Configuration
You can now lock or unlock the configuration of a Cohesity view. The lock or unlock feature provides additional security checks on the view's configuration. Only users with the Data Security privilege can lock or unlock a view. You can lock or unlock a Cohesity view using the Cohesity CLI only. For more information, see view for view-related CLI operations:
l view lock l view unlock When a view is locked, no users can perform configuration-related operations such as: l Access the properties of the view l Create, edit, or delete aliases of the view l Enable or disable user or directory quotas
Overwrite a View
You can use the Cohesity CLI view overwrite command to overwrite a View with the contents of another View in the same Cohesity cluster. The target View becomes a clone of the source View. This is useful if you want to maintain a View on a remote Cohesity cluster (used for replication) that has information from the latest replication of the source View. For example, you might manually create a View on the remote Cohesity cluster and then overwrite that View with a View snapshot after each replication task runs. To overwrite a View:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 9: SmartFiles (File and Object Services)

Cohesity Views

1. Start the Cohesity CLI remotely or locally as described in the Cohesity CLI Reference Guide. Specify the static IPv4 or IPv6 address of one of the Cohesity nodes. For example, if the CLI was downloaded to a Linux system, you might use the following command. Provide a Cohesity cluster username and password. ./iris_cli -server 172.16.3.101 -username=admin
2. Overwrite the target View with the source View contents by using the following Cohesity CLI command: admin>view overwrite source-view-name=<view1> target-view-name=<view2>
Delete a View
You can delete a View if you do not need the data in a View. When you delete a View permanently all data stored in the View such as files, Snapshots and Cloned VM files.

Remote Views are always read-only. By default, Remote Views are visible to clients and visible in the Cohesity GUI. To disable Remote Views visibility on clients for all protocols:

SMB Shares
