Work with Kerberos Security enabled primaries for data protection
If your primary cluster to be protected is not Kerberos security enabled, then you can ignore this section. Otherwise, please go through this section before attempting to register a data source in Cohesity. Typical flow of this process is:
a. Obtain Kerberos principal name(s), the corresponding keytab file(s) and Kerberos configuration file (krb5.conf) for your kerberos realm.
b. Ensuring the Kerberos KDC server hostname is resolvable from NoSQL and Hadoop Service pods.
c. Adding the keytab and the kerberos realm to NoSQL and Hadoop Service using a command line tool called imanis_cli.sh.
d. Register the data source in Cohesity.
Obtain Kerberos Principal(s), keytab file(s) and krb5.conf
Verify with your primary cluster administrators about one or more kerberos principals to be used by NoSQL and Hadoop service for connecting to their cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 30: NoSQL and Hadoop Service

Post Installation Procedures

Note: NoSQL and Hadoop service recommends using a single principal exclusively for NoSQL and Hadoop service access. This is to ensure better control over what access permissions are granted to this principal and can also be useful for auditing purposes. For example, one can create a principal such as imanis@REALMNAME in the KDC server for exclusive use by NoSQL and Hadoop Service software.
However, in some cases, while protecting Hadoop clusters like CDH or HDP, some deployments may prefer to create 3 separate kerberos principals for allowing access to hdfs, hbase and hive respectively as follows:
l imanis_hdfs@REALMNAME - Kerberos principal used for HDFS workflows l imanis_hbase@REALMNAME - Kerberos principal used for HBase workflows l imanis_hive@REALMNAME - Kerberos principal used for Hive workflows
In such cases, you may end up with 3 different keytab files corresponding to these 3 principals as opposed to a single keytab file in case of using a single principal.
The key thing to ensure is that the principal(s) given to NoSQL and Hadoop Service have full access permissions granted on the primary cluster, for listing, reading files, tables, keyspaces, databases, collections and write access while restoring a backup from NoSQL and Hadoop Service.
Note: Replace REALMNAME with the actual realm name used in your kerberos cluster. You can use any other existing principal name such as hdfs@REALMNAME , instead of imanis. New principles are created in KDC servers by Kerberos admin.
Ensure Kerberos KDC server hostname is resolvable from NoSQL and Hadoop Service pods
We must ensure that the Kerberos KDC server hostname is resolvable from the NoSQL and Hadoop Service kubernetes pods. This is generally not a problem if the DNS is setup properly and we use FQDN for the Kerberos KDC server. However, if this is not the case, then one can also add this hostname and IP address to /etc/hosts on the pods running NoSQL and Hadoop Service. Use imanis_cli.sh -c hosts add option to perform this step:
$ pwd /home_cohesity_data/athena/mounts/_internal_view_mount/imanis $ cat $PWD/hosts 10.14.20.237 im39-vm1.cohesity.com $ imanis_cli.sh -c hosts add $PWD/hosts

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 30: NoSQL and Hadoop Service

Post Installation Procedures

Add a keytab and Kerberos realm to NoSQL and Hadoop Service
You need to perform this step every time you want to register a new kerberos enabled data source with NoSQL and Hadoop Service. However, if the principal that you plan to use is the same as other data sources that have already been registered, then you can skip this step. Run a command line tool called imanis_cli.sh on any one Cohesity cluster node. The following options are supported by imanis_cli.sh for the kerberos operations:
$ imanis_cli.sh -c kerberos usage: imanis_cli.sh -c kerberos addrealm imanis_cli.sh -c kerberos deleterealm realm_name imanis_cli.sh -c kerberos validatekeytab [local keytabpath] imanis_cli.sh -c kerberos import krb5_keytab_dirpath
For adding a new kerberos principal, we use the add realm option. There are two ways in which the information about the new Kerberos realm to be added is given as input to this script.
l By pointing the script to an existing krb5.conf file. The conf file will be read and parsed to extract the relevant information. Download the krb5.conf file from your primary node to the node on NoSQL and Hadoop Services
l In case you do not have access to krb5.conf file, you can type the required information manually by confirming the prompts. Download the keytab file(s) and krb5.conf (if you have one) to one of the Cohesity cluster nodes under the directory as follows:
cd /home_cohesity_data/athena/mounts/_internal_view_mount/imanis/ mkdir kerberos cd kerberos scp ip_or_hostname:/path/to/keytab_and_krb5_conf_files .
Here, replace the ip_or_hostname with the IP address or hostname of the server where the keytab and krb5.conf files are present. This is usually your primary cluster itself or any other server where administrators have generated these files and saved.
Note: It is important to download and keep these files under this specific mount point only. This cannot be changed, however you can create any sub directory.
/home_cohesity_data/athena/mounts/_internal_view_mount/imanis/
You must have one or more keytabs and/or krb5.conf file in the present working directory as follows:
$ pwd /home_cohesity_data/athena/mounts/_internal_view_mount/imanis/kerberos $ ls

Manage SSL enabled NoSQL primary clusters
In general, two entities (client, server programs in our case) that are communicating with one another must ensure the following:
1. Client to ensure that it is talking to an authentic server. 2. Server to ensure that it is talking to an authentic client. 3. The data client-server exchange must not be seen by anyone else in the middle.
See FAQs on NoSQL and Hadoop Services for details on the most frequently asked questions about SSL enabled NoSQL primary clusters.
Certificate file formats supported
NoSQLandHadoop uses PEM format for certificates and keys for importing.
PEM or Privacy Enhanced Mail is a Base64 encoded DER certificate. So you can open it in your favorite editor to check. Generally when a PEM encoded file is opened in a text editor, it contains very distinct headers and footers as below:
A private key in PEM format is as shown below:
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED DEK-Info: DES-EDE3-CBC,E1537934256F0AAE aNLbkgsTZLESaRTPvpgh3lMRm4ltJ9rOZaZCn3msw22iVUec5u+dpr9FM8jY6y7J m4MB203AfRexnFwmL3FrIki4vylRmVp7HWMxQLLYBxBPPPEi7QVB6EE6GNKEf973 ... ... ... cy3sLxHa7+IGD/c4pnETQ+9Zna/wrHEyt8WDtFzJ4sL9f1u3peh2ip9OG+Gh6F6Y SDK129oSj5FF/uY///zkzAneHZwDSuAbNJfJfrKMUDZEWA292DqGJI03MFaHlq2f -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----

Work with NoSQLandHadoop Services using SSL tool
NoSQL and Hadoop services provide a CLI tool called imanis_cli.sh which can be found on the Cohesity nodes where NoSQL and Hadoop Service is installed. This tool is used to set up keystore and truststore on the NoSQL and Hadoop Service app. Following are the options to imanis_cli.sh -c ssl command. Log in to one of the Cohesity cluster nodes where NoSQL and Hadoop Service is installed and run the following:
$ imanis_cli.sh -c ssl
Fetching ImanisData cluster config from athena-1:imanis-nodemanager-0
Usage : imanis_cli.sh -c ssl import port hostname1 [ hostname2 hostname3 ...] download certificate(s) from remote server(s) and import them into Imanis Truststore automatically arguments: port : SSL port where server is listening hostname : list of hostnames of the servers to download SSL certificates
imanis_cli.sh -c ssl import-manual alias1 /path/to/certificate/file1 alias2 /path/to/certificate/file2 ... Import SSL certificates manually into Imanis truststore NOTE: You need to copy the certificates to one of the Imanis nodes manually Use this only if the automatic import fails arguments: alias : short hostname from where the certificate is importedfile : path to certificate file
imanis_cli.sh -c ssl generate-keystore Generate self-signed SSL certificates and use it for Imanis keystore
imanis_cli.sh -c ssl import-keystore /path/to/key/file /path/to/cert/file Import CA signed SSL certificate+key into Imanis keystore, Use this when self-signed certificate is not good enough arguments: /path/to/key/file : path to file containing private key in PEM format /path/to/cert/file: path to corresponding certificate file in PEM format NOTE: If you have a single file containing both key and certificate,

imanis_cli.sh -c ssl list [truststore|keystore] List the certificates from Imanis Truststore/Keystore

imanis_cli.sh -c ssl delete [truststore|keystore]Delete the truststore/keystore, if it exists
Setting up truststore: The truststore contains certificates from the SSL enabled servers to which we want to connect to. There are a couple of ways in which you can build the truststore:
a. Importing certificates from servers automatically: In this case, you run the imanis_cli.sh tool by specifying the port and the list of server hostnames or IP addresses. The tool will connect to the specified port on each server and download the SSL certificate presented by the server. IPv4 Example: you have three servers in your MongoDB cluster with IP address 10.14.20.87, 10.14.20.88 10.14.20.89 and they are listening on port 27221 $ imanis_cli.sh -c ssl import 27221 10.14.20.87 10.14.20.88 10.14.20.89

Setting up keystore A keystore must have a private key and a corresponding certificate. To set up the keystore:

Scale Nodemanager Pods
Sometimes, you may want to increase (scale up) the number of nodemanager replicas to use the additional resources available after adding a new compute node. In such cases, you can utilize the additional resources by launching more nodemanager replicas using the command given below:
$ imanis_cli.sh -c scale --help INFO : Checking reachability of pod imanis-nodemanager-0 --------------------------------------------------------------------Performing scale operation of node manager pods. --------------------------------------------------------------------Usage: To scale up number of nodemanager pods, imanis_cli.sh -c scale up --nmcount To scale down number of nodemanager pods, imanis_cli.sh -c scale down --nmcount --nmcount: Number of expected node manager pods. ---------------------------------------------------------------------

$ imanis_cli.sh -c scale up 4 INFO : Checking reachability of pod imanis-nodemanager-0 --------------------------------------------------------------------Performing scale operation of node manager pods. --------------------------------------------------------------------NM pods scaled up to 4 successfully. INFO: Scale up performed successfully ---------------------------------------------------------------------
You can also reduce the number of running nodemanager pods by reducing the replica count using the following command.
$ imanis_cli.sh -c scale down 2 INFO : Checking reachability of pod imanis-nodemanager-0 --------------------------------------------------------------------Performing scale operation of node manager pods. --------------------------------------------------------------------NM pods scaled down to 2 successfully. INFO: Scaled down performed successfully ---------------------------------------------------------------------

Configuring Continuous Data Protection (CDP) for MongoDB
Ensure that the NoSQL and Hadoop Service app is installed and running. To enable MongoDB CDP service, use the following command: $ imanis_cli.sh -c mongocdp enable --cpu <cpu-cores> --memory <memory-GB> -replica <num-replicas>
l cpu-cores: Number of CPU cores allocated to each MongoCDP service instance l memory-GB: Amount of memory allocated to each MongoCDP service instance l num-replicas: Number of MongoCDP service instances. Depending on the load on
MongoDB primary and the recovery point objective, one or more MongoDB CDP services can be provisioned. The use of multiple smaller CDP services can help RPO in case of nodes going down. For example, the below command enables MongoDB CDP with single replicas of 1core/2GB memory. $ imanis_cli.sh -c mongocdp enable --cpu 1 --memory 2 --replica 1 INFO : Checking reachability of pod imanis-nodemanager-0 INFO : Log File : /tmp/imanis-cli-workdir.10686/cli/imanis-mongo-cdp.log INFO : Enabling MongoCDP pods deployment INFO : Reading allocatable cluster resources INFO : Total allocatable Memory(GB) : 239 INFO : Total allocatable CPUs : 47 INFO : Number of MongoCDP replicas : 1 INFO : CPUs per MongoCDP replica : 1 INFO : Memory per MongoCDP replica(GB) : 2 INFO : Total CPUs for MongoCDP replicas : 1 INFO : Total Memory for MongoCDP replicas(GB): 2 INFO : Total Memory for Other Services(GB) : 15 INFO : Total CPUs for Other Services : 10 INFO : Small-Nodemanager instance config : 16GB/4 CPUs INFO : Medium-Nodemanage instance config : 32GB/8 CPUs INFO : Large-Nodemanager instance config : 40GB/10 CPUs Please confirm above configurations for 'NoSQL & Hadoop Service' app deployment with MongoCDP Pods Do you want to continue (yes/no) yes ? yes

Megafile Support for Cassandra
Megafile allows fast backup and recovery for large files, helping reduce backup times as well as downtime when recovering from a disaster. Megafile distributes files across all nodes in a cluster. Megafile breaks large files into smaller chunks for parallel backup and recovery across nodes. The minimum size of these chunks is optimized to maximize performance.
Cassandra backup and recovery of size tiered tables generally contains data files which are in tens or hundreds of GBs. These data files are backed up or recovered as Megafiles. Cassandra uses different approaches for backup and recovery. The Megafile approach is used only if scp is being used for backup and recovery.
By default, Megafile support for Cassandra backup and recovery is disabled.
Enable or Disable Megafile for Cassandra Backup
Run the following command to enable Megafile for Cassandra backup:
imanis_cli.sh -c megafile --connector cassandra-backup --workdir /tmp/imanis --enable true

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 30: NoSQL and Hadoop Service

Additional Configuration for NoSQL and Hadoop Services

where, -workdir specifies the directory on the primary cluster nodes where Cassandra can copy the binaries. Run the following command to disable Megafile for Cassandra backup: imanis_cli.sh -c megafile --connector cassandra-backup --enable false Enable or Disable Megafile for Cassandra Recovery A file is restored as a Megafile only if it is backed up as a Megafile. Otherwise, Cassandra uses the normal recovery workflow to recover Cassandra objects. Run the following command to enable Megafile for Cassandra recovery: imanis_cli.sh -c megafile --connector cassandra-restore --workdir /tmp/imanis --enable true where, -workdir specifies the directory on the primary cluster nodes where Cassandra can copy the binaries. Run the following command to disable Megafile for Cassandra recovery: imanis_cli.sh -c megafile --connector cassandra-restore --enable false Megafile Status The pulse log shows the following when Megafile is enabled for backup and recovery: - Megafile support is enabled The pulse log shows the following after a protection run or recovery: CASSANDRA_MEGAFILES_COPIED=2 CASSANDRA_MEGAFILES_FAILED=2 CASSANDRA_ MEGAFILES_DATA_COPIED=4931999383 where
l CASSANDRA_MEGAFILES_COPIED - Number of Megafiles successfully copied. l CASSANDRA_MEGAFILES_FAILED - Number of Megafiles for which copy failed. l CASSANDRA_MEGAFILES_DATA_COPIED - Total data copied as Megafile.

Config Save and Restore
After terminating the app, any modification made to any of the config files is lost. This tool allows you to restore configs from previous instances of an app if it is saved with the save option.
l config save is used to save config and patches from the running imanis instance. l config restore is used to restore config/patches from the previous instance to the
current running instance. Save Config and Patches Perform the following steps to save config and patches from the running instance:
1. Log in to the Cohesity cluster where the NoSQL & Hadoop Service app is running. 2. Run the following command:
$ imanis_cli.sh -c config 3. Run the following command to save config and patches:
$ imanis_cli.sh -c config save Restore Config and Patches Perform the following steps to restore config and patches to the running instance:
1. Log in to the Cohesity cluster where the NoSQL & Hadoop Service app is running. 2. Run the following command:
$ imanis_cli.sh -c config 3. Run the following command to restore config and patches:
$ imanis_cli.sh -c config restore

Monitor the NoSQL and Hadoop Service Health
To ensure that the NoSQL and Hadoop Service is healthy, Cohesity constantly monitors the following services running on the Kubernetes pods: zookeeper, YARN, api-server, and mongocdp (if enabled for MongoDB protection). These services are required to enable and perform the backup and restore operations. If any of these services encounter issues, an error message with an error code appears on the Cohesity UI, which can be used for troubleshooting. The status of the NoSQL and Hadoop Service is displayed as either Running or Not Healthy depending on the status of these services. The status of the NoSQL and Hadoop Service specifies the following:
l Running - The NoSQL and Hadoop Service is healthy and running. l Not Healthy - The NoSQL and Hadoop Service is not healthy and have some issues.
To view the health of the NoSQL and Hadoop service from the Coheity UI, navigate to Marketplace > My Apps and then click the All Instances tab. Running State:

Not Healthy State: Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

NoSQL and Hadoop Service Error Codes
This section covers the NoSQL and Hadoop Service error codes and the troubleshooting steps.
Important: Ensure that you have Host Shell access on the Cohesity cluster to perform the troubleshooting steps.
NoSQL_0000 Issue: The NoSQL and Hadoop service health check feature cannot report the health of the service. The NoSQL and Hadoop service might be in a Running or Not Healthy state, and the health check feature cannot detect the service's current status. Troubleshooting: Contact Cohesity Support if the issue persists. NoSQL_0001 Issue: The NoSQL and Hadoop service, zookeeper, is down on one or more of the pods: imaniszookeeper-0, imanis-zookeeper-1, and imanis-zookeeper-2. Troubleshooting:
1. Login to the pod using the following command: kubectl.sh exec -it -n <athena-namespace> imanis-zookeeper-0 -/bin/bash
2. Run the following command to find the pod on which the zookeeper service is down:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 30: NoSQL and Hadoop Service

Monitor the NoSQL and Hadoop Service Health

talena-services.sh status zookeeper
3. Log in to the pod on which the zookeeper service is down and verify zookeeper log files in $LOG_DIR to determine the reason for the issue. For example: The log files to look for, if zookeeper is down on imanis-zookeeper-0 pod: $LOG_DIR/zookeeper-hdfs-server-imanis-zookeeper-0.log $LOG_DIR/zookeeper-hdfs-server-imanis-zookeeper-0.out
4. Also, you can collect the logs from the Cohesity cluster for further debugging by running the following command using the cohesity user on the cluster: imanis_cli.sh -c explorer -n 1 -s logs -l zookeeper /home/cohesity
5. Try restarting the zookeeper service to fix the issue. Run the following command on any of the pods to restart the zookeeper service: talena-services.sh restart zookeeper
6. Check the status of the zookeeper service to verify if the issue is resolved using the following command: talena-services.sh smoke zookeeper
Contact Cohesity Support if the issue persists. NoSQL_0002 Issue: The NoSQL and Hadoop group of services YARN, is down on one or more of the mentioned pods: imanis-resourcemanager-0, imanis-resourcemanager-1, imanis-nodemanager-*, and imanis-historyserver-0. Troubleshooting:

FAQs on NoSQL and Hadoop Services
The following are some of the frequently asked questions about managing SSL enabled NoSQL primary clusters:
1. What is alias which is used while importing the certificates ? Does it have to match the hostname ?
Alias is just a name or a tag for the entry in the truststore. It is used only by users to identify the certificate they are looking for. It could be any unique string for a given certificate entry. Usually the hostname of the machine to which the certificate belongs is preferred as it makes it easy to identify the same.
2. Can I import the certificates into NoSQL and Hadoop Service in PKCS12 format ?
No, the certificates should be in PEM format for importing into NoSQL and Hadoop service.
3. My primary server certificate is signed by an intermediate CA and the intermediate CA certificate is signed by another root CA. So do I need to import these two certificates as well into NoSQL and Hadoop service?

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 30: NoSQL and Hadoop Service

FAQs on NoSQL and Hadoop Services

Yes, root CA, intermediate CA certificates should also be imported into NoSQL and Hadoop service truststore. If you import using an automatic method, then usually all the certificates in the chain are downloaded from the server and imported into NoSQL and Hadoop service truststore. 4. How do I know what format my certificate is in ? If you cat the file and find text wrapped in headers such as -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- or -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----, then the certificate is in PEM format. 5. How do I verify if my private key and certificate match each other ?
openssl x509 -noout -modulus -in /path/to/cert | openssl md5
openssl rsa -noout -modulus -in /path/to/key | openssl md5
If both the sums match, then they match each other.
Note: When importing a keystore into NoSQL and Hadoop service, this check is done by the script.
6. How do I check if I have already imported a certificate into NoSQL and Hadoop Service truststore ?
# imanis_cli.sh -c ssl list truststore
and check if the entry exists. 7. I am importing a CA signed certificate and the corresponding private key into NoSQL
and Hadoop service as keystore. What should be the hostname ( CN ) ? The hostname for NoSQL and Hadoop Service app usually start with imanis*.imanis-cluster.*.svc.cluster.local. But these hostnames are not resolvable outside the Athena app. So for hostname, you can use the Cohesity hostnames on which NoSQL and Hadoop Service app has been deployed. 8. My server certificates have expired. How do I remove the old certificates and re import new ones ? Using imanis_cli.sh -c ssl list command, you can list the entries and delete the ones which you want using the specific alias as follows:
# imanis_cli.sh -c ssl delete alias
9. If I delete keystore or truststore while the protection runs are in progress, what happens ? Protection runs may fail. This should be done only when you are sure that there are no protection runs connecting to SSL enabled primaries on your NoSQL and Hadoop cluster.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 30: NoSQL and Hadoop Service

FAQs on NoSQL and Hadoop Services

10. What is the difference between password and passphrase for the private key I am importing ? How do I verify if my password and passphrase are correct before importing ?
Password is set for the keystore or truststore that you import into NoSQL and Hadoop service. Please set a good password and remember it.
Passphrase is always associated with a private key. It is usually set when you generate a private key. The passphrase you enter should match with the passphrase that was set for the given key. You can not change this afterwards.
11. When do I need to import certificates into NoSQL and Hadoop Service?
You need to do it before you register your data source into Cohesity UI.
12. Can I only import certificates from my server into NoSQL and Hadoop service? Is importing or generating keystore mandatory ?
In some environments, there is no requirement for the client to present its certificate to server and server having to carry out the validation. In such environments, you do not need to import NoSQL and Hadoop service certificate into your primary cluster.
However, in some cases, like in cassandra, the setting required_client_auth=true in yaml configuration file mandates that validation be done both ways. In this case, you have to copy the certificate from NoSQL and Hadoop node into your primary nodes and import it using the methods prescribed by your respective primary setup.
13. Which one should I use ? A self-signed certificate or a CA signed certificate for NoSQL and Hadoop Service?
This depends on the security requirements of your organization. Self-signed certificate is good enough, if the requirement is to encrypt the data transferred between the NoSQL and Hadoop running cluster and your primary cluster being protected. But if the requirement is not only encrypted data transmission on the wire but also to validate that the server and client are authentic, then you need CA signed certificates.

Test & Dev Overview

Test & Dev Overview
Cohesity empowers developers to instantiate the latest backup of their production application stack and run it directly off Cohesity, providing a unified foundation for copy data management. Instant, zero-space clones enable businesses to quickly spin up test/dev environments from a backup or existing file share, enabling rapid test and development from actual data without any capacity overhead. Because clones are designed with performance in mind, access time is identical regardless of the number of snapshots or clones that are made.
Cohesity provides the ability to clone objects from snapshots created by a Protection Group. The cloned objects are copied to a new location, rehydrated and restored to a running state. For example when a VMware object is cloned in an on-premises Cohesity cluster, new VM files (such as VMDKs) are created from snapshots and stored in a view on the Cohesity cluster. This view becomes the datastore for these VM files. The Cohesity cluster creates new VMs in the selected resource pool by mounting the view containing the new VMDKs as the datastore on the ESXi hosts. During cloning, VMware is responsible to select the ESXi hosts that have access to the required Datastore based on load balancing.
Note the following about Cohesity Cloning:
l When cloning in an on-premises Cohesity cluster, in a single Clone task you can only clone Protection Groups and VMs that belong to the same Storage Domain and Source.
l You can select only one Snapshot of a VM to clone. While configuring a Clone task, you cannot select two Snapshots that were created from the same VM.
For instructions on how to use Cohesity to Clone VMs, see Clone VMs.
The following example depicts cloning Snapshots of VMware VMs. You want to clone a set of Engineering VMs for use by the QA department for testing. You can select a mix of individual Snapshots and Job Snapshots to clone. In the figure below, the following Snapshots are cloned:
l The individual Snapshot created of VM1 on 03/21/2025 03:00AM l The individual Snapshot created of VM3 on 03/21/2025 05:10AM
After the testing is complete, you may want to tear down the cloned VMs. For more information, see About Tearing Down Cloned VMs.

numbered squares: .

Clone Views
You can make a clone of an existing view. After cloning, the two versions of the data are unique. Changes made to the data in the new view are not replicated in the original view and changes made to the original view are not replicated in the new view. Data within a DataLock view is immutable. You can also clone a view from a view Snapshot. For more information, see Clone a View From a Snapshot.
Before you can clone Protected Objects (Views), Snapshots must exist. To create Snapshots, create and run a Protection Group.
To clone a view:

Clone Views

1. Navigate to Test & Dev. 2. Click Clone located at the top right of the page. 3. Click Views. 4. Select Views to Clone. 5. Set Clone Options.
Select Views to Clone
In this section you select Views to clone. Before you can clone Protected Objects (Views), Snapshots must exist. To create Snapshots, create and run a Protection Group. To select Views to clone:
1. Search for Views to clone. Enter characters of the View name and a list of items displays. (You can optionally specify the wildcard character * in the search.) Select an item from the list. You can also optionally narrow the search results by specifying filter criteria. For example, you can filter the search results by a specific Protection Group. Click Change Filters, specify Filter by criteria and click Add.
2. Click a View.
Set Clone Options
In this section you select the options for the clone task. To set clone options:
1. Select the clone's Purpose. Select Clone as DataLock View if you want to clone a view as write once read many. Data within a DataLock view is immutable, and most view properties cannot be edited. (Note that view-level DataLock is different than file-level DataLock, as described in File-level DataLock for NFS and SMB Views.)
2. In the Task Name field, you can optionally change the default name for the clone task.
3. View Name: If you are creating or cloning a new view, specify a name for the view. Forward slashes (/) are not allowed in the view name.
Important: Renaming a view changes its default share name. Clients won't be able to mount the view unless they use the new share name. Clients using a share alias are not affected by the rename.

For a DataLock view, select a date for lock expiration. During the lock period, data within the view cannot be edited by any user.
During the lock period, users with Data Security privileges can delete the view (unless File DataLock is enabled for the view, in which case the view cannot be deleted), extend the lock period (it cannot be reduced) , add IPs in the allowlist and change the description. After the lock period expires, the view can be deleted by any user that has permission to delete it. 4.

Clone VMs
Cohesity provides the ability to clone objects from snapshots created by a Protection Group. The cloned objects are copied to a new location, rehydrated and restored to a running state. For example when a VMware object is cloned in an on-premises Cohesity cluster, new VM files (such as VMDKs) are created from snapshots and stored in a view on the Cohesity cluster. This view becomes the datastore for these VM files. The Cohesity cluster creates new VMs in the selected resource pool by mounting the view containing the new VMDKs as the datastore on the ESXi hosts. During cloning, VMware is responsible to select the ESXi hosts that have access to the required Datastore based on load balancing.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 31: Test & Dev (Cloning)

Clone VMs

To learn more, see Test & Dev Overview and About Tearing Down Cloned VMs.
Tip: You can also watch the VMware VM Test & Dev (Cloning) video to learn how to clone VMware objects.
You can clone or migrate any DataProtect VM to any Cohesity supported cloud.
Note the following about Cloning VMs:
Prerequisite
For Windows VMs, prepare the VM that is ready for cloning by running the Microsoft Sysprep (System Preparation) tool. This process generalizes the virtual disk and generates a new machine SID.
Considerations:
l Attached CDROM or floppy drives are not recovered or cloned. When recovering or cloning a Snapshot of a VM that had an attached CDROM or floppy drive with data (such as an ISO file), when the VM is recovered or cloned the attached drives are not created and the data is not available.
l Cloning or recovering VMs may fail if the maximum number of mounted NFS Datastores on a VMware ESXi Host is exceeded. Till 6.7, the default value is 8 and from 7.0, the default value is 32. If an ESXi Host already has the maximum number of NFS datastores mounted, the Cohesity View (datastore) does not mount on the ESXi Host during the Cloning or Recovery process. For more information including instructions on increasing the limit, see Increasing the default value that defines the maximum number of NFS mounts on an ESXi/ESX host (2239).
l During VM Recovery or the Cloning of VMs, the Cohesity cluster stores the VMDK and VMX files in different directories on the Cohesity datastore (View), due to a VMware vSphere issue. The VMDK files are placed in the taskname/vmname directory and the VMX files are placed in the vmname directory, where taskname is the Task Name you specify for the Recover task and the vmname is the name of the VM. For example, if a Clone is created with the Task Name of QA that creates clones of the VMs called Build and Test, the VMDK and VMX files are stored in the following directories in the Cohesity datastore (View): QA/Build/Build.vmdk, QA/Test/Test.vmdk, Build/Build.vmx and Test/Test.vmx. However, when recovering a VM, after bringing up the VM on the Cohesity datastore (View), the Cohesity cluster does a Storage vMotion migration of the VM back to its original primary datastore. After the Storage vMotion migration completes, both the VMX and VMDK files end up in the vmname directory and the VMDK files are no longer stored in the taskname directory. This VM recovery example assumes that the VMDK files were originally located in the default directory (and not in some special directory) when the backup was performed.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 31: Test & Dev (Cloning)

Clone VMs

l For some conditions, the VMware vSphere reports an error that there is a mismatch between the actual Content ID of Parent VM and the Parent Content ID stored by the Child VM. If you see this error, follow the instructions to fix this issue provided in the following VMware Knowledge Base article: Resolving the CID mismatch error: The parent virtual disk has been modified since the child was created (1007969).
l During the recovery of a single VM that has multiple networks or datastores, VMware does not check if the VM and the ESXi Host's network and datastore are compatible when assigning the VM to the ESXi Host. This can cause the recovery to fail.
l Due to a VMware issue, specific VM recovery scenarios can cause storage migration (and recovery) to fail. l Using default settings to recover a VM to the same datastore. If the recovered VM belongs to a local datastore, migration may fail because VMware does not register the local datastore to all ESX Hosts within the Resource Pool.
l Using custom settings to recover a VM to a selected Resource Pool and datastore. If the recovered VM belongs to a datastore that is not mounted on all ESX Hosts in the Resource Pool, migration may fail because VMware does not check the compatibility of the ESX Host (within the Resource Pool) with the given datastore while registering the VM.
l When the Cohesity cluster clones a VM, the Cluster makes a request to the vCenter Server to create the new VM. The vCenter Server selects an ESXi host from the specified resource pool to host the new VM. However, the VMware vSphere version of the ESXi host, which was selected by the vCenter Sever, may be incompatible with the VMware vSphere version of the original VM. When this happens, the clone of the VM fails with the following error: A component of the virtual machine is not accessible on the host.
l If VMs with the same VM name (but different relative VMDK paths) are cloned, the Cohesity cluster retains the original VM name for one VM and renames the rest by adding _X to the end of the VM names, where X is an increasing number such as 1, 2, or 3. For example if you clone three VMs called QA, the Cluster names the VMs as QA, QA_1 and QA_2. However, cloning VMs with the same relative path is not supported.
l Cloning not supported with the same relative path and VMDK file name. You cannot clone VMs that have the same relative path and the same VMDK name from two different primary datastores. For example, Protection Groups create Snapshots of test.vmdk stored in qa/testing on datastore1 and test.vmdk stored in qa/testing on datastore2. If you attempt to Clone these two Snapshots, the Clone fails with an error message. The Clone fails because relative path and VMDK names are used to store both VMDKs in the Cohesity datastore and the Cluster cannot store them in same location. In addition, if two VMs have reference the same Hard disk, the Clone also fails. For example if VM1 included a Hard Disk that was then removed (not deleted) from VM1 and added to VM2. These two VMs cannot be Cloned because the relative path and reference to the Hard Disk is the same.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 31: Test & Dev (Cloning)

Clone VMs

l Linked clones of VMware Virtual Machines can be backed up, recovered and cloned by the Cohesity cluster but the linking between the VMs is not preserved. The Cohesity cluster supports the Backup, Recovery and Cloning of linked clones of VMware Virtual Machines. However, the linking between the VMs is not preserved and full Snapshots of the VMs are created. In a single Recover task, you can recover a single linked clone VM but not multiple linked clone VMs.
l Cloning VMs within a vApp is not currently supported; they will be cloned under a specified Resource Pool similar to regular VMs.
l vApp VMs can be recovered to their original location (under the same vApp where the original VM that was backed up was present). When vApp VMs are recovered to an alternate location, they can be recovered to the specified Resource Pool only and the user must then move the VMs to the desired vApp.
l Currently, when a VM with multiple NICs is cloned or recovered to an alternate location, Cohesity creates the VM with only one NIC. This will be fixed in a future release.
l For VMware VMs, Virtual RDM disks are recovered as flat disks. l Cohesity supports recovery only from VM to VM. Recovering VM to physical server and
vice-versa is not supported. l A workaround is needed for Hyper-V VM recovery in SCVMM configurations using test
and development (cloning) scenarios, since the initial recovery may report issues with unsupported configurations. To avoid this, the Cohesity file share needs to be added to the recognized file shares for the host/cluster on SCVMM. Once the file share is successfully configured and a VM refresh is completed, the unsupported configuration issue of the VM is resolved. If a clone view is already added to known file shares and is used to perform subsequent clones, this workaround is not necessary.
Note: The file share must adhere strictly to the following format: \\<clustervip>\<storageDomain>.<cloneViewName>.fs Example file share path: \\dptest.domain.com\DefaultStorageDomain.new.fs
Before you can clone Protected Objects (VMs), Snapshots must exist. To create Snapshots, create and run a Protection Group. To learn more, see Replicate and Clone VMs in AWS Cloud Edition and Clone VMs from OnPremises to AWS Cloud Service (On Demand CloudSpin) .
Best Practice for Cloning VMs
Cohesity recommends the following best practice for cloning a VM: Do not delete the existing VM source while cloning.

l Windows
l You can clone as many disks as the selected VM supports. For example, if you select a Standard_DS1_v2 VM, four disks can be cloned.
l For a Windows VM, if you want to access the newly created VM in the Cloud service using Remote Desktop, enable the Windows Remote Desktop on the VM prior to capturing the Snapshots of a Windows VM.
l When backing up Windows VMs with multiple disks, before a Protection Group captures the Snapshot, the Cohesity agent and VMware tools must be installed on the VM and the VM must be running. The Cohesity agents installed must be of the same version as the Cohesity Cluster version. For more information, see Install and Manage the Agent on Windows Servers. About Tearing Down Cloned VMs
Cohesity provides the ability to clone objects from snapshots created by a Protection Group. The cloned objects are copied to a new location, rehydrated and restored to a running state. For example when a VMware object is cloned in an on-premises Cohesity cluster, new VM files (such as VMDKs) are created from snapshots and stored in a view on the Cohesity cluster. This view becomes the datastore for these VM files. The Cohesity cluster creates new VMs in the selected resource pool by mounting the view containing the new VMDKs as the datastore on the ESXi hosts. During cloning, VMware is responsible to select the ESXi hosts that have access to the required Datastore based on load balancing. Cohesity also provides the ability to tear down (delete) the set of VMs created by a clone task. The teardown procedure of a VMware VM clone is described below. You create Clones of VMs by creating a clone task. For example, you might clone a set of development VMs for QA to use for testing as shown in the following figure.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 31: Test & Dev (Cloning)

Clone VMs

After the testing is completed, you may want to tear down the cloned VMs created by the clone task. You can initiate a clone teardown as described in Tear Down Clones. The actions that occur during a teardown are described in the following procedure:
1. The Cohesity cluster deletes the compute instances of the cloned VMs in the ESXi host.
2. The VM files (such as VMDK and VMX) are deleted on the view acting as a datastore. 3. If no VMs are using the view (datastore), the view is umounted from all ESXi hosts.
The steps in the preceding procedure are represented in the following figure with blue
numbered squares: .

If a cloned VM has been altered after being created by a clone task, the VM may not be automatically cleaned up during a clone teardown. For more information, see VM Not Deleted if Cloned VM is Altered.
Tear Down Clones
Cohesity provides the ability to clone objects from snapshots created by a Protection Group. The cloned objects are copied to a new location, rehydrated and restored to a running state. For example when a VMware object is cloned in an on-premises Cohesity cluster, new VM files (such as VMDKs) are created from snapshots and stored in a view on the Cohesity cluster. This view becomes the datastore for these VM files. The Cohesity cluster creates new VMs in the selected resource pool by mounting the view containing the new VMDKs as the datastore on the ESXi hosts. During cloning, VMware is responsible to select the ESXi hosts that have access to the required Datastore based on load balancing.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 31: Test & Dev (Cloning)

Clone VMs

Cohesity also provides the ability to tear down (delete) the set of VMs created by a clone task. To learn more, see About Tearing Down Cloned VMs.
Note: The teardown of an MS SQL clone database removes it from the SQL server; the user does not have to do this beforehand. However, in the rare instance you created other additional databases with files on the mounted drive that the cloned database is on, those additional databases should be deleted first through the SQL Server Management Studio.
Tear Down a Clone
1. Navigate to Test & Dev. 2. Click a Task Name link in the table. 3. Click Tear Down Clone located at the top right of the page.
The clone teardown process of a VMware VM clone completes the following steps:
1. The Cohesity cluster deletes the compute instances of the cloned VMs in the ESXi host.
2. The VM files (such as VMDK and VMX) are deleted on the view acting as a datastore. 3. If no VMs are using the view (datastore), the view is umounted from all ESXi hosts.
After the teardown, the clone task remains visible in the Cohesity UI. If a clone teardown fails and does not delete all the VMs or VM files, you can restart the clone teardown by repeating the procedure above. For example, if the ESXi host that contains the cloned VMs is not available on the network when the clone teardown first runs, you can run the clone teardown again when the ESXi host becomes available and the VMs will be deleted. The Test & Dev workflow for VMware VMs provides two options when objects are cloned:
1. Use an existing view 2. Create a new view
If an existing view is used, it may contain other data. If a new view is created, it may be used for other purposes, or for future Test & Dev clones. So in either case, the views are not deleted on clone teardown. Further, it does not hinder any other process or action. The user can still clean up the view manually.
VM Not Deleted if Cloned VM is Altered
If a cloned VMware VM has been altered after being created by a clone task, the VM may not be automatically cleaned up during a clone teardown. These special cases are described below:
1. The VM is using files found in an additional external datastore besides the original datastore (view) that is storing the cloned VM. Here are some examples:

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 31: Test & Dev (Cloning)

Clone Databases

l A directory has been NFS mounted onto the VM and the VM is using files in that directory.
l The original VM files were moved to an additional external datastore using Storage vMotion.
2. The VM was converted to a VMware template. 3. The Fault Tolerant (FT) setting was enabled for the VM. To delete the altered VMs, you can either manually delete the VMs or revert the changes made to the VMs and run the clone teardown again.

Pfile Parameters

The Pfile parameters option allows you to see the target database parameters before the clone job is initiated. The Pfile inherits some source database parameters to the target database and allows you to edit the target database parameters based on your requirement by specifying the additional parameters as a key=value pair. The Pfile lists the following parameters:
l Default Parameters: Default parameters of the target database and you can edit the default
l Inherited Parameters: Parameters from the source database and you can edit the inherited parameters, if required.
l Restricted Parameters: You cannot edit the restricted parameters in the Pfile. The following are the restricted parameters: l INSTANCE_NAME l DB_NAME l DB_UNIQUE_NAME l DB_BLOCK_SIZE l MAX_STRING_SIZE l COMPATIBLE If you edit the following values in the Clone Oracle GUI, You must click the Reset button on the top-right corner to reset the Pfile and get the updated parameter values in the Pfile box. l Oracle Home l Oracle Base l Database Name Target database will be created with the specified parameters in the Pfile. For example, if SGA_TARGET is specified as a part of the pfile parameters, the clone operation will use the value specified in the pfile during the cloning of the source database.

SGA (System Global Area)

The SGA is an area of memory (RAM) allocated to an Oracle Instance when it starts up. Ideally, SGA's value varies from 1024M to 102400M.

Change DBID

If this option is disabled, the cloned database UUID will be the same as the source database and it will not be displayed on the Source page. Later, If the cloned databases are required to be discovered by Cohesity, then follow the steps below:
1. Start the database in MOUNT mode. 2. Run the following query to get the DBID:
"select DBID from GV$database". 3. Change the database DBID using the NID command. 4. Run the following query "select DBID from GV$database" and confirm that the DBID
is different from the one we obtained in step 2. 5. Once confirmed, start the database in OPEN mode. 6. Add the database entry in the oratab file. 7. Do a source refresh. 8. The database should be listed there now. If none of the other databases on the Oracle host have DBID the same as that of the cloned database then, skip steps 1 to 5.

Cloning vCloud Director (vCD) VMs using Cohesity involves integrating Cohesity's data protection platform with your vCD environment. Cohesity allows users to clone vCD VMs and vApps from backups for Test & Dev use cases.
Considerations
l Clone vCD VMs should only use the "Detach network" option for all users, tenants, and administrators.
Note: Administrators can use attach options until they select a network that is part of the vApp being cloned.
l Cloning templates as templates is not supported for all tenants and administrators. l The option "Detach Network" will prevent the original VM NIC cards from being
reattached after cloning. l If you cannot attach NICs/Org vDC networks during the cloning workflow, please
contact Cohesity support for assistance. l While cloning VMs to the target, the original IP address and IP mode are not recovered
to the NIC cards. By default, the IP mode is set to "none" and the IP address remains empty. Contact Cohesity support to recover the original IP addresses for the clone operation.

Performance
The performance statistics page helps you to view the performance of the Cohesity cluster, Storage Domains, and Nodes with respect to the attributes such as CPU, memory, IOPS, throughput, and latency. By default, the page provides performance statistics for the entire cluster. You can view performance statistics by selecting System > Performance.
Cluster Performance Statistics
To view Cluster performance statistics, select Cluster from the top navigation pane of the performance page.

The overview tab of the Cluster performance screen shows the performance graph of the following attributes:
l CPU--The total CPU utilization of the Cluster. l Memory-- The total memory utilization of the Cluster. l IOPS--The read and write I/O operations of the Cluster. l Throughput--The throughput of the Cluster. l Latency--The average response time for read and write operations for Views
configured with TestAndDev High QoS policy.
Following are the characteristics of the performance statistics screen of a cluster:

l You can zoom in on part of the graph by dragging the mouse across a section of the graph or by clicking the Zoom icon.
l From each attribute performance page, you can use the Adapters and Tasks dropdown lists or use the search option and filter the jobs or activities that are displayed.

Monitor Performance of Workloads
Cohesity now provides component-level logical statistics and granular-level statistics that enable you to inspect resource usage and workload distribution across the I/O Operations service. Statistics available on the System > Performance > Workloads tab help you:
l Check the overall performance of the Cohesity cluster l Inspect the resource usage across various components l Detect whether the cluster is overloaded l Debug workload-level performance issues l Debug replication performance issues l Debug intermittent performance issues Historical data is available for up to 30 days. This enables you to go back in time and debug issues. For example, if the SmartFiles workload was experiencing high latency at a certain time, you can go back to that particular point in time and view the granular statistics to identify the root cause. You can select one of the following time ranges: l Past hour l Past 12 hours l Past 24 hours l Past 7 days l Past 30 days

Configure and Test SNMP
You can enable Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) on the Cohesity cluster to further integrate Cohesity into your data center and enterprise management solutions. Whenever events occur on the Cohesity cluster, SNMP notifications are sent to your network management system.
Prerequisites and Considerations
l Cohesity supports SNMP versions 2 and 3. l The Cohesity cluster supports SNMP polling and notifications. l Ports 161 (UDP, incoming) and 162 (UDP, outgoing) must be open.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 32: Monitoring

Configure and Test SNMP

l The SNMP network management system must be accessible from the Cohesity cluster.
l Disabling SNMP stops the notification broadcasts but does not clear the existing SNMP configuration information.
l For a list of SNMP Object Identifiers (OIDs), see Alerts Reference.
Configure SNMP
1. In the Cohesity Dashboard, select Settings > Summary and click SNMP > Configure SNMP.

This is the port the SNMP agent listens on. The default is 161. This is the SNMP trap destination port. The default is 162.
l V3 - More secure (supports encryption and authentication) l V2C - Basic security with community strings.

Verify SNMP Transmission to Network Management Systems

3. Run the following tcpdump command from alerts master node: sudo tcpdump -ni any port 161 or 162 -vv

Note: Port 161 is used for SNMP packets and port 162 is used for SNMP traps.
4. Use the following object ID to generate a non-impacting event: LogsDiskSpaceLow 1.3.6.1.4.1.47421.0.6 This event is triggered when the logs partition reaches over 95% full. Use the following steps to determine available space in the logs partition. df -h /home/cohesity/logs logs=/home/cohesity/logs ; df -h $logs ; fallocate -l 38g $logs/foo df -h $logs ; sleep 300 ; rm $logs/foo ; df -h $logs
5. This page reports on the following Cohesity cluster data statistics:

Metrics Logical Data

Description
Data Protection: The combined total of data in the objects that are protected by Cohesity. These metrics are different depending on workload type.
l VMs: The data size reported by VMware is the provisioned amount, not the actual data residing in the VM. For examples, if a VM is provisioned for 1TB but contains only 100GB of data, VMware reports it as 1TB.
l All Other Workloads: The data size reported is the actual front end data residing on the server. If a server with 1TB capacity contains 100GB of data, the server reports 100GB.
Note: l These metrics do not include unprotected objects. l Currently, the logical data value shown on the UI is a sum of the logical data values captured across all the protection runs. For instance, if the source has 100GB of logical data, and assuming it remains at 100GB for the first 10 protection runs, Cohesity would report, after 10 runs, the Logical Data to be 1000GB (1TB).
SmartFiles: Size of total unique logical data of active filesystem as residing on Cohesity. This does not count the space consumed by the Data Protection runs (i.e. snapshots) that may be protecting the active filesystem.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 32: Monitoring

Storage Statistics

Metrics Data Read
Data In
Data Written Resiliency Impact

Description
Data Read is the size of the set of protected objects as read by Cohesity for a single backup run. This number is a per protection run statistic and is not additive across backup runs.
Note: The Data Read column displays 0 bytes for view-based backups as the protected data resides within a Cohesity view on the cluster and is not read from an external source.
Total unique logical data residing on the Cohesity cluster. For Data Protection, this is the sum of your first full backup and subsequent change data captured by Cohesity. For SmartFiles, some customers, such as SPs and enterprise customers with multiple tenants, may want to use this as the Logical Data so that snapshot capacity is included in the chargeback.
Data written on the Cohesity cluster after the unique logical data has been reduced by data deduplication and data compression. For SmartFiles, this metric value carries the name of Physical Data.
Note: This number reflects unique data written, before resiliency operations.
The space required to honor resiliency settings (Erasure Coding / Replication Factor) in addition to the data written. For example, if the Data Written is 100GB and resiliency setting is RF3, the Resiliency Impact is 200GB. That is, to honor the resiliency setting, you will need an additional 200GB on top of the 100GB for the Data Written.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 32: Monitoring

Storage Statistics

Metrics Storage Consumed
Storage Reduction
Storage Consumed Local and Cloud Storage Saved Total Capacity Available

Description
The total size of data stored on the Cohesity file system after all operations on the data (data deduplication, data compression, and data resiliency) have been accounted for. This data can be stored either all locally or as a combination of local storage and in the Cloud Tier (if Cloud Tier is enabled). For example, if the Data Written is 100GB and resiliency is set to RF3, leading to the need for an additional 200GB of space, the resulting Storage Consumed is 300GB. If the Data Written is 100GB and resiliency is set to EC4:2, leading to the need for an additional 50GB (as for every 4 data fragments, 2 parity fragments are added), the resulting Storage Consumed is 150GB.
Note: If you have enabled Cloud Tiering, then Storage Consumed is the sum of space consumed on local storage and space consumed on the cloud tier. In such cases, the sum of Storage Consumed value and Capacity Available value for the cluster can exceed the cluster capacity.
The ratio of Logical Data to Storage Consumed. For Data Protection, this reflects all operations performed by Cohesity on source data, which include snapshotting, change tracking and ingest, data deduplication, data compression, and data resiliency. For SmartFiles, this reflects all operations performed on the Cohesity hosted active filesystem, which include logical data writes, change tracking, data deduplication, data compression, and data resiliency.
If you have enabled Cloud Tiering, then this metric is the sum of space consumed on local storage and space consumed on the cloud tier.
The space owing to data deduplication and data compression. For example, if Data In is 100GB, deduplication ratio is 4x, compression is 2x, then Data Written is 12.5GB. Therefore, the Storage Saved is 100GB - 12.5GB = 87.5GB.
The total physical capacity of all storage devices after subtracting the space reserved for Cohesity software operations.
The amount of space still available on the Cohesity cluster, calculated by subtracting the Storage Consumed (Locally and not on Cloud Tier) from the Total Capacity.

l VMs: The data size reported by VMware is the provisioned amount, not the actual data residing in the VM. For example, if a VM is provisioned for 1TB but contains only 100GB of data, VMware reports it as 1TB.
l All Other Workloads: The data size reported is the actual front end data residing on the server. If a server with 1TB capacity contains 100GB of data, the server reports 100GB.

Note: l These metrics do not include unprotected objects.
l Currently, the logical data value shown on the UI is a sum of the logical data values captured across all the protection runs. For instance, if the source has 100GB of logical data, and assuming it remains at 100GB for the first 10 protection runs, Cohesity would report, after 10 runs, the Logical Data to be 1000GB (1TB).

SmartFiles:
Size of total unique logical data of active filesystem as residing on Cohesity. This does not count the space consumed by the Data Protection runs (i.e. snapshots) that may be protecting the active filesystem.

Data In

Total unique logical data residing on the Cohesity cluster.
For Data Protection, this is the sum of your first full backup and subsequent change data captured by Cohesity.
For SmartFiles, some customers, such as SPs and enterprise customers with multiple tenants, may want to use this as the Logical Data so that snapshot capacity is included in the chargeback.

Data Reduction

The ratio of Data In to Data Written. This ratio reflects the data deduplication and data compression operations.

Storage Consumed Local and Cloud

If you have enabled Cloud Tiering, then this metric is the sum of space consumed on local storage and space consumed on the cloud tier.

Growth

The physical data written to the storage domain over the number of days specified in the Growth field.

Storage Consumed

Description
The name of the consumer.
The total size of data stored on the Cohesity file system after all operations on the data (data deduplication, data compression, and data resiliency) have been accounted for. This data can be stored either all locally or as a combination of local storage and in the Cloud Tier (if Cloud Tier is enabled). For example, if the Data Written is 100GB and resiliency is set to RF3, leading to the need for an additional 200GB of space, the resulting Storage Consumed is 300GB. If the Data Written is 100GB and resiliency is set to EC4:2, leading to the need for an additional 50GB (as for every 4 data fragments, 2 parity fragments are added), the resulting Storage Consumed is 150GB.

Health Dashboard
The Health dashboard provides detailed information about the health of your Cohesity cluster. You can use this information to identify your Cohesity cluster's potential problems and address them before becoming severe. The dashboard provides an overview of the number of Critical, Warning, and Healthy (Info) alerts triggered by the Cohesity cluster. It collates all the alerts triggered by your cluster, categorizes them based on the alert category, and then displays them as the following components:
l Hardware l Software l Maintenance l Data Service
In each of these components, the alert categories are displayed as individual cards and contain the number of alerts triggered for the category. The alert categories are color-coded based on the severity of the alerts:
l Red - Critical l Yellow - Warning l Green - Informational (Info)

l Memory l CPU l NIC l Firmware l Disk l Power Supply l Fan l Temperature l Chassis l Node l Cluster
For more information on the alert categories, see Alerts Reference.

Alerts
The Cohesity cluster creates an alert when:
l It finds a potential problem or when it exceeds the defined threshold. l A Protection Group is configured to trigger an alert indicating the success or failure of
the job.
You can configure general alert email notifications in the System > Health > Settings tab and job-specific email notifications in a Protection Group. Each alert has a severity rating that indicates the seriousness of the problem:
l Critical--Immediate action is required because it detects a severe problem that might be imminent or major functionality is not working, such as a disk failure.
l Warning--Action is required, but the affected functionality is still working, such as the disk space on the Cohesity cluster is 80% to 90% full.
l Informational--Immediate action is not required, and the alert provides an informational message.
The Alerts tab displays all the alerts that are generated by the Cohesity cluster. Alerts are grouped into one alert (with multiple occurrences) if the alerts are of the same type, and they are reporting the same Object and occur within the specified time-frame of the alert.
Analyze the Alert
From the Alerts tab, you can click on an alert and view the alert details on the Details for <Alert_Name> page. The Details for <Alert_Name> page includes a timeline view that shows the date and time when the alert was triggered. The page also provides the following details of the alert:

Details Alert Code

Description The alert code. You can click on the alert code for detailed information about the alert.

Important: In multi-tenant deployments, the rules for alert notifications work as follows:
l If the notification rules are set up at the organization level, only alerts raised at that level will trigger notifications.
l If the notification rules are set up at the cluster level, and alerts are raised at the organization level, all organizations' alerts will trigger notifications.
Additionally, notifications will be sent if the alert's category, severity, and name match the specified filters.
Note: Alert notifications are sent once per active alert within the dedup interval.

Add Alert Notification Rule
You can add different alert notification rules that send emails, SNMP, Syslog, and/or cURL HTTP POST requests to a webhook URL based on the alert categories, severities, and names. Rules can be configured at both the service provider and the tenancy level.
Prerequisites
Before you add an alert notification rule, make sure that you:
l Configure an SMTP Server on the Cohesity cluster, if you plan to send email notifications when an alert is triggered. For details on configuring the SMTP server, see Configure Settings.
l Configure the SNMP setting on the Cohesity cluster, if you plan to send SNMP notifications to your network management system when an alert is triggered. For details on configuring SNMP settings, see Configure and Test SNMP.
l Add a Syslog server to the Cohesity cluster, if you plan to send Syslog notifications to the server when an alert is triggered. For details on configuring the Syslog server, see Add a Syslog Server.
To add an alert notification rule:
1. Navigate to System > Health and click the Settings tab. 2. Click Add Alert Notification Rule. 3. On the Add Alert Notification Rule page, do the following:
1. Rule Name: Type a descriptive name for the rule, for example, Cluster Disk Offline or Backup Job Failure.
2. Alert Category: Optional. Select one or more categories from the drop-down. Otherwise, all alerts in any category will trigger the rule.
3. Alert Severities: Optional. Select one or more severities from the drop-down. Otherwise, all alerts with any severity will trigger the rule.
4. Alert Name: Optional. Select one or more names from the drop-down. Otherwise, any Alert name will trigger the rule. If you selected any categories, the list includes only alerts in those categories.
5. Email: Optional. Click Add and from the drop-down menu, perform the following: 1. Select To and type an email address or distribution list of the recipients to whom you plan to send the email notification. 2. Select CC and type an email address or distribution list of the recipients to whom you plan to send a copy of the email notification.
6. SNMP: Optional. Toggle on if you want the rule to send SNMP notifications when the alert is triggered.
7. Syslog: Optional. Toggle on if you want the rule to send Syslog notifications when the alert is triggered.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 32: Monitoring

Health Dashboard

8. Webhook: Optional. Toggle on and provide the URL and cURL details if you want the rule to send a web callback to a server. Type the URL for the server and type any cURL options you want to use. When an alert is triggered, the Cohesity cluster sends an HTTP request to the server. Your application can then interpret the request. For example, the webhook might notify the server about a critical disk alert, and your application might open a trouble ticket to track the problem. For more information, see Configuring Webhooks.
4. Click Save.
Edit Alert Notification Rule
You can edit an existing alert notification rule and update the following: Change the rule name.
l Select or discard alert categories from the Alert Categories list. l Select or discard alert severities from the Alert Severities list. l Select or discard alert names from the Alert Name list. l Add or remove email addresses l Enable or disable SNMP notification l Enable or disable Syslog notification l Enable or disable Webhook.
The updated alert notification rule is applied from the next alert that is triggered. To edit an existing alert notification rule:
1. Navigate to System > Health and click the Settings tab. 2. Click the edit icon next to the rule. 3. On the Edit Alert Notification Rule page, update the settings as per your
requirement. 4. Click Save.
Delete Alert Notification Rule
You can delete the alert notification rules that you do not want to use for alert notifications. To delete alert notification rule:
1. Navigate to System > Health and click the Settings tab. 2. Click the delete icon next to the rule. 3. In the Delete Alert Notification Rule dialog box, click Delete.
Configuring Webhooks
Webhooks are HTTP callbacks which are usually triggered by some event. Webhooks are configured on one website and when an event occurs on this website, an HTTP request is made to the configured URL which invokes action on the other website.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 32: Monitoring

Health Dashboard

You can enable webhooks for Cohesity alerts by creating an alert notification rule. When the alert is triggered and meets the criteria in the rule, the cluster sends an HTTP request to the specified website. Your application can then interpret the request. For example, the webhook might notify the website about a critical disk alert and your application might open a trouble ticket to track the problem.

To create an alert notification rule and enable a webhook: 1. Navigate to System > Health and select the Alerts tab. The Alerts summary page is displayed. 2. Select the Settings tab, and click Add Alert Notification Rule. 3. Configure the following details:

Alert Request
When an alert is triggered, a sample payload as shown below will be available at the configured URL: CURL Request:
Curl -XPOST https://test-service-now.com/api/x_hesin_cohesity_c/cohesitywebhook
The Payload sent to the above URL:
{ "alertType": "1060", "alertId": "437441:1665640208440874", "alertName": "DnsServerUnReachable", "alertDescription": "DNS server is not reachable.", "alertSeverity": "WARNING", "alertCategory": "Networking", "alertCause": "DNS servers [10.2.0.1] unreachable. Please update DNS
Server.", "alertHelpText": "Check and provide alternate DNS server.",

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 32: Monitoring

Health Dashboard

"languageCode": "en-us", "alertUrl": "https://cluster-ip/health/alert-info/437441:1665640208440874", "clusterName": "cohesity", "clusterId": "4398906079065976", "alertCode": "CE03601060", "alertProperties": {
"cluster_id": "4398906079065976", "alert_message": "DNS servers [10.2.0.1] unreachable. Please update DNS Server." }, "firstOccurrenceUsecs": "1665640208440874", "lastOccurrenceUsecs": "1665640208440874" }
Note: prod-cluster.eng.cohesity.com refers to the IP address of the cluster.
Customized Template for URL Request and Data Payload
Webhook also supports template options for both URL requests and data payload. Data payload can be sent in any customized format as a template with placeholders. These placeholders are replaced with the actual values of the generated alert. The placeholders can be any of the following:
"$alertType", "$alertId", "$alertName", "$alertDescription", "$alertSeverity", "$alertCategory", "$alertCause", "$alertHelpText", "$languageCode", "$alertUrl", "$clusterName", "$clusterId", "$alertCode", "$alertProperties", "$firstOccurrenceUsecs", "$lastOccurrenceUsecs"
The following is an example of a template for a Slack channel:
--template {"blocks": [{ "type": "section", "fields": [{"type": "plain_ text", "text": "alert name" }, {"type": "mrkdwn", "text": "*$alertName*"}, {"type": "plain_text", "text": "alertSeverity"}, {"type": "mrkdwn", "text": "*$alertSeverity*"}, {"type": "plain_text", "text": "alertCategory"}, {"type": "mrkdwn", "text": "*$alertCategory*"}, {"type": "plain_text", "text": "alertDescription" }, {"type": "mrkdwn", "text": "*$alertDescription*" }, {"type": "plain_text", "text": "alertCause" }, {"type": "mrkdwn", "text":"*$alertCause*"}]}]}
Webhook URL path can also be customized with placeholders. Example: "http://example.webhooksite.com?alertName=$alertName", where alertName=$alertName is the placeholder. [content type]

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 32: Monitoring

Health Dashboard

If the content-type is not specified, by default, it is application/json. If a content-type is specified it must be acceptable by the webhook server. Example:
-H content-type:text/html
[curl options] For security reasons, valid webhook options can only be -H( or --header), -d(or -data)and --template. If --template is provided then -d(or --data) is ignored. If -template is not provided then the payload in --data is merged with the default alert JSON content. Ensure that you provide a valid JSON entry for the -d(or --data) option. Example:
-d {"accountId": 12345, "accountName": "test" }
Resolving Alerts
When an alert is triggered at the Cohesity cluster side, the above data as shown in the sample payload must be notified to the configured URL. Using the above payload, the alerts can be resolved at the target based on the alertID. This eliminates the need to switch back to the Cohesity cluster to manage and resolve alerts. To resolve alerts, the alertURL from the sample payload must be extracted and used in the API request as shown below: URL Request:
https://prod-cluster.eng.cohesity.com/irisservices/api/v1/public/alertResolutions
Method : POST Payload :
{"resolutionDetails":{"resolutionSummary":"Resolved at 11/1, high priority"},"alertIdList":["157373326:1577990357283489"]}
Note: alertIdList refers to the alertID in the payload. Resolved at 11/1, high priority is a user defined string.

Disk Alerts
CE00101009 MissingDisk
Alert Description: The node is missing disks. Reason: This alert is generated when the number of disks assigned to a node does not match the number of disks supported by the hardware model of the node. The alert is triggered once per hour as long as a disk is missing. This alert can be caused by one of the following conditions. l The Cohesity cluster was created with fewer disks than supported by the hardware
model of the node. l A node with fewer disks than supported by the hardware model of the node, is added
to the Cohesity cluster. The disk(s) may be pulled out or not completely inserted. Action: Find the node with the issue and add enough disks as supported by the hardware model of the node. This may involve pushing in a partially pulled-out disk or inserting a new disk if a slot in the node is empty and following the instructions in the hardware replacement procedure. Severity: Warning Related Error Code: Not Applicable

CE00302123 NodeFailureIsNotTolerated
Alert Description: Effective usage space in the cluster is high, the cluster may not have enough space to heal if a node failure happens. Reason: This alert is triggered when the Cohesity cluster detects that a potential node failure could result in an effective Cohesity cluster disk usage of 95% or greater. This alert Cause field indicates the current actual disk usage, which is typically less than 95%. If a node in the Cohesity cluster fails, its contents need to be copied to the other nodes. If the Cohesity cluster detects that the contents of a potentially failed node cannot be copied to the remaining nodes due a lack of disk space, this alert is triggered to indicate that node failures cannot be tolerated. Action: Do one or more of the following:
l Add more nodes to your Cohesity cluster. l Clean up Snapshots that are no longer required. l Archive Snapshots to an External Target. l Configure Cloud Tier to hold rarely used data. l Consider changing Storage Domains to use Erasure Coding. Capacity utilization will be
reduced over time in the background. l See the Alert: CE03802121/CE03802122 Cluster Space Usage High KB article.

CE00401149 NetworkInterfaceFlaky
Alert Description: The number of network interface flaps is exceeding the limit. Reason: This alert is triggered when a network interface exhibits "flaky" behavior. A physical interface is considered flaky when it repeatedly transitions between an up and down state within a specific time period, exceeding a defined threshold. Definition of Flaky Behavior The network interface transitions up or down more than n times within a t-second window. These thresholds are defined by default as, n = 10 transitions and t = 60 seconds. Both values are configurable using a GFLAG. Example of Flaky Behavior If the interface undergoes transitions like this: [U D U D U D U D U D U]. This results in 11 counts (each up and down counts individually) within 60 seconds, which exceeds the default threshold of 10. Consequently, the alert is raised to signal potential instability or hardware issues. Action: If you encounter this alert, follow these steps to identify and address the issue: - Inspect the Physical Link: Verify the physical connection of the network interface.

Cohesity User Guide 7.4.1

Chapter 32: Monitoring

Health Dashboard

- Examine the Network Interface Card (NIC): Confirm that the NIC is functioning correctly. - Check the Peer Router or Switch: Investigate the device connected to the interface (peer router or switch). If the issue persists after the initial checks, contact Cohesity Support for assistance. Related Error Code: Not Applicable Severity: Critical Dedup Interval: 3600 seconds SNMP OID: 1.3.6.1.4.1.47421.0.444 Platform: All

CE02806028 ImbalanceThresholdExceededAlert
Alert Description: Imbalance threshold exceeded for chunkfiles. This can cause increase in the cluster usage. Reason: There is sub-optimal erasure coding overhead of greater than 100GB in an erasure coding enabled view box. When the minimum data stripe size and maximum data stripe size of the erasure coded chunk files differ a lot, the erasure coding involves space overhead when compared to an ideal case where all data stripes are of the same size. Such EC imbalance space overheads are automatically reclaimed in the background by the MapReduce and Space Reclamation service. This alert is caused when the overheads are not reclaimed in a timely manner. Action: Contact Cohesity Support for assistance. Related Error Code: Not Applicable Severity: Warning SNMP OID: 1.3.6.1.4.1.47421.0.387 Platform: All

CE02809069 ClockSkewBetweenClusterAndDC
Alert Description: A big clock skew between the Cohesity cluster and Domain Controller, causing the authentication to fail. Reason: The clock skew between the Cohesity cluster (or Hyx node if existent) and the DC controller is more significant than a threshold.
Important: Time synchronization is crucial for Kerberos authentication. Kerberos tickets use timestamps to prevent replay attacks by rejecting old or expired tickets. If system clocks are out of sync, attackers can exploit the gap to gain unauthorized access. Keeping all systems synchronized ensures security and prevents authentication vulnerabilities.
Action: Perform the following: - Verify the NTP server configuration on both the Cohesity cluster and the Domain Controller to ensure they are using the same NTP server. - Use the iris_cli cluster sync-ntp command to synchronize the NTP servers on the Cohesity cluster. - Check the network connectivity between the Cohesity cluster and the NTP server to ensure there are no issues. Related Error Code:

Error Codes kDomainController

Description
If the clock skew between the Cohesity cluster (or Hyx node if existent) and the DC controller is more significant than a threshold, authentication will fail through this DC. Thus, the time skew is periodically monitored. If it gets close to the threshold, The alert is raised as a reminder to sync up the clock on the DC.

Severity: Critical SNMP OID: 1.3.6.1.4.1.47421.0.405
